quote: Intuitively, [Y1 ← y1 , . . . ,Yk ← yk ]ϕ says that ϕ would hold if Yi were set to yi , for i = 1, . . . , k.
formula: (M,\vec u)\models[\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y]\varphi\iff(M_{\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y},\vec u)\models\varphi,\qquad F^{\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y}_{Y_i}=y_i.
assumptions: Recursive causal model, fixed context, distinct intervention variables and admissible values; other equations remain unchanged.
gloss: Evaluate a claim after replacing the selected variables’ equations with constant assignments.
relation: Special case of the paper’s extended counterfactual semantics when the antecedent is a conjunction of primitive events.

quote: Definition 2.1: ⃗X =⃗x is an actual cause of ϕ in the causal setting (M,⃗u) if the following three conditions hold:
formula: \begin{aligned}\mathrm{AC1}:&\ (M,\vec u)\models(\vec X=\vec x)\land\varphi.\\\mathrm{AC2}:&\ \exists\vec W\subseteq\mathcal V\setminus\vec X,\vec w^*,\vec x' :\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec W=\vec w^*\ \land\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w^*]\neg\varphi.\\\mathrm{AC3}:&\ \nexists\vec X'\subsetneq\vec X\text{ whose actual assignment satisfies AC2}.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Known recursive causal model and actual context. Witness variables are fixed at actual values. The PDF’s AC2 quantifier prints an unprimed alternative; the intervention uses x′.
gloss: An actual, minimal event prevents the outcome when changed while some other variables retain their actual values.
relation: Recovered by abstract actual causation in Theorem 4.2; generalized to suitable recursive counterfactual structures in Theorem 4.5.

quote: A ccf M is a family of models or structures (we use the latter two words more or less interchangeably) such that each model M ∈ M has a set of possible states or worlds, and there is a semantics that allows us to define (M, w) |= ϕ for all formulas in a language L M . We require that L M include primitive events in some signature S , and be closed under conjunction and negation (so contains L (S )) and basic counterfactuals, so that if ϕ and ψ are in L (S ), then ϕ → ψ ∈ L M .
formula: \forall M\in\mathcal M:\ (M,w)\models\varphi\text{ is defined for every state }w\text{ of }M\text{ and every }\varphi\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal M};\quad\mathcal L(\mathcal S)\subseteq\mathcal L_{\mathcal M};\quad\varphi,\psi\in\mathcal L(\mathcal S)\Rightarrow(\varphi\to\psi)\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal M}.
assumptions: Models with states, primitive-event interpretations and a truth semantics supporting the stated Boolean and counterfactual language.
gloss: A shared semantic framework in which causal definitions can use counterfactuals without requiring structural equations.
relation: Includes causal models and Lewis-style counterfactual structures; supports abstract actual causation and abstract explanation.

term: counterfactual in causal models with an arbitrary Boolean antecedent
quote: To give semantics to a counterfactual of the form ϕ → ψ ∈ L + (S ), we proceed as follows: Let ⃗Y be the endogenous variables that appear in ϕ. Then we take (M,⃗u) |= ϕ → ψ iff there exists a vector ⃗y of values such that ϕ ∧ ⃗Y = ⃗y is consistent (when viewed as a propositional formula) and (M,⃗u) |= [⃗Y ←⃗y]ψ.
formula: (M,\vec u)\models\varphi\to\psi\iff\exists\vec y\in\mathcal R(\vec Y):\ \operatorname{Consistent}(\varphi\land\vec Y=\vec y)\land(M,\vec u)\models[\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y]\psi,\quad\vec Y=\operatorname{Vars}(\varphi).
assumptions: Recursive causal model; intervene on exactly the endogenous variables occurring in the antecedent; consistency is propositional.
gloss: Some complete assignment satisfying the antecedent must make the consequent true when imposed.
relation: Extends basic causal formulas; differs from universal closest-world semantics for nonbinary negated antecedents.

quote: That is, (M, s) |= ϕ → ψ if in all the closest states to s satisfying ϕ, ψ also holds. (It follows that (M, s) |= ϕ → ψ vacuously if there are no states t such that (M,t) |= ϕ.)
formula: M=(S,R,\pi),\quad t\preceq_s u\iff(s,t,u)\in R;\qquad(M,s)\models\varphi\to\psi\iff\forall t\in\operatorname{Min}_{\preceq_s}\{v:(M,v)\models\varphi\},\ (M,t)\models\psi.
assumptions: Finite state set; reflexive, transitive closeness relations; each state is strictly closer to itself than any other state.
gloss: The consequent must hold in every closest world where the antecedent holds.
relation: An alternative counterfactual semantics supporting the same abstract causation and explanation definitions; can allow backtracking.

term: actual cause with respect to CX
quote: Definition 4.1: Given a ccf M and set CX ⊆ L M of formulas, ϕ is an actual cause of ψ with respect to CX in a model M ∈ M and state s if the following three conditions hold:
formula:
egin{aligned}\mathrm{AC1'}:&\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi.\\mathrm{AC2'}:&\ \exists	au\in C_X:\ (M,s)\models	au\land((
eg\varphi\land	au)	o
eg\psi).\\mathrm{AC3'}:&\ 
exists\varphi'\in C_X:\ (\models\varphi\Rightarrow\varphi')\land(
ot\models\varphi'\Rightarrow\varphi)\land\mathrm{AC2'}(\varphi',\psi).\end{aligned}
assumptions: Chosen ccf, model, state, counterfactual semantics and admissible witness language C_X. Logical implication and counterfactual implication are distinct.
gloss: A true, logically minimal condition is causally necessary once an admissible true witness is retained.
relation: Generalizes modified HP actual causation; allows complex causes and depends on the witness language.

quote: As is standard, we say that an agent knows ϕ if ϕ is true at all the settings in K .
formula: \operatorname{Knows}_K(\varphi)\iff\forall\vec u\in K:\ (M,\vec u)\models\varphi.
assumptions: Epistemic state K consisting of contexts of a fixed causal model; the agent’s uncertainty is represented by membership in K.
gloss: An agent knows a statement when it holds in every situation the agent considers possible.
relation: Makes explanation agent-relative and motivates the additional nontriviality condition.

quote: Definition 6.1: ⃗X = ⃗x is an explanation of ψ in a model M relative to a set K of contexts in M if the following conditions hold:
formula: \begin{aligned}\mathrm{EX1(a)}:&\ \forall\vec u\in K,\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\psi\Rightarrow\exists(X=x)\in(\vec X=\vec x),\vec Y=\vec y:\ X=x\land\vec Y=\vec y\text{ is a cause of }\psi.\\\mathrm{EX1(b)}:&\ \forall\vec u'\in K,\ (M,\vec u')\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x]\psi.\\\mathrm{EX2}:&\ \nexists\vec X'\subsetneq\vec X\text{ satisfying EX1(a), EX1(b) with the restricted assignment}.\\\mathrm{EX3}:&\ \exists\vec u\in K:\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\psi.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Known recursive causal model, epistemic context set K and modified HP actual causation. Causes may contain additional conjuncts outside the explanation.
gloss: An explanation is minimally sufficient throughout the agent’s possibilities and contains something causally relevant wherever it actually holds.
relation: The HP explanation definition reviewed by the paper; generalized by Definition 6.3.

term: nontrivial explanation in a causal model
quote: The explanation is nontrivial if it also satisfies EX4.
formula: \mathrm{EX1\text{--}EX3}\quad\land\quad\exists\vec u'\in K:\ (M,\vec u')\models\neg(\vec X=\vec x)\land\psi.
assumptions: An explanation satisfying Definition 6.1 and an epistemic state containing an outcome-compatible context where the explanation is false.
gloss: Observing the outcome does not already tell the agent that the explanation holds.
relation: Adds an epistemic informativeness requirement to explanation; mirrored by EX4′ in the abstract framework.

quote: Definition 6.3: Given a ccf M and set CX ⊆ L M of formulas, ϕ is an explanation of ψ with respect to CX in a model M ∈ M and state s relative to a set K of states in M if the following three conditions hold:
formula:
egin{aligned}\mathrm{EX1(a)'}:&\  orall s\in K,\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi\Rightarrow\exists	au_1,	au_2\in C_X:\ 
ot\models	au_1,\ \models\varphi\Rightarrow	au_1,\ \models	au_2\Rightarrow	au_1,\ \operatorname{Cause}_{C_X}(	au_2,\psi;M,s).\\mathrm{EX1(b)'}:&\  orall s'\in K,\ (M,s')\models\varphi	o\psi.\\mathrm{EX2'}:&\ 
exists\varphi':\ (\models\varphi\Rightarrow\varphi')\land(
ot\models\varphi'\Rightarrow\varphi)\land\mathrm{EX1'}(\varphi',\psi).\\mathrm{EX3'}:&\ \exists s\in K:\ (M,s)\models\varphi\land\psi.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Ccf and counterfactual semantics, admissible formula set C_X, epistemic state set K and Definition 4.1 causation. Minimality ranges over formulas, not merely variable subsets.
gloss: A minimally sufficient formula must share a nontrivial logical consequence with an actual cause wherever explanation and outcome coexist.
relation: Generalizes Definition 6.1 under Theorem 6.4’s language restriction; Theorem 6.5 establishes correspondence for compatible recursive structures.

term: nontrivial explanation with respect to CX
quote: Again, the explanation is nontrivial if EX4′ .
formula: \mathrm{EX1'\text{--}EX3'}\quad\land\quad\exists s'\in K:\ (M,s')\models\neg\varphi\land\psi.
assumptions: An abstract explanation and an epistemic state permitting the outcome without the explanation.
gloss: The explanation supplies information not already settled by the outcome.
relation: Abstract counterpart of EX4 in Definition 6.1.

quote: Elsewhere I have called this interpretation of sufficiency weak sufficiency (Beckers, 2021).
formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ is weakly sufficient for }\vec Y=\vec y\iff\forall\vec u\in\mathcal R(\mathcal U):\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x]\vec Y=\vec y.
assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; no interventions on other variables; quantification over every context.
gloss: Setting the proposed cause guarantees the outcome across backgrounds while everything else follows its equations.
relation: Implied by strong sufficiency; equivalent to direct sufficiency under agreement and Independence.

quote: In the context of causal models I have coined this direct sufficiency (Beckers, 2021).
formula: \vec C=\mathcal V\setminus(\vec X\cup\vec Y);\qquad\forall\vec c\in\mathcal R(\vec C),\vec u\in\mathcal R(\mathcal U):\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec C\leftarrow\vec c]\vec Y=\vec y.
assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; arbitrary interventions on all remaining endogenous variables.
gloss: The proposed cause guarantees the outcome regardless of interventions on any other endogenous variables.
relation: Stronger than strong and weak sufficiency; strong sufficiency applies direct sufficiency to an entire protected network.

quote: I call the relevant notion of causal sufficiency at work strong sufficiency (Beckers, 2021), which can be formally defined as follows:
formula: \vec Y\subseteq\vec N\quad\land\quad\exists\vec n\supseteq\vec y:\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is directly sufficient for }\vec N=\vec n.
assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive causal model; the network N is safeguarded from intervention and its whole assignment is determined by X=x.
gloss: The cause fixes a complete causal network containing the outcome, despite interventions outside that network.
relation: Intermediate between direct and weak sufficiency; forms the basis of sufficient explanations.

term: sufficient explanation; actual sufficient explanation; direct sufficient explanation; part of an explanation
quote: Using strong sufficiency we can define a sufficient explanation so that it specifies all the required elements for it to be action-guiding.
formula: \begin{aligned}(\vec X=\vec x,\vec N)\text{ is a sufficient explanation of }Y=y&\iff\vec X=\vec x\text{ is strongly sufficient for }Y=y\text{ along }\vec N.\\\text{It is actual in }(M,\vec u)&\iff(M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x.\\\text{It is direct}&\iff\vec N=\{Y\}.\\\vec X'=\vec x'\text{ is a part}&\iff\vec X'\subseteq\vec X,\ \vec x'=\vec x|_{\vec X'}.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive model; a selected safeguarded network. Actuality additionally requires a context.
gloss: An explanation states both a sufficient intervention and the network that must remain undisturbed; actuality and directness add explicit restrictions.
relation: Uses strong sufficiency; supplies the objects ordered by dominance and used in counterfactual explanations and actual causation.

quote: Of course we do not want to add redundant parts to a sufficient set, as a good explanation should be as concise as possible.
formula: E_i=(\vec X_i=\vec x_i,\vec N_i);\quad E_1\succeq E_2\iff\bigl(E_1,E_2\text{ explain the same }Y=y\bigr)\land\vec X_1\subseteq\vec X_2\land\vec N_1\subseteq\vec N_2;\quad E_1\succ E_2\iff E_1\succeq E_2\land\neg(E_2\succeq E_1).
assumptions: Two sufficient explanations in the same causal model. Definition 9 compares variable sets and does not separately require matching assigned values.
gloss: One sufficient explanation dominates another of the same outcome when its intervened variables and its safeguarded network are subsets of the other's.
relation: Defines the ordering used by good sufficient explanations and replacement.

quote: This allows us to define what makes for a good sufficient explanation of an observed output.
formula: \operatorname{Good}(E;M,\vec u,y)\iff E\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\ \land\ \nexists E'\ne E:\ E'\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\land E'\succeq E.
assumptions: Fixed causal setting and outcome, sufficient explanations and Definition 9 dominance. The definition says 'not dominated by any other', rather than 'not strictly dominated'.
gloss: An actual sufficient explanation is good when no other actual sufficient explanation of the outcome uses a subset of its intervened variables and a subset of its safeguarded network.
relation: Adds minimality to actual sufficient explanation; actual causes are particular parts of good sufficient explanations.

quote: Formally the causal notion that this third interpretation relies on is the latest definition of actual causation by Halpern, which is best understood as a generalization of counterfactual dependence in the following way.
formula: (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land\vec W=\vec w\land Y=y,\qquad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w]Y\ne y,\qquad\vec X\text{ minimal};\quad\vec W\text{ is a witness}.
assumptions: Known deterministic strongly recursive model and actual context; disjoint cause and witness variables; alternative values differ componentwise from actual values.
gloss: Changing a minimal cause changes the outcome when a specified witness retains its actual values.
relation: Generalizes standard and direct counterfactual dependence; corresponds to modified HP actual causation, but differs from the paper’s Definition 15.

quote: Here I will call this relation direct counterfactual dependence.
formula: \vec W=\mathcal V\setminus(\vec X\cup\{Y\})\quad\text{in Definition 11};\qquad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w]Y\ne y.
assumptions: Definition 11 actuality and minimality; all other endogenous variables can be held at their actual values.
gloss: Change the proposed cause while fixing every other endogenous variable except the outcome.
relation: Special case of Definition 11 with the largest witness. The paper calls it a deterministic version of the direct effect (Pearl 2001); with the actual value as reference it matches Pearl's unit-level natural direct effect (Definition 4).

quote: This relation is standardly referred to as counterfactual dependence (Pearl, 2009).
formula: \vec W=\varnothing\quad\text{in Definition 11};\qquad(M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x\land Y=y,\quad(M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x']Y\ne y,\quad\vec X\text{ minimal}.
assumptions: Known causal setting; no interventions beyond changing the proposed cause; other variables follow their equations.
gloss: Changing the cause changes the outcome without fixing any additional variables.
relation: Special case of generalized counterfactual dependence with an empty witness.

quote: Therefore I define counterfactual explanations as counterfactual analogs of sufficient explanations.
formula: \begin{aligned}\vec X=\vec x\text{ rather than }\vec X=\vec x'\text{ explains }Y=y\text{ relative to }(\vec W=\vec w,\vec N)\iff&\ ((\vec X=\vec x,\vec W=\vec w),\vec N)\text{ is an actual sufficient explanation of }Y=y\\&\land\exists y'\ne y:\ ((\vec X=\vec x',\vec W=\vec w),\vec N)\text{ is a sufficient explanation of }Y=y'.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Known causal setting; componentwise different alternatives; same witness values and safeguarded network in the factual and alternative explanations.
gloss: The actual intervention guarantees this outcome, while the alternative guarantees another outcome under the same safeguards.
relation: Combines two sufficient explanations; good counterfactual explanations characterize Definition 11 dependence existentially over witnesses and networks.

quote: Just as with sufficient explanations, we want an explanation to be as concise as possible.
formula: E_i=(\vec X_i=(\vec x_i,\vec x_i'),\vec W_i=\vec w_i,\vec N_i);\quad E_1\succeq E_2\iff\bigl(E_1,E_2\text{ explain the same }Y=y\bigr)\land\vec X_1\subseteq\vec X_2\land\vec W_1\subseteq\vec W_2\land\vec N_1\subseteq\vec N_2;\quad E_1\succ E_2\iff E_1\succeq E_2\land\neg(E_2\succeq E_1).
assumptions: Counterfactual explanations in one causal setting; comparison uses cause, witness and safeguarded-network sets.
gloss: One counterfactual explanation dominates another of the same outcome when its changed variables, witness and safeguarded network are all subsets of the other's.
relation: Extends sufficient-explanation dominance by adding a witness-set comparison.

quote: A counterfactual explanation is good if it is not dominated by any other counterfactual explanation.
formula: \operatorname{GoodCF}(E)\iff\operatorname{CFExplanation}(E)\land\nexists E'\ne E:\ \operatorname{CFExplanation}(E')\land E'\succeq E.
assumptions: Fixed causal setting, outcome and Definition 13 dominance; retains the paper’s non-strict 'dominated' wording.
gloss: No other counterfactual explanation of the outcome uses subsets of its changed variables, witness and safeguarded network.
relation: Theorem 2 relates its existence to generalized counterfactual dependence.

quote: First I make precise how changing the values of some variables can turn a sufficient explanation into a better one.
formula: \begin{aligned}E&=((\vec X=\vec x,\vec W=\vec w),\vec N);\\\vec X=\vec x'\text{ can replace }\vec X=\vec x&\iff\exists E':\ E'\text{ sufficiently explains the same }Y=y,\ E'\succeq E,\ E'\text{ includes }(\vec X=\vec x',\vec W=\vec w).\end{aligned}
assumptions: A sufficient explanation, its partition into changed and retained assignments, and sufficient-explanation dominance. The replacement explanation need not be actual.
gloss: Alternative values can replace actual ones when they preserve the outcome in an explanation at least as economical.
relation: Non-replaceability distinguishes actual causes from arbitrary parts of good sufficient explanations.

quote: Therefore I define actual causes as parts of explanations that sit in between counterfactual and sufficient explanations: they are parts of good sufficient explanations such that there exist counterfactual values which would not have made the explanation better.
formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ rather than }\vec X=\vec x'\text{ is an actual cause of }Y=y\iff\exists E:\ E\text{ is a good sufficient explanation of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u),\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of }E,\ \neg\operatorname{Replace}_E(\vec x',\vec x).
assumptions: Known deterministic causal setting, good sufficient explanations, replacement criterion and componentwise distinct alternative values.
gloss: A cause belongs to a good sufficient explanation and has an alternative that cannot preserve that explanation’s guarantees.
relation: Weaker than counterfactual explanation; differs from generalized counterfactual dependence in Definition 11; largely equivalent to Beckers’s 2021 causation definition.

quote: An obvious strengthening of actual causation is to replace the existential quantifier over counterfactual values with a universal one, so that the actual values are the optimal values in terms of explanations.
formula: \exists E:\ E\text{ is a good sufficient explanation of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u),\ \vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of }E,\ \forall\vec x'\text{ differing componentwise from }\vec x:\ \neg\operatorname{Replace}_E(\vec x',\vec x).
assumptions: Known causal setting; one good sufficient explanation must resist every admissible alternative assignment.
gloss: The actual values cannot be replaced by any alternative in the relevant good explanation.
relation: Strengthens actual causation by universally quantifying over alternatives.

concepts: actual causation; explanation; direct and indirect effects
quote: Finally, replacing strong sufficiency with direct sufficiency offers a notion of direct causation .
formula: \vec X=\vec x\text{ is a direct cause of }Y=y\text{ in }(M,\vec u)\iff\vec X=\vec x\text{ is part of an actual direct good sufficient explanation of }Y=y.
assumptions: Known causal setting; goodness and actuality; a direct sufficient explanation has safeguarded network containing only the outcome.
gloss: A direct cause belongs to a minimal actual explanation that does not rely on an intermediate safeguarded network.
relation: Proposition 3 gives an alternative making every direct cause an actual cause; direct causation need not imply optimal causation.

quote: Definition 1. A nondeterministic causal model M is a 3tuple (V, G, PM ), where V is a set of variables (each with their own domain), G is an acyclic directed graph such that there is one node for each variable in V
formula: M=(\mathbf V,G,P_M),\qquad P_M(\mathbf V)=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P_M(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\qquad G\text{ acyclic}.
assumptions: Specified variable domains and DAG; probabilities represent nondeterministic mechanisms rather than ignorance about deterministic mechanisms.
gloss: A directed acyclic causal system specifies stochastic mechanisms directly.
relation: Alternative to the deterministic causal-model representation; supports Definition 2 counterfactual semantics.

quote: This formalizes the simple idea that the only information the actual world gives us about counterfactual worlds is that the actual parents resulted in their actual children, and nothing more.
formula: \begin{aligned}P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X=x\mid\mathbf{pa}_X)&=1,\\P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)&=P(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)\quad(\mathbf{pa}_X^*\ne\mathbf{pa}_X),\\P^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V)&=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\\P^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)&=P^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*).\end{aligned}
assumptions: Nondeterministic causal model, complete factual assignment and imposed counterfactual root values. Actual local input-output pairs are retained; unobserved parent settings retain prior mechanisms.
gloss: Preserve observed responses to actual parent values, but reuse the original stochastic mechanism for changed parent values.
relation: General nondeterministic semantics; reduces to simple semantics for the paper’s LLM representation and is recovered by unrestricted selection.

quote: In other words, the simple semantics states that the counterfactual distribution does not depend on the factual result at all and takes on the same form as the prior, factual, distribution.
formula: \forall\mathbf r^*,\mathbf v\text{ with }\mathbf r^*\not\subseteq\mathbf v:\quad P_M^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)=P_M(\mathbf V=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R=\mathbf r^*).\qquad P^*(Y^*=y^*\mid Y=y,X=x,X^*=x^*)=P(Y=y^*\mid X=x^*)\ (x^*\ne x).
assumptions: Genuinely changed root input. Theorem 2 establishes the condition for the idealized autoregressive LLM representation, not arbitrary stochastic systems.
gloss: A changed-prompt counterfactual is distributed like an ordinary new run on that prompt.
relation: Special property of the general nondeterministic semantics; differs from conditioning on factual evidence in deterministic latent-noise models.

quote: Definition 4. A deterministic causal model M is a 5-tuple (V, U, G, f, PU ), where V and G are as before, U is a set of variables called exogenous (V are called endogenous), f is a function f : (u, r) → v mapping values for the exogenous and root variables to values of the endogenous variables such that r ⊆ f (u, r) (i.e., f is the identity function for R), and PU is a probability distribution over U satisfying positivity.
formula: M=(\mathbf V,\mathbf U,G,f,P_{\mathbf U}),\quad f:(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\mapsto\mathbf v,\quad\mathbf r\subseteq f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r),\quad P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)>0;\qquad\mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\text{ defines a solution}.
assumptions: Specified acyclic graph, deterministic response function, exogenous variables and positive exogenous distribution.
gloss: Outputs are deterministic once root inputs and latent background variables are fixed.
relation: Contrasts with nondeterministic causal models; implementations using pseudorandom generators admit this literal representation.

quote: Probabilities of counterfactuals – of the same restricted form as before – are now defined as:
formula: P^*(\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf v,\mathbf r^*)=\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v^*=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r^*)\}}P(\mathbf u\mid\mathbf v)=\frac{\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v^*=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r^*),\ \mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\}}P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)}{\sum_{\{\mathbf u:\mathbf v=f(\mathbf u,\mathbf r)\}}P_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf u)},\quad\mathbf r\subseteq\mathbf v.
assumptions: Deterministic causal model, specified latent-variable distribution and factual evidence of positive probability; the same latent values are used counterfactually.
gloss: Infer latent backgrounds from the observed run, then change the root input while retaining those backgrounds.
relation: Pearl-style semantics appropriate to deterministic mechanisms; generally not identified by an LLM’s observational distribution alone.

quote: Definition 5. Given a family of distributions P (Y|X), observed values x, y, and a counterfactual value x∗ , we define the set of stable values as
formula: \operatorname{St}(y,x,x^*)=\{y\}\cup\left\{y':\frac{P(y\mid x^*)}{P(y\mid x)}<\frac{P(y'\mid x^*)}{P(y'\mid x)}\right\}.
assumptions: Factual input-output pair, counterfactual input and conditional output probabilities. Ratios need defined denominators or a zero-probability convention.
gloss: Keep the factual output and alternatives whose relative probability increase exceeds its increase.
relation: Defines the allowed support for Counterfactual Stability and the stable selection function.

quote: Informally, CS means that all counterfactual values whose relative increase in prior probability – when moving from the actual to the counterfactual setting – is lower than that of the actual value are excluded.
formula: P^*(Y\notin\operatorname{St}(y,x,x^*)\mid y,x,x^*)=0.
assumptions: Conditional observational distributions, a factual input-output pair and the stable-value set. The formal strict inequality also excludes nonfactual ties.
gloss: The counterfactual distribution puts no probability outside the stable-value set.
relation: Optional restriction on counterfactual distributions; Gumbel-Max models impose additional constraints beyond stability.

quote: Definition 6. Given a causal model M and a variable X ∈ V, a selection function SX for X is a function that maps values (x, paX , paX ∗ ) to subsets of X’s domain that include x, and such that S(x, paX , paX ) = {x}. We define S := ∪{X∈V} {SX }, and call S a selection function for M .
formula: S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*)\subseteq\mathcal R(X),\quad x\in S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*),\quad S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X)=\{x\};\qquad S=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf V}\{S_X\}.
assumptions: Known variable domains, factual local assignments and counterfactual parent assignments.
gloss: A selection function specifies which alternative child values are admissible after changing its parents.
relation: Parameterizes biased counterfactual probabilities, including unrestricted and counterfactually stable semantics.

quote: A selection function can be used to straightforwardly refine the general nondeterministic semantics from Definition 2: one simply conditions on the fact that counterfactual values are restricted to those in S.
formula: \begin{aligned}P_S^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*)&:=P(X\mid\mathbf{pa}_X^*,X\in S_X(x,\mathbf{pa}_X,\mathbf{pa}_X^*)),\\P_S^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V)&=\prod_{X\in\mathbf V}P_S^{(x,\mathbf{pa}_X)}(X\mid\mathbf{Pa}_X),\\P_S^*(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*)&=P_S^{\mathbf v}(\mathbf V^*=\mathbf v^*\mid\mathbf R^*=\mathbf r^*).\end{aligned}
assumptions: Nondeterministic model, complete factual assignment and selection function; selected conditional events must have positive probability.
gloss: Restrict each counterfactual mechanism to selected outputs, renormalize, and combine the resulting local distributions.
relation: Generalizes Definition 2 through selection; described as Bayesianized Imaging.

term: unbiased nondeterministic semantics; counterfactually stable semantics
quote: Choosing S U defines the unbiased nondeterministic semantics, and choosing St defines the counterfactually stable semantics.
formula: S_X^U(x,\mathbf{pa},\mathbf{pa}^*)=\begin{cases}\{x\},&\mathbf{pa}^*=\mathbf{pa},\\\mathcal R(X),&\mathbf{pa}^*\ne\mathbf{pa};\end{cases}\qquad S_X^{\mathrm{St}}=\operatorname{St};\qquad P^*_{S^U}\text{ is unbiased},\quad P^*_{\mathrm{St}}\text{ is counterfactually stable}.
assumptions: Definition 7 construction; unrestricted selection is set-maximal subject to Definition 6. Stable selection uses local conditional distributions.
gloss: One specialization permits every alternative; the other limits alternatives to stable values.
relation: Unbiased semantics recovers Definition 2 and simple semantics for LLMs; stable semantics need not equal a Gumbel-Max counterfactual distribution.

quote: To see why, note first that all semantics under consideration satisfy consistency, meaning that PS∗ (Y ∗ = y|X = x, Y = y, X ∗ = x) = 1.
formula: P_S^*(Y^*=y\mid X=x,Y=y,X^*=x)=1.
assumptions: Factual input-output observation; counterfactual input equals the factual input.
gloss: Leaving the input unchanged reproduces the factual output with certainty.
relation: Shared by the compared semantics; explains why Definition 3 restricts simple semantics to genuinely changed inputs.

term: selection function for good counterfactual explanations
quote: For example, one natural method for generating good counterfactual explanations (Wachter, Mittelstadt, and Russell, 2017; Beckers, 2022) is to consider only those outcomes that are significantly different from the actual outcome – relative to the difference in the prompt – and yet are at least as likely under their respective prompt, resulting in the following selection function (where distance function d(., .) and threshold ϵ > 1 are task-specific parameters):
formula: S^{\mathrm{CE}}_{d,\epsilon}(y,x,x^*)=\left\{y':\frac{d(y',y)}{d(x^*,x)}\ge\epsilon\ \land\ P(y\mid x)\le P(y'\mid x^*)\right\},\qquad\epsilon>1.
assumptions: Task-specific distances, threshold, output probabilities and nonzero prompt distance. As printed, this proposed filter can exclude factual y and therefore need not satisfy Definition 6’s inclusion requirement.
gloss: Seek large output changes from small prompt changes without lowering the probability of the selected output.
relation: Proposed alternative to closeness-seeking counterfactual stability; implementation is deferred to future work.

term: nondeterministic causal model of an autoregressive LLM
quote: Therefore we can represent the process with a causal model consisting of variables V = {X, T1 , . . . , Tk , Y} and the following equations and distributions: (T1 , . . . , Tlx ) = X for i ∈ {lx + 1, . . . , k}: P (Ti |T1 , . . . , Ti−1 ) Y = (T1 , . . . , Tk )
formula: \mathbf V=\{X,T_1,\ldots,T_k,Y\};\quad(T_1,\ldots,T_{l_x})=X;\quad T_i\sim P(T_i\mid T_1,\ldots,T_{i-1})\ \ (i=l_x+1,\ldots,k);\quad Y=(T_1,\ldots,T_k).
assumptions: Fixed length k with an empty token; the prompt X is the only root and Y the only leaf; idealized sampling (each token is a random variable distributed as P(T|s)); sampling parameters held fixed. Only interventions on the prompt are considered.
gloss: Each generated token is a stochastic mechanism whose parents are the prompt and all earlier tokens; the output is the token sequence.
relation: Theorem 2: this model satisfies the simple semantics (Definition 3) for changed prompts, because the prompt is a parent of every generated token. Intermediate tokens are variables of the model, but the paper does not treat interventions on them.

concepts: completeness of explanation; faithfulness of reasoning; counterfactuals; other: causal sufficiency
quote: Definition 2 (Sufficiency, PS) Sufficiency measures whether the reasoning chain S = (s1 , . . . , sn ) is sufficient to produce the correct answer y.
formula: \operatorname{PS}(S,q)=P\bigl(A_{\operatorname{do}(S)}=y\mid A\ne y,\bar S,q\bigr).
assumptions: Known correct answer y, baseline chain bar S yielding an incorrect answer with positive probability, and meaningful counterfactual chain interventions.
gloss: Among baseline failures, how often would inserting this chain have produced the correct answer?
relation: Adapts Pearl’s probability of sufficiency to whole reasoning chains; distinct from the binary correctness proxy used by the algorithm.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning; counterfactuals; other: causal necessity
quote: Definition 3 (Necessity, PN) Necessity quantifies whether a specific reasoning step st is required for producing the correct answer a = y.
formula: \operatorname{PN}(S,s_t,q)=P\left(A_{\operatorname{do}(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})}\ne y\mid A=y,S,q\right).
assumptions: A factually correct chain, specified incorrect replacement bar s_t and downstream continuation generated conditional on that replacement.
gloss: Given a successful chain, how often would corrupting this step and regenerating its continuation cause failure?
relation: Adapts probability of necessity to individual reasoning steps; under perfect sufficiency it supplies the paper’s PNS computation.

term: Probability of Necessary and Sufficient Cause (PNS) in CoT
concepts: faithfulness of reasoning; counterfactuals; other: causal necessity and sufficiency
quote: Inspired by the counterfactual definition [46], we define the Probability of Necessary and Sufficient Cause (PNS) for the step st as:
formula: S'=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t}),\qquad\operatorname{PNS}(S,s_t,q):=P(A_S=y,A_{S'}\ne y).
assumptions: Joint potential outcomes for original and replacement chains, a correct-answer target and a specified downstream-adaptive intervention. Bar s_t disambiguates the replacement step.
gloss: The original chain succeeds and the chain with the replaced step fails in the same counterfactual comparison.
relation: Joint necessity-and-sufficiency object. Appendix A identifies it by interventional differences under monotonicity, or by replacement failure probability under perfect original-chain success.

concepts: completeness of explanation; other: causal sufficiency
quote: We approximate CoT trace sufficiency as binary: PS = 1 if chain S yields the correct answer (equivalent to P (A = y | do(S), q) = 1; Appendix A), else PS = 0.
formula: \widehat{\operatorname{PS}}(S,q)=\mathbf 1\{\widehat y_{\mathrm{init}}=y\},\qquad\widehat y_{\mathrm{init}}=\operatorname{Rollout}(S,q).
assumptions: Ground-truth answer and a generated answer under the chain. One observed success does not itself establish success probability one.
gloss: Treat a chain as sufficient when its evaluated answer is correct.
relation: Operational proxy for PS; the paper invokes Appendix A’s perfect-intervention criterion to motivate the approximation.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning; counterfactuals; other: causal necessity and sufficiency
quote: Each S is assessed by validation model V for coherence and logical integrity (beyond just final answer correctness).
formula: \widehat{\operatorname{PNS}}(S,s_t,q)=1-\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}V\bigl(\bar S^{(i)}\bigr),\qquad\bar S^{(i)}=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s_{>t}^{\prime(i)}).
assumptions: Original chain deemed sufficient; k replacement rollouts; replacements and descendants semantically disjoint from the originals; validator scores intended to represent successful coherent reasoning.
gloss: Estimate a step’s contribution as one minus average validity of alternative continuations.
relation: Estimates PNS using the perfect-sufficiency reduction; validator judgments go beyond the final-answer event in Definition 4.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning; other: causal necessity
quote: Nodes with PNS score below threshold α (and their downstream nodes) are pruned iteratively until all retained nodes satisfy necessity.
formula: s_t\text{ retained}\iff\widehat{\operatorname{PNS}}(S,s_t,q)>\alpha;\qquad s_t\text{ skipped otherwise}.
assumptions: A chain passing the sufficiency gate, an estimated PNS score and chosen threshold alpha. Algorithm 1 skips ties.
gloss: Keep a step only when its estimated causal contribution exceeds the chosen threshold.
relation: Turns the PNS estimator into the pruning rule; thresholded empirical necessity differs from a universal logical necessity claim.

concepts: counterfactuals; faithfulness of reasoning; other: exogeneity
quote: Definition 5 (CoT Exogeneity) When generating each reasoning step st , the generation of the current step depends only on the previous reasoning steps s<t and the question q, and not on any external variables.
formula: P(s_t\mid\operatorname{do}(s_{<t}),q)=P(s_t\mid s_{<t},q).
assumptions: The previous reasoning and question capture the relevant causes of current-step generation; interventions are interpreted as specified by the paper.
gloss: Conditioning on a reasoning prefix gives the same step distribution as intervening to impose it.
relation: Used in the paper’s PNS identification arguments and claimed perfect-intervention/full-sufficiency equivalence.

concepts: counterfactuals; faithfulness of reasoning; other: monotonicity
quote: This condition states that altering a reasoning step to an incorrect version cannot result in correcting a previously incorrect final answer. Equivalently, whenever the modified chain S yields a correct answer, the original unaltered chain S must also yield a correct answer, ensuring monotonic progression toward correctness.
formula: \forall t,\bar s_t:\quad P(A_S\ne y,A_{\bar S}=y)=0,\qquad\bar S=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t}).
assumptions: Joint potential outcomes under original and corrupted-step chains; applies to every considered step and corruption with regenerated downstream reasoning.
gloss: Corrupting a step can never repair an answer that the original chain would get wrong.
relation: Together with exogeneity, yields the PNS difference formula in Lemma 2; Lemma 3 instead assumes perfect original-chain success.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning; counterfactuals; other: causal sufficiency
quote: This means the intervention do(S) guarantees A = y in all worlds compatible with q.
formula: \text{Perfect Intervention}:\ P(A=y\mid\operatorname{do}(S),q)=1;\qquad\text{Full Sufficiency}:\ \operatorname{PS}(S,q)=1.
assumptions: Appendix A.4 assumes exogeneity and positive baseline failure probability. Its converse argument additionally treats the correct chain as robustly successful; exogeneity alone does not generally establish the claimed equivalence.
gloss: Perfect intervention guarantees success everywhere; full sufficiency guarantees correction within the specified baseline-failure condition.
relation: The paper claims these criteria are equivalent and uses that claim to motivate its PS gate; they should remain distinct from single-run correctness.

quote: We will use the counterfactual notation Yx (u) to de­ note the value that Y would attain in unit (or situa­ tion) U = u under the control regime do(X = x). See Pearl (2000, Chapter 7) for formal semantics of these counterfactual utterances.
formula: Y_x(u):=\text{the value of }Y\text{ in unit }U=u\text{ under }\operatorname{do}(X=x).
assumptions: Structural causal model supporting interventions and unit-specific outcomes; background unit u remains fixed.
gloss: The outcome this particular unit would have under a specified intervention.
relation: Basic potential-outcome notation used in all controlled, natural and path-specific effects.

quote: the total effect measures the probability that response variable Y would take on the value y when X is set to x by external intervention.
formula: P(Y_x=y)=P(Y=y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x));\qquad\operatorname{TE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_x)-E(Y_{x^*}).
assumptions: A structural intervention semantics; reference level x* for contrasts; population distribution over units for expectations.
gloss: The overall outcome distribution under an intervention, or its mean change relative to a reference intervention.
relation: Combines direct and indirect pathways. In nonlinear models, Theorem 3 decomposes it using an effect for the reverse transition.

quote: A variable X is said to have a controlled direct effect on variable Y in model M and situation U if there exists a setting Z = z of the other variables in the model and two values of X, x"' and x, such that =
formula: \exists z,x^*,x:\quad Y_{x^*z}(u)\ne Y_{xz}(u).
assumptions: Known unit-level structural model; controllable setting z for other variables. Restricting Z to Y’s parents other than X leaves the definition unchanged.
gloss: Changing X can change this unit’s outcome even while the other relevant variables are fixed.
relation: Qualitative counterpart of the controlled direct-effect magnitude in Definition 2; differs from naturally choosing each unit’s mediator setting.

quote: Given a causal model M with causal graph G, the controlled direct effect of X on Y in unit U = u and setting Z = z is given by
formula: \operatorname{CDE}_z(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{xz}(u)-Y_{x^*z}(u).
assumptions: Structural model, fixed unit u, reference x*, specified mediator setting z and a numeric outcome scale. Z contains Y’s parents other than X.
gloss: The unit’s outcome difference between two X settings while mediators are fixed at z.
relation: Quantifies Definition 1. The paper also permits ratios or proportional differences as alternative magnitude conventions.

quote: (Average controlled direct effect) Given a probabilistic causal model (M, P(u)), the con­ trolled direct effect of event X = x on Y is defined as:
formula: \operatorname{CDE}_z(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{xz}-Y_{x^*z}).
assumptions: Probabilistic causal model and population distribution P(u); the same prescribed z is used across units. Identification requires appropriate experiments or causal assumptions.
gloss: Average the controlled direct-effect contrast across the population.
relation: Population counterpart of Definition 2; contrasts with average natural direct effect’s unit-specific mediator settings.

quote: (Unit-level natural direct effect; qualitative) An event X x is said to have a natural direct effect on variable Y in situation U if the following inequality holds
assumptions: Unit-level structural model supporting nested counterfactuals; reference x*; mediators fixed at the values that this same unit would attain under x*.
gloss: Changing X matters when mediators retain this unit’s own reference-condition values.
relation: Natural counterpart of qualitative controlled direct effect; variable-level effect exists when some pair x*, x satisfies the inequality.

quote: If one is interested in the magnitude of the natural direct effect, one can take the difference
formula: \operatorname{NDE}(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{x,Z_{x^*}(u)}(u)-Y_{x^*}(u).
assumptions: Numeric outcome, unit u and nested structural counterfactuals sharing the unit’s background conditions.
gloss: Measure the outcome change from changing X while preserving the unit’s reference mediator behavior.
relation: Quantifies Definition 4; its population expectation is Definition 5.

quote: (Average natural direct effect) The average natural direct effect of event X on a response variable Y, denoted N DE(x, x*; Y), is de­ fined as
formula: \operatorname{NDE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{x,Z_{x^*}})-E(Y_{x^*}).
assumptions: Probabilistic structural model, population distribution, reference x* and nested potential outcomes. Identification needs assumptions beyond ordinary treatment randomization.
gloss: Average the direct effect while each unit keeps its own mediator values under the reference intervention.
relation: Population version of Equation (5); differs from average controlled direct effect by natural rather than uniform mediator assignment.

quote: (Unit-level indirect effect; qualitative) An event X = x is said to have an indirect effect on variable Y in situation U = u if the following inequal­ ity holds
assumptions: Unit-level structural model and reference x*; X stays at x* while mediators receive their values under x.
gloss: The outcome changes when only the mediator response to changing X is transferred to the reference condition.
relation: Natural indirect counterpart of Definition 4; no analogous variable-fixing controlled indirect effect is supplied.

quote: Taking the difference between the two sides of Eq. (18), we can define the unit level indirect effect as
formula: \operatorname{NIE}(x,x^*;Y,u)=Y_{x^*,Z_x(u)}(u)-Y_{x^*}(u).
assumptions: Numeric outcome and nested unit-level counterfactuals; the mediator values under x are evaluated while X is fixed at x*.
gloss: Measure the outcome change caused by transferring the intervention-induced mediator values alone.
relation: Quantifies Definition 6 and averages to Definition 7.

quote: (Average indirect effect) The average indirect effect of event X = x. on variable Y, denoted NIE(x,x*; Y), is defined as
formula: \operatorname{NIE}(x,x^*;Y)=E(Y_{x^*,Z_x})-E(Y_{x^*}).
assumptions: Probabilistic structural model, population distribution and nested counterfactuals. Experimental or observational identification requires the conditions analyzed in Section 3.6.
gloss: Average the outcome change from altering mediator behavior while preserving the reference treatment.
relation: Population version of Equation (19); generally not TE minus same-direction NDE, although that additive relation holds in linear models.

quote: Let G be the the causal graph associated with model M, and let g be an edge-subgraph of G containing the paths selected for effect analysis. The g-specific effect of x on Y (relative to reference x*) is defined as the total effect of x on Y in a modified model M; formed as follows.
formula: \begin{aligned}PA_i&=\{PA_i(g),PA_i(\bar g)\},\\f_i^*(pa_i,u;g)&=f_i\bigl(pa_i(g),pa_i^*(\bar g),u\bigr),\qquad pa_i^*(\bar g)=PA_i(\bar g)_{x^*}(u),\\\operatorname{SE}_g(x,x^*;Y,u)_M&=\operatorname{TE}(x,x^*;Y,u)_{M_g^*}.\end{aligned}
assumptions: Structural model and graph, selected edge-subgraph g, fixed unit u and reference intervention x*. Inputs along excluded edges are replaced by their original-model reference values.
gloss: Allow influence through selected edges while supplying reference-world inputs along the excluded edges.
relation: Generalizes natural direct and indirect effects; unlike those special cases, some path-specific effects remain unidentified even in Markovian models.

quote: A (deterministic) causal model is a pair M = (Σ, {FX }X∈V ), such that Σ is a signature and {FX }X∈V is a set of mechanisms, with FX : ValV → ValX assigning a value to X as a function of the values of all the variables, including X itself.
formula: M=(\Sigma,\{F_X\}_{X\in\mathbf V}),\qquad F_X:\operatorname{Val}_{\mathbf V}\to\operatorname{Val}_X.
assumptions: A signature specifying variables and their nonempty value ranges; deterministic mechanisms.
gloss: A collection of variables and equations specifying their causal mechanisms.
relation: Underlying model class for exact transformation and constructive abstraction; permits cycles and self-dependence.

quote: The resulting order ≺ captures a notion of direct causation, which can be extended to indirect causation by taking its transitive closure ≺∗ .
formula: Y\prec X\iff\exists\mathbf z,y,y'\;F_X(\mathbf z,y)\ne F_X(\mathbf z,y'),\qquad\mathbf Z=\mathbf V\setminus\{Y\};\qquad\prec^*=\operatorname{TC}(\prec).
assumptions: Known deterministic mechanisms; other variables held fixed while varying Y.
gloss: Direct causation is functional dependence; indirect causation follows chains of such dependence.
relation: Defines the graphical structure induced by the causal model; distinct from an actual-causation definition.

quote: Given M = (V, {FX }X∈V ), the set of solutions, called Solve(M), is the set of all v ∈ ValV such that all the equations ProjX (v) = FX (v) are satisfied for each X ∈ V.
formula: \operatorname{Solve}(M)=\{\mathbf v\in\operatorname{Val}_{\mathbf V}:\forall X\in\mathbf V,\ \operatorname{Proj}_X(\mathbf v)=F_X(\mathbf v)\}.
assumptions: Known mechanisms; cyclic models may have no solution or multiple solutions.
gloss: All complete states that satisfy the model's equations simultaneously.
relation: Exact transformations preserve these sets after corresponding interventions.

quote: Define a hard intervention to be a partial setting i ∈ ValI for finite I ⊆ V.
formula: F_X^{\mathbf i}(\mathbf v)=\begin{cases}\operatorname{Proj}_X(\mathbf i),&X\in\mathbf I,\\F_X(\mathbf v),&X\notin\mathbf I.\end{cases}
assumptions: A causal model and a finite set of variables to fix.
gloss: Replace selected mechanisms with constants.
relation: Special case of soft intervention and interventional.

quote: We define a soft intervention on some finite set of variables X ⊆ V to be a family of functions {IX }X∈X where IX : ValV → ValX for each X ∈ X.
formula: I=\{I_X\}_{X\in\mathbf X},\quad I_X:\operatorname{Val}_{\mathbf V}\to\operatorname{Val}_X;\qquad F_X^I=I_X\ \text{for }X\in\mathbf X.
assumptions: Replacement mechanisms on a finite set of variables.
gloss: Replace selected mechanisms with new functions.
relation: Generalizes hard intervention; special case of interventional.

quote: We define an interventional on some finite set of variables X ⊆ V to be a family of functions I = {IX }X∈X where IX : SoftX → SoftX for each X ∈ X.
formula: I=\{I_X\}_{X\in\mathbf X},\qquad I_X:\operatorname{Soft}_X\to\operatorname{Soft}_X,\qquad F_X^I=I_X\langle F_X\rangle.
assumptions: Access to mechanisms; transformations may depend on the mechanisms being replaced.
gloss: Transform mechanisms using functions of the original mechanisms.
relation: Generalizes soft interventions beyond mechanism replacement.

quote: An intervention algebra formalizes the notion of a set of separable components with distinct mechanisms, satisfying the fundamental algebraic properties of commutativity and left-annihilativity (see (a) and (b) in Definition 16).
formula: (\Lambda,\oplus)\text{ is an intervention algebra}\iff\exists\Sigma\;(\Lambda,\oplus)\simeq(\Phi_\Sigma,\circ)
assumptions: A binary operation; ΦΣ is the algebra of finite hard interventions for some signature.
gloss: An intervention system with the same algebraic structure as hard interventions.
relation: Restricts general interventionals so they behave like interventions on separable variables.

quote: These two properties highlight an important sense in which hard interventions are modular: when intervening on two different variables, the order does not matter; and when intervening on the same variable twice, the second undoes any effect of the first intervention.
formula: X\ne Y\Rightarrow x\circ y=y\circ x;\qquad X=Y\Rightarrow x\circ y=y.
assumptions: Atomic interventions; composition follows the paper's left-to-right intervention convention.
gloss: Different components can be edited independently; a later edit of one component replaces its earlier edit.
relation: Characterizes the modular behavior captured by intervention algebras.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: Then M∗ is an exact transformation of M under (τ, ω) if for all I ∈ Domain(ω), the following diagram commutes:
formula: \forall I\in\operatorname{Domain}(\omega),\qquad\tau\bigl(\operatorname{Solve}(M_I)\bigr)=\operatorname{Solve}\bigl(M^*_{\omega(I)}\bigr).
assumptions: Intervention algebras on both models; partial surjections τ and ω; ω preserves the intervention order. Undefined τ values receive a distinguished bottom value.
gloss: Intervening and then translating yields exactly the same states as translating the intervention and running the other model.
relation: Deterministic variant of Rubenstein et al.'s exact transformation (cf. Beckers and Halpern's uniform transformation, Def. 3.5), generalized to interventionals; bijective translation and constructive abstraction are special cases.

quote: We say that τ (M) is the bijective translation of M under τ .
formula: F_{X^*}^{\tau(M)}(\mathbf v^*)=\operatorname{Proj}_{X^*}\!\left(\tau\left(F_{\mathbf V}(\tau^{-1}(\mathbf v^*))\right)\right).
assumptions: A bijection between complete state spaces; known mechanisms.
gloss: Rewrite the same mechanisms in an invertibly transformed state space.
relation: Lossless special case of exact transformation; supplies access to distributed modular features.

quote: In words, the set ΠXH consists of those low-level variables that are ‘aligned’ with the high-level variable XH , and πXH tells us how a given setting of the low-level cluster ΠXH corresponds to a setting of the high-level variable XH .
formula: \Pi=\{\Pi_X:X\in\mathbf V_H\}\cup\{\Pi_\bot\}\text{ partitions }\mathbf V_L;\quad\Pi_X\ne\varnothing;\quad\pi_X:\operatorname{Val}_{\Pi_X}\rightharpoonup\operatorname{Val}_X\text{ is surjective}.\qquad\tau^\pi(\mathbf v)=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf V_H}\pi_X(\operatorname{Proj}_{\Pi_X}(\mathbf v)).
assumptions: Nonoverlapping variable clusters; a possibly empty forgotten cluster; partial surjective value maps.
gloss: Specify which low-level variables realize each high-level variable and how their values correspond.
relation: Canonically induces the state map τπ and intervention map ωπ used in constructive abstraction.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: We say that H is a constructive abstraction of L under an alignment ⟨Π, π⟩ iff H is an exact transformation of L under (τ π , ω π ).
formula: \forall\mathbf i\in\operatorname{Domain}(\omega^\pi),\qquad\tau^\pi(\operatorname{Solve}(L_{\mathbf i}))=\operatorname{Solve}(H_{\omega^\pi(\mathbf i)}).
assumptions: An alignment; ωπ acts on interventions targeting complete aligned cells, excluding the forgotten cell.
gloss: The high-level model preserves interventions under a specified clustering of low-level variables.
relation: Special case of exact transformation; permits partial value maps unlike Beckers and Halpern's original constructive abstraction.

quote: Marginalization is essentially a matter of ignoring a subset X of variables.
formula: \mathbf V^*=\mathbf V\setminus\mathbf X,\qquad\Pi_\bot=\mathbf X,\qquad\Pi_Y=\{Y\},\quad\pi_Y(y)=y\quad(Y\notin\mathbf X).
assumptions: A signature and a proper subset of variables to forget.
gloss: Forget selected variables while retaining the values of the others.
relation: One of three operations sufficient to decompose any alignment.

quote: Next, variable merge collapses each cell of a partition into single variables.
formula: \operatorname{Val}_{X^*}^*=\operatorname{Val}_{\Pi_{X^*}},\qquad\Pi_\bot=\varnothing,\qquad\pi_{X^*}(\mathbf y)=\mathbf y.
assumptions: A partition of low-level variables indexed by the new high-level variables.
gloss: Replace each variable cluster with one variable retaining the cluster's complete joint value.
relation: One of the three alignment-decomposition operations; does not itself discard values.

quote: Finally, value merge alters the value space of each variable, potentially collapsing values:
formula: \delta_X:\operatorname{Val}_X\rightharpoonup\operatorname{Val}_X^*\text{ surjective},\qquad\Pi_X=\{X\},\quad\Pi_\bot=\varnothing,\quad\pi_X=\delta_X.
assumptions: A partial surjective map to a new value space for each variable.
gloss: Coarsen variable values while retaining the variables.
relation: Complements marginalization and variable merge in decomposing constructive alignments.

quote: Composition of alignments is defined, as expected, via composition of their maps.
formula: \Pi''_{X''}=\bigcup_{X'\in\Pi'_{X''}}\Pi_{X'},\qquad\Pi''_\bot=\bigcup_{X'\in\Pi'_\bot\cup\{\bot\}}\Pi_{X'},\qquad\pi''_{X''}(\mathbf y)=\pi'_{X''}\!\left(\bigcup_{X'\in\Pi'_{X''}}\pi_{X'}(\operatorname{Proj}_{\Pi_{X'}}(\mathbf y))\right).
assumptions: Two alignments with matching intermediate signatures.
gloss: Combine two successive abstraction alignments into one.
relation: Used in the decomposition of alignments into marginalization, variable merge and value merge.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: Taken together, we can construct a metric that quantifies the degree to which M∗ is an approximate transformation of M in a single number:
formula: \mathcal S_{I\sim P}\!\left[\operatorname{Sim}\!\left(\tau(\operatorname{Solve}(M_I)),\operatorname{Solve}(M^*_{\omega(I)})\right)\right].
assumptions: Partial surjective state and order-preserving intervention maps; a similarity function, intervention distribution P and real-valued aggregation statistic S; evaluable solved states.
where: §2.4, Definition 41, Eq. 6, [P224]–[P226]; interpretation as graded faithfulness in §3.2, [P592]
gloss: Grade an interpretation by aggregating agreement under corresponding interventions.
relation: Graded version of exact transformation; encompasses interchange intervention accuracy, LIME fidelity and other choices of comparison metric.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: If this number is above a particular cutoff η, we can say that M∗ is an η-approximate abstraction of M.
formula: \mathcal S_{I\sim P}[\operatorname{Sim}(\tau(\operatorname{Solve}(M_I)),\operatorname{Solve}(M^*_{\omega(I)}))]>\eta.
assumptions: The approximate-transformation score and a threshold; the quoted direction assumes larger scores indicate better agreement.
gloss: Accept an abstraction when its graded score exceeds a specified threshold.
relation: Thresholded approximate transformation; the paper states an above-threshold convention despite also allowing distance-valued comparisons.

quote: Specifically, the causal model is provided a ‘base’ input and an intervention is performed that fixes some variables to be the values they would have if different ‘source’ inputs were provided.
formula: \operatorname{IntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf s_1,\ldots,\mathbf s_k\rangle,\langle\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_k\rangle)=\bigcup_{j=1}^k\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_j}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf s_j})).
assumptions: Input variables; disjoint noninput target sets; source computations supplying definite target values.
gloss: Patch selected variables with values produced by other inputs.
relation: Base case for recursive interchange interventions and distributed interchange interventions.

quote: We take interchange interventions as a base case and generalize to recursive interchange interventions, where variables are fixed to be the value they would have if a recursive interchange intervention (that itself may be defined in terms of other interchange interventions) were performed.
formula: \operatorname{RecIntInv}_{m+1}(M,\langle\mathbf s_j\rangle,\langle\mathbf X_j\rangle,\langle\mathbf i_j\rangle)=\bigcup_{j=1}^k\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_j}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf s_j\circ\mathbf i_j}));\qquad\operatorname{RecIntInv}_0=\operatorname{IntInv}.
assumptions: Disjoint target sets and depth-m interventions used in the source computations.
gloss: Patch with values obtained from computations that themselves contain patches.
relation: Generalizes interchange intervention; expresses path patching and causal scrubbing operations.

quote: Geiger et al. (2023) generalize interchange interventions to distributed interchange interventions that target variables distributed across multiple causal variables.
formula: F_X\leftarrow\left[\mathbf v\mapsto\operatorname{Proj}_X\!\left(\tau^{-1}\!\left(\operatorname{Solve}\!\left(\tau(M)_{\operatorname{IntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf s_1,\ldots,\mathbf s_k\rangle,\langle\mathbf X_1^*,\ldots,\mathbf X_k^*\rangle)}\right)\right)\right)\right].
assumptions: An input-preserving bijective translation and disjoint targets in the translated space. Formula follows the printed Definition 46, including its use of M inside IntInv.
gloss: Translate to a feature space, patch there, and translate back.
relation: Extends interchange interventions to distributed features using bijective translation.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: Geiger et al. (2022b) propose interchange intervention accuracy, which is simply the proportion of interchange interventions where the low-level and high-level causal models have the same input–output behavior (see Section 2.6 for an example).
formula: \operatorname{IIA}(H,L,(\Pi,\pi))=\mathbb E_{\mathbf i\sim P(\operatorname{Domain}(\omega^\pi))}\!\left[\mathbf1\!\left[\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_H^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\tau^\pi(L_{\mathbf i}))=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_H^{\mathrm{Out}}}(H_{\omega^\pi(\mathbf i)})\right]\right].
assumptions: An aligned model pair and a distribution over aligned interventions; intervened-model notation denotes its resulting state.
gloss: How often corresponding patches make the two models produce matching outputs.
relation: Special case of approximate transformation with output equality and expectation; ordinary accuracy results when base and source inputs coincide.

quote: We propose to define modular features as any set of variables that form an intervention algebra accessed by a bijective translation.
formula: \text{Modular features are variables of }\tau(M)\text{ accessed through bijective }\tau\text{ whose interventions form an intervention algebra}.
assumptions: A bijective translation and an intervention algebra; no linearity restriction.
gloss: Separable causal components exposed by an invertible change of representation.
relation: Uses bijective translation and intervention algebra to generalize neuron-aligned and linear features.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; causal abstraction
quote: The LIME fidelity of using H to interpret L on the input x is given as:
formula: \operatorname{LIME}(H,L,\Delta_{\mathbf x})=\frac1{|\Delta_{\mathbf x}|}\sum_{\mathbf x'\in\Delta_{\mathbf x}}\operatorname{Distance}\!\left(\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_L^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\operatorname{Solve}(L_{\mathbf x'})),\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_H^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\operatorname{Solve}(H_{\mathbf x'}))\right).
assumptions: Identical input/output spaces; a finite neighborhood of inputs and an output-distance function.
gloss: Average local output disagreement between an interpretable model and the model it explains.
relation: Special case of approximate transformation restricted to input interventions; does not establish agreement of internal mechanisms.

term: completeness axiom of the integrated gradients method
concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; other: attribution completeness
quote: The completeness axiom of the integrated gradients method is formulated as follows:
formula: \sum_{i=1}^{|\mathbf Y|}\operatorname{IG}_i(\mathbf y,\mathbf y')=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X^{\mathrm{Out}}}(M_{\mathbf x\cup\mathbf y})-\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X^{\mathrm{Out}}}(M_{\mathbf x\cup\mathbf y'}).
assumptions: The integrated-gradients setup and conditions under which the path integral is defined.
gloss: Attributions sum to the output change caused by replacing the baseline hidden state.
relation: Completeness of numerical attribution, rather than completeness of a natural-language reasoning explanation.

quote: The fundamental notions involved in mediation are total, direct, and indirect effects, which can be defined with interchange interventions.
formula: \begin{aligned}\operatorname{TotalEffect}(M,\mathbf x,\mathbf x',\mathbf Y)&=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x'}))-\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x})),\\\operatorname{DirectEffect}(M,\mathbf x,\mathbf x',\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)&=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x'\cup\operatorname{IntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf x\rangle,\langle\mathbf Z\rangle)}))-\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x})),\\\operatorname{IndirectEffect}(M,\mathbf x,\mathbf x',\mathbf Y,\mathbf Z)&=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x\cup\operatorname{IntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf x'\rangle,\langle\mathbf Z\rangle)}))-\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf Y}(\operatorname{Solve}(M_{\mathbf x})).\end{aligned}
assumptions: Disjoint X, Y and Z; subtraction of Y values is defined; source and intervened computations have definite solutions.
gloss: Compare the full input change with changes that freeze or selectively change the mediator.
relation: Defines mediation effects using interchange interventions; complete mediation equates indirect and total effects.

concepts: direct and indirect effects; causal abstraction
quote: The following are equivalent: 1. The hidden vector H completely mediate the causal effect of inputs on outputs:
formula: \operatorname{IndirectEffect}(L,\mathbf x,\mathbf x',\mathbf X^{\mathrm{Out}},\mathbf H)=\operatorname{TotalEffect}(M,\mathbf x,\mathbf x',\mathbf X^{\mathrm{Out}}),\qquad M=L.
assumptions: A neural network, specified inputs/outputs and candidate hidden mediator; the displayed equation switches from L to M for the same network.
gloss: Changing the mediator alone reproduces the entire effect of changing the input.
relation: Remark 53: equivalent to the high-level model obtained by variable merge and marginalization of L having no direct edge from input X to output Y (a chain X→Z→Y).

quote: To perform a path patch, we use a recursive interchange intervention on a model M processing a base input b that simulates ‘sender’ variables H taking on intervened values from a source input s, restricting the effect of this intervention to receiver variables R while freezing variables F.
formula: \mathbf i_R=\operatorname{IntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf s,\mathbf b\rangle,\langle\mathbf H,\mathbf F\setminus\{R\}\rangle);\qquad\mathbf j=\operatorname{RecIntInv}(M,\langle\mathbf b,\ldots,\mathbf b\rangle,\langle R_1,\ldots,R_2\rangle,\langle\mathbf i_{R_1},\ldots,\mathbf i_{R_k}\rangle).
assumptions: Base/source inputs, sender/receiver sets and frozen variables. The printed receiver list ends in R2 although the text indexes k receivers.
gloss: Patch a sender's influence into selected receivers while freezing alternative routes.
relation: An application of recursive interchange interventions.

quote: If performing an ablation on H to erase the concept C leads L to have the degraded behavior AC without changing other behaviors, then the ablation was successful.
formula: \operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_L^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\operatorname{Solve}((L_I)_{\mathbf x}))=\begin{cases}A_C(\mathbf x),&\mathbf x\in\operatorname{Domain}(A_C),\\\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_L^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\operatorname{Solve}(L_{\mathbf x})),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
assumptions: A proposed concept-erasing ablation and a specified partial function describing the behavioral degradation expected from erasing that concept.
gloss: Erasure causes the concept-specific deficit while preserving other behavior.
relation: Equivalent to exact transformation by the section's three-variable ablation model.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; other: circuit sufficiency
quote: The high-level causal model H is an exact transformation of the low-level neural model L under (τ, ω) exactly when the subcircuit C preserves the behavior B.
formula: \forall\mathbf x\in\operatorname{Domain}(B),\qquad\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbf X_L^{\mathrm{Out}}}(\operatorname{Solve}((L_{I_{\overline C}})_{\mathbf x}))=B(\mathbf x),\qquad\overline C=\mathbf V\times\mathbf V\setminus C.
assumptions: A candidate circuit, a target behavior and specified ablation values for connections outside the circuit.
gloss: The candidate circuit still realizes the target behavior after its complement is ablated.
relation: Expressed as exact transformation by a three-variable ablation model; causal scrubbing uses a different intervention scheme.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; causal abstraction
quote: Chan et al. (2022b) propose to measure the faithfulness of H by appeal to the proportion of performance maintained by L under interventionals determined by Scrub.
formula: \mathbb E_{I\sim P}\!\left[\mathbf1\!\left[\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathrm{Out}}(\tau(\operatorname{Solve}(L_I)))=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathrm{Out}}(\operatorname{Solve}(H^*_{\omega(I)}))\right]\right].
assumptions: The Scrub algorithm, its source-sampling distributions, the target behavior and the auxiliary ablation model H* constructed in §3.5.2.
gloss: Measure behavior preserved after recursively resampling connections according to a proposed interpretation.
relation: Special case of approximate transformation with indicator similarity and expectation; H* differs from the interpretation H used to choose resamples.

quote: Intuitively, [Y1 ← y1 , . . . , Yk ← yk ]ϕ says that ϕ would hold if Yi were set to yi , for i = 1, . . . , k.
formula: (M,\mathbf u)\models[\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y]\varphi\iff(M_{\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y},\mathbf u)\models\varphi.
assumptions: A recursive causal model; a fixed exogenous context; φ is a Boolean combination of endogenous-variable assignments.
gloss: Evaluate a claim after replacing selected structural equations with fixed values.
relation: Counterfactual semantics underlying the intervention-outcome distances.

quote: In the formal definition, we need two additional functions: τU : RL (UL ) → RH (UH ), which maps exogenous states of ML to exogenous states of MH , and ωτ : IL → IH , which maps low-level interventions to high-level interventions.
formula: \operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V,\mathbf x)=\{\mathbf v\in\mathcal R(\mathbf V):\mathbf v|_{\mathbf X}=\mathbf x\};\qquad\omega_\tau(\mathbf X\leftarrow\mathbf x)=\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y\iff\tau(\operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V_L,\mathbf x))=\operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V_H,\mathbf y).\qquad\mathcal I_L^\tau=\operatorname{Domain}(\omega_\tau),\quad\mathcal I_H^\tau=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_L^\tau).
assumptions: A low-to-high state map; ωτ is undefined when the image is not a high-level restriction set.
gloss: Derive intervention correspondence directly from which states each intervention fixes.
relation: Reproduces Beckers and Halpern's induced intervention map; used in τ-consistency and τ-abstraction.

quote: We capture all of them by requiring the two causal models to be τ -consistent:
formula: \tau:\mathcal R_L(\mathbf V_L)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal R_H(\mathbf V_H),\qquad\mathcal I_H=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_L),\qquad|\mathcal R_L(\mathbf U_L)|\ge|\mathcal R_H(\mathbf U_H)|.
assumptions: Two causal-model signatures, allowed intervention sets and a state map.
gloss: Require compatible state spaces, intervention sets and enough low-level contexts to cover high-level contexts.
relation: Necessary structural prerequisites for exact and approximate τ-abstraction.

quote: Abstraction means that for each possible low-level context-intervention pair, the two ways of moving up “diagonally” to a high-level endogenous state always lead to the same result.
formula: \exists\tau_U:\mathcal R_L(\mathbf U_L)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal R_H(\mathbf U_H)\;\forall\mathbf u_L,i\in\mathcal I_L,\quad\tau(M_L(\mathbf u_L,i))=M_H(\tau_U(\mathbf u_L),\omega_\tau(i))
assumptions: τ-consistent models; the context quantifier ranges over all low-level contexts, independently of the intervention quantifier.
gloss: Every allowed intervention has exactly corresponding outcomes at both levels in every context.
relation: Inherited from Abstracting Causal Models; recovered by zero-error deterministic approximate abstraction.

quote: If MH is a τ -abstraction of ML then we say it is constructive if τ is constructive and IL = ILτ .
formula: \mathbf V_L=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n+1}\mathbf Z_i,\quad\mathbf Z_i\ne\varnothing\ (i\le n),\quad\tau(\mathbf v_L)=\tau_1(\mathbf v_L|_{\mathbf Z_1})\cdots\tau_n(\mathbf v_L|_{\mathbf Z_n}),\quad\tau_i:\mathcal R(\mathbf Z_i)\to\mathcal R(Y_i).\qquad\text{Constructive abstraction additionally requires }\mathcal I_L=\mathcal I_L^\tau.
assumptions: High-level variables Y1,…,Yn; a partition with a possibly empty forgotten cell.
gloss: Each high-level variable is computed from its own disjoint low-level variable cluster.
relation: Restated from Beckers and Halpern (2019); supplies the constructive special case in which an approximate abstraction decomposes into an approximation followed by an exact abstraction (Thm. 5.6).

quote: Thus, M1 is a dmax -α approximation of M2 if the predictions of M1 are always within α of the predictions of M2 .
formula: d_{\max}(M_1,M_2)=\max_{i\in\mathcal I,\ \mathbf u\in\mathcal R(\mathbf U)}d_{\mathbf V}(M_1(\mathbf u,i),M_2(\mathbf u,i));\qquad d_{\max}(M_1,M_2)\le\alpha.
assumptions: Similar deterministic models; a metric on their common endogenous state space.
gloss: Bound the largest prediction discrepancy over all contexts and allowed interventions.
relation: Identity-map special case of deterministic τ-α approximate abstraction.

quote: MH is a τ -α approximate abstraction of ML if dτ (ML , MH ) ≤ α.
formula: d_\tau(M_L,M_H)=\min_{\tau_U\ \mathrm{surjective}}\max_{i\in\mathcal I_L,\ \mathbf u_L\in\mathcal R_L(\mathbf U_L)}d_{\mathbf V_H}\!\left(\tau(M_L(\mathbf u_L,i)),M_H(\tau_U(\mathbf u_L),\omega_\tau(i))\right);\qquad d_\tau(M_L,M_H)\le\alpha.
assumptions: Finite τ-consistent models; fixed surjective τ; a high-level state metric; optimize over surjective context maps.
gloss: Choose the best context correspondence, then bound the worst high-level intervention-outcome discrepancy.
relation: Generalizes exact τ-abstraction; α=0 recovers it.

quote: A probabilistic causal model M = (S, F, I, Pr) is just a causal model together with a probability Pr on contexts ~u.
formula: M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F,\mathcal I,\Pr),\qquad\Pr^i(\mathbf v)=\Pr(\{\mathbf u:M(\mathbf u,i)=\mathbf v\}).
assumptions: A recursive causal model and a distribution over exogenous contexts.
gloss: Add uncertainty over contexts to deterministic structural equations.
relation: Supports expected-error and tail-probability generalizations of deterministic approximation.

quote: Definition 4.1: Define a distance function dmax on pairs of similar probabilistic causal models by taking
formula: d_{\max}(M_1,M_2)=\max_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal R(\mathbf U)}\Pr(\mathbf u)d_{\mathbf V}(M_1(\mathbf u,i),M_2(\mathbf u,i));\qquad d_{\max}(M_1,M_2)\le\alpha.
assumptions: Similar probabilistic models sharing their context distribution and state metric.
gloss: Bound expected prediction error for the worst allowed intervention.
relation: Replaces deterministic dmax's worst context with an expectation.

quote: Definition 4.2: Define a distance function dβ on pairs of similar probabilistic causal models by taking
formula: d_\beta(M_1,M_2)=\max_{i\in\mathcal I}\Pr\!\left(\{\mathbf u:d_{\mathbf V}(M_1(\mathbf u,i),M_2(\mathbf u,i))\ge\beta\}\right);\qquad d_\beta(M_1,M_2)\le\alpha.
assumptions: Similar probabilistic models; a state metric; an error-severity threshold β.
gloss: Bound the probability of a discrepancy at least β under the worst intervention.
relation: Alternative to expected-distance approximation, emphasizing large errors.

quote: In the probabilistic notion, we require that the two different probability distributions obtained by the two ways of lifting an intervention be equal.
formula: \forall i\in\mathcal I_L,\qquad\tau_\#\Pr_L^i=\Pr_H^{\omega_\tau(i)}.
assumptions: τ-consistent probabilistic models; pushforward of low-level interventional outcome distributions.
gloss: Corresponding interventions induce identical high-level outcome distributions.
relation: Distributional counterpart of deterministic τ-abstraction.

quote: We can now extend our definitions to the approximate scenario just as we did for deterministic causal models.
formula: d_\tau(M_L,M_H)=\min_{\tau_U:\tau_{U\#}\Pr_L=\Pr_H}\max_{i\in\mathcal I_L}\sum_{\mathbf u_L}\Pr_L(\mathbf u_L)d_{\mathbf V_H}\!\left(\tau(M_L(\mathbf u_L,i)),M_H(\tau_U(\mathbf u_L),\omega_\tau(i))\right);\qquad d_\tau(M_L,M_H)\le\alpha.
assumptions: τ-consistent probabilistic models; a high-level state metric; a context map with the prescribed pushforward distribution.
gloss: Minimize expected abstraction error over distribution-compatible context mappings, retaining the worst intervention.
relation: Probabilistic generalization of deterministic approximate abstraction; extended by intervention-distribution averaging.

quote: Definition 4.7 : Given a surjective map τ : R(VL ) → R(VH ), an intervention distribution PrI is a distribution on IL × IH such that
formula: \Pr_{\mathcal I}(i_L\mid i_H)>0\iff\omega_\tau(i_L)=i_H.
assumptions: A surjective abstraction map and low/high allowed intervention sets.
gloss: Specify how likely each compatible low-level implementation of a high-level intervention is.
relation: Adds uncertainty over implementation to uncertainty over contexts.

quote: MH is a probabilistic τ -αapproximate abstraction of ML if the distance between the expectations of these distributions is less than α.
formula: d_\tau^{\Pr_{\mathcal I}}(M_L,M_H)=\min_{\tau_U:\tau_{U\#}\Pr_L=\Pr_H}\max_{i_H\in\mathcal I_H}\sum_{\mathbf u_L}\Pr_L(\mathbf u_L)\sum_{i_L\in\mathcal I_L}\Pr_{\mathcal I}(i_L\mid i_H)\,d_{\mathbf V_H}\!\left(\tau(M_L(\mathbf u_L,i_L)),M_H(\tau_U(\mathbf u_L),\omega_\tau(i_L))\right).
assumptions: τ-consistent probabilistic models, a state metric, an intervention distribution and a distribution-compatible context map.
where: §4, Definition 4.8, [P45]–[P46]; quote from the Fig. 4 caption, [P45]
gloss: Average over contexts and low-level implementations, then take the worst high-level intervention.
relation: Generalizes probabilistic dτ by replacing worst-case low-level implementation with an implementation distribution.

quote: A basic causal model M is a pair (S, F ), where S is a signature and F defines a function that associates with each endogenous variable X a structural equation FX giving the value of X in terms of the values of other endogenous and exogenous variables (discussed in more detail below). A causal model M is a tuple (S, F , I), where (S, F ) is a basic causal model and I is a set of allowed interventions (also discussed in more detail below).
formula: M_{\mathrm{basic}}=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F),\quad\mathcal S=(\mathbf U,\mathbf V,\mathcal R),\quad F_X:\mathcal R(\mathbf U\cup\mathbf V\setminus\{X\})\to\mathcal R(X);\qquad M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F,\mathcal I).
