assumptions: Exogenous/endogenous variables with nonempty ranges; the paper restricts to recursive models.
gloss: Structural equations plus a specified set of interventions of interest.
relation: Basic models omit intervention restrictions; strong abstraction is formulated between basic models.

quote: Intuitively, [Y1 ← y1 , . . . , Yk ← yk ]ϕ says that ϕ would hold if Yi were set to yi , for i = 1, . . . , k.
formula: (M,\mathbf u)\models[\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y]\varphi\iff(M_{\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y},\mathbf u)\models\varphi;\qquad(M,\mathbf u)\models X=x\iff M(\mathbf u)_X=x.
assumptions: Recursive model and a fixed exogenous context; φ is a Boolean combination of primitive assignments.
gloss: A counterfactual claim is evaluated in the model modified by the proposed intervention.
relation: Provides the semantics for comparing causal outcomes and probabilistic causal models.

quote: A probabilistic causal model M = (S, F , I, Pr) is just a causal model together with a probability Pr on contexts.
formula: M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal F,\mathcal I,\Pr),\qquad\Pr^i(\mathbf v)=\Pr(\{\mathbf u:M(\mathbf u,i)=\mathbf v\}).
assumptions: A causal model and a probability distribution over exogenous-variable assignments.
gloss: A structural model whose uncertainty comes from its context distribution.
relation: Exact transformation relates probabilistic models; uniform transformation removes dependence on one particular context distribution.

quote: With this background, we can give the RW+ definition of exact transformation.
formula: \forall i\in\mathcal I_L,\qquad\Pr_H^{\omega(i)}=\tau_\#\Pr_L^i,\qquad(\tau_\#\Pr)(\mathbf v_H)=\Pr(\{\mathbf v_L:\tau(\mathbf v_L)=\mathbf v_H\}).
assumptions: Probabilistic causal models; a state map τ; an order-preserving surjection ω between allowed interventions.
gloss: Corresponding interventions produce identical distributions after low-level outcomes are translated.
relation: Definition attributed to Rubenstein et al.; weakened relative to uniform transformation and τ-abstraction.

quote: Definition 3.5: If ML and MH are deterministic causal models, ω is an order-preserving, surjective mapping ω : IL → IH , and τ : RL (VL ) → RH (VH ), then MH is a uniform (τ ω)-transformation of ML if, for all PrL , there exists PrH such that (MH , PrH ) is an exact (τ -ω)-transformation of (ML , PrL ).
formula: \forall\Pr_L\;\exists\Pr_H\;\forall i\in\mathcal I_L,\qquad\Pr_H^{\omega(i)}=\tau_\#\Pr_L^i.
assumptions: Fixed deterministic models, fixed τ, and a fixed order-preserving surjective intervention map.
gloss: The transformation must work for every low-level context distribution.
relation: Strengthens exact transformation; characterized by a compatible context map in Theorem 3.8.

quote: The next result provides a characterization of when MH is a uniform (τ -ω)-transformation of ML .
formula: \forall\mathbf u_L\in\mathcal R_L(\mathbf U_L),\ \forall i\in\mathcal I_L,\qquad\tau(M_L(\mathbf u_L,i))=M_H(\tau'(\mathbf u_L),\omega(i)).
assumptions: A proposed context map τ′ and fixed state/intervention maps.
gloss: A context map makes corresponding interventions agree pointwise in every low-level context.
relation: Existence characterizes uniform transformation; τ-abstraction additionally requires a surjective compatible map.

quote: More generally, we define below a natural way in which a mapping τ on states induces a mapping ω on allowed interventions.
formula: \operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V,\mathbf x)=\{\mathbf v\in\mathcal R(\mathbf V):\mathbf v|_{\mathbf X}=\mathbf x\};\qquad\omega_\tau(\mathbf X\leftarrow\mathbf x)=\mathbf Y\leftarrow\mathbf y\iff\tau(\operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V_L,\mathbf x))=\operatorname{Rst}(\mathbf V_H,\mathbf y).\qquad\mathcal I_L^\tau=\operatorname{Domain}(\omega_\tau),\quad\mathcal I_H^\tau=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_L^\tau).
assumptions: A state map; matching high-level restriction sets must exist, otherwise ωτ is undefined.
gloss: An intervention corresponds to the high-level restriction induced by its set of possible states.
relation: Constrains ω using τ, addressing a freedom allowed by exact and uniform transformations.

quote: Definition 3.13: (MH , IH ) is a τ -abstraction of (ML , IL ) if the following conditions hold:
formula: \tau\text{ surjective};\qquad\exists\tau_U:\mathcal R_L(\mathbf U_L)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal R_H(\mathbf U_H)\text{ compatible with }\tau;\qquad\mathcal I_H=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_L).
assumptions: Deterministic causal models; intervention correspondence induced by τ.
gloss: Require surjective state/context mappings and pointwise causal agreement under state-induced intervention correspondence.
relation: Strengthens uniform transformation; foundation for strong and constructive abstractions.

quote: We can strengthen the notion of τ -abstraction to define a relation on basic causal models, by considering the largest possible sets of allowed interventions.
formula: \mathcal I_H^\tau=\mathcal I_H^*\quad\text{and}\quad(M_H,\mathcal I_H^\tau)\text{ is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }(M_L,\mathcal I_L^\tau).
assumptions: Basic causal models; I*H contains all high-level interventions; all low-level interventions on which ωτ is defined are included.
gloss: An abstraction valid over the full induced low-level intervention set and every high-level intervention.
relation: Strengthens τ-abstraction; required by constructive τ-abstraction.

quote: Finally, we define constructive abstraction, which is the special case of strong abstraction where the mapping from lowlevel states to high-level states partitions the low-level variables and maps each cell to a unique high-level variable.
formula: M_H\text{ is a strong }\tau\text{-abstraction of }M_L;\quad\mathbf V_L=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n+1}\mathbf Z_i,\quad\mathbf Z_i\ne\varnothing\ (i\le n);\quad\tau(\mathbf v_L)=\tau_1(\mathbf v_L|_{\mathbf Z_1})\cdots\tau_n(\mathbf v_L|_{\mathbf Z_n}),\quad\tau_i:\mathcal R_L(\mathbf Z_i)\to\mathcal R_H(Y_i).
assumptions: High-level variables Y1,…,Yn; a disjoint low-level partition with a possibly empty ignored cell.
gloss: A strong abstraction in which each high-level variable has its own low-level realization cluster.
relation: Special case of strong τ-abstraction; the converse is conjectured but not proved.

quote: An SCM models reality with a collection of mechanisms and exogenous distributions.
formula: M=\langle\mathbf U,\mathbf V,\mathcal F,P(\mathbf U)\rangle,\qquad v_i\leftarrow f_{V_i}(\mathbf{pa}_{V_i},\mathbf u_{V_i}),\qquad\mathcal F:\mathcal D_{\mathbf U}\to\mathcal D_{\mathbf V}.
assumptions: Recursive mechanisms; finite discrete endogenous domains; exogenous variables may be dependent.
gloss: Structural equations and latent uncertainty jointly specify observations, interventions and counterfactuals.
relation: Semantic foundation for the Pearl Causal Hierarchy and projected abstraction.

quote: An SCM M = ⟨U, V, F, P (U)⟩ induces a family of joint distributions over V, one for each intervention x. For each Y ⊆ V:
formula: P^M(\mathbf y_{\mathbf x})=\int\mathbf1\{\mathbf Y_{\mathbf x}(\mathbf u)=\mathbf y\}\,dP(\mathbf u),\qquad\mathcal F_{\mathbf x}=\{f_V:V\notin\mathbf X\}\cup\{f_X\leftarrow x:X\in\mathbf X\}.
assumptions: An SCM; hard interventions replace the selected mechanisms.
gloss: Outcome distributions after fixing variables by intervention.
relation: Subset of Layer 3 involving one common intervention.

quote: An SCM M = ⟨U, V, F, P (U)⟩ induces a family of joint distributions over counterfactual events Y1[x1 ] , Y2[x2 ] , . . . for any Yi , Xi ⊆ V:
formula: P^M(\mathbf y_{1[\mathbf x_1]},\mathbf y_{2[\mathbf x_2]},\ldots)=\int\mathbf1\{\mathbf Y_{1[\mathbf x_1]}(\mathbf u)=\mathbf y_1,\mathbf Y_{2[\mathbf x_2]}(\mathbf u)=\mathbf y_2,\ldots\}\,dP(\mathbf u).
assumptions: The same exogenous draw is shared across all intervened submodels.
where: §1.1, Definition 2, Eq. 1, [P20]–[P27]; Appendix A.2, Definition 12, Eq. 25, [P161]–[P162]
gloss: Joint probabilities of outcomes in different hypothetical worlds for the same latent circumstances.
relation: Contains Layers 1 and 2; generalized queries extend its hard-intervention notation to soft interventions.

quote: In words, intervariable clusters group low-level variables together to form high-level variables while intravariable clusters group low-level values together to form high-level values.
formula: \mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_n\}\text{ partitions a subset of }\mathbf V;\qquad\mathcal D=\{\mathcal D_{C_i}:C_i\in\mathcal C\},\quad\mathcal D_{C_i}=\{D_{C_i}^1,\ldots,D_{C_i}^{m_i}\}\text{ partitions }\mathcal D_{C_i}^{\mathrm{domain}}.
assumptions: Variable domains; admissibility requires that no descendant outside a cluster be an ancestor of a variable inside it.
gloss: Group variables into macrovariables and group their joint values into macrovalues.
relation: Defines the partitions underlying constructive abstraction functions.

quote: A function τ : DVL → DVH is said to be a constructive abstraction function w.r.t. inter/intravariable clusters C and D iff
formula: \mathbf v_H=\tau(\mathbf v_L)=(\tau_{C_i}(\mathbf c_i):C_i\in\mathcal C),\qquad\tau_{C_i}(\mathbf c_i)=v_{H,i}^j\iff\mathbf c_i\in D_{C_i}^j.
assumptions: A bijection between clusters and high-level variables, and between each value partition's cells and that variable's high-level values.
gloss: Map each disjoint low-level cluster to its corresponding high-level variable and value.
relation: A structural property of τ; unlike constructive τ-abstraction, does not itself require causal agreement.

quote: The abstract invariance condition (AIC) states, in words, that two low-level values cannot map to the same high-level value if they have different downstream effects.
formula: \tau(\mathbf v_1)=\tau(\mathbf v_2)\Rightarrow\forall\mathbf u,\ C_i\in\mathcal C:\quad\tau_{C_i}\!\left((f_V^L(\mathbf{pa}_V^{(1)},\mathbf u_V):V\in C_i)\right)=\tau_{C_i}\!\left((f_V^L(\mathbf{pa}_V^{(2)},\mathbf u_V):V\in C_i)\right).
assumptions: A known low-level SCM and constructive abstraction function; parent assignments are taken from v1 and v2.
gloss: Merged low-level states must induce the same abstract mechanism outputs in every latent context.
relation: Required by ordinary exact abstraction; projected abstraction accommodates its violations.

quote: In words, a partial SCM projection of M over Wo is essentially a smaller version of M defined only on the variables of W ⊆ V, where each Wi ∈ W is only partially represented in the projection.
formula: M'=\langle\mathbf U\cup\mathbf W^u,\mathbf W^o,\mathcal F',P(\mathbf U')\rangle;\qquad\mathbf w_{\mathbf x}^o=M'_{[\mathbf x^o]}(\mathbf u,\mathbf x^u,\mathbf z^u),\quad\delta(\mathbf w_{\mathbf x}^o,\mathbf w_{\mathbf x}^u)=\mathbf W_{\mathbf x}(\mathbf u),\quad\delta(\mathbf x^o,\mathbf x^u)=\mathbf x,\quad\mathbf Z^u=\mathbf W^u\setminus\mathbf X^u.
assumptions: Surjective reconstruction maps δi from observed/unobserved components to each retained original variable; zᵘ is drawn from the corresponding original-world values.
where: §2.1, Proposition 1, Eq. 6, [P63]–[P69]; repeated in Appendix A.4, [P199]–[P201]
gloss: Retain coarse variable components while moving the discarded components into latent inputs.
relation: Generalizes SCM projection; projected abstraction is a partial projection of a τ-abstraction.

quote: An SCM MH is a projected abstraction of ML if and only if it is a partial SCM projection of a τ -abstraction (Beckers & Halpern, 2019, Def. 3.13) (also Def. 14 in App. A) of ML .
formula: M_H\text{ is a projected abstraction of }M_L\iff\exists M'\;[M'\text{ is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }M_L\ \land\ M_H\text{ is a partial SCM projection of }M'].
assumptions: A τ-abstraction and a partial SCM projection; choosing a particular projection additionally requires latent and intervention interpretations.
gloss: An abstraction that represents lost information through latent components rather than requiring abstract invariance.
relation: Generalizes τ-abstraction to lossy representations through partial SCM projection.

term: low-level soft intervention corresponding to a high-level intervention
quote: In words, a high-level intervention should be equivalent to a distribution over the corresponding low-level interventions that assigns probability to each possible intervention based on their prior probabilities given their parents.
formula: P(\sigma_{C_i}=\mathbf c_i)=P(\mathbf c_i\mid\tau(\mathbf c_i)=v_{H,i},\mathbf{pa}_{V_{H,i}},\mathbf u^c_{V_{H,i}}),\qquad\mathbf u^c_{V_{H,i}}=R_{\mathbf V_H^c(V_{H,i})}(\mathbf u_{C_i}).
assumptions: A low-level distribution, abstraction fibers, parent values and the confounded-neighbor response information defined in Appendix B.2. Repeated identical interventions share one sample.
gloss: Resolve an ambiguous macrointervention by sampling compatible microinterventions with context-sensitive probabilities.
relation: Provides the intervention semantics for generalized queries and the constructive projected-abstraction algorithm.

quote: Denote YL,∗ as a set of counterfactual variables over VL .
formula: \mathbf Y_{L,*}=(\mathbf Y_{L,1[\sigma_{\mathbf X_{L,1}}]},\mathbf Y_{L,2[\sigma_{\mathbf X_{L,2}}]},\ldots),\quad\mathbf Y_{H,*}=\tau(\mathbf Y_{L,*});\qquad Q=\sum_{\mathbf y_{L,*}:\tau(\mathbf y_{L,*})=\mathbf y_{H,*}}P(\mathbf Y_{L,*}=\mathbf y_{L,*}),\quad\tau(Q)=P(\mathbf Y_{H,*}=\mathbf y_{H,*}).
assumptions: Outcome/intervention variable sets are unions of clusters; corresponding low-level soft interventions are specified.
gloss: Pair a high-level counterfactual query with the aggregate low-level soft-intervention query that represents it.
relation: Extends prior abstraction query definitions from hard to soft interventions.

quote: In short, given a low level query Q (Eq. 19) and its high-level counterpart τ (Q) (Eq. 18), MH is said to be Q-τ consistent with ML if QML = τ (Q)MH .
formula: Q^{M_L}=\tau(Q)^{M_H},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\sum_{\mathbf y_{L,*}:\tau(\mathbf y_{L,*})=\mathbf y_{H,*}}P^{M_L}(\mathbf Y_{L,*}=\mathbf y_{L,*})=P^{M_H}(\mathbf Y_{H,*}=\mathbf y_{H,*}).
assumptions: SCMs, a constructive abstraction function and a specified corresponding query pair.
gloss: The two models agree on the particular causal query being abstracted.
relation: Query-specific abstraction; Li-τ consistency requires it for every corresponding query in a causal-hierarchy layer.

quote: Furthermore, if MH is Q-τ consistent with ML for all Q ∈ Li (ML ) of the form of Eq. 27, then MH is said to be Li -τ consistent with ML .
formula: \forall Q\in\mathcal L_i(M_L)\text{ of the specified corresponding-query form},\qquad Q^{M_L}=\tau(Q)^{M_H}.
assumptions: A constructive abstraction function and correspondence for all queries in the selected layer.
where: Appendix A.3, Definition 17, [P182]; main-text continuation in [P102]
gloss: All corresponding queries at a chosen causal-hierarchy layer agree.
relation: Generalizes Q-τ consistency; L3-τ consistency connects distributional abstraction with constructive τ-abstraction.

quote: Then, construct GC† = ⟨VH , E†C ⟩ as follows.
formula: E_{\mathcal C}^\dagger\leftarrow E_{\mathcal C};\quad\text{for each }X\in\mathbf V_H^\dagger:\quad\begin{cases}Z\to X\to Y&\Rightarrow\text{ add }Z\to Y,\\Z\leftrightarrow X\to Y&\Rightarrow\text{ add }Z\leftrightarrow Y\text{ and }X\leftrightarrow Y,\\Z\leftarrow X\to Y&\Rightarrow\text{ add }Z\leftrightarrow Y.\end{cases}\quad\text{Repeat to closure.}
assumptions: A cluster causal diagram and the set of AIC-violating high-level variables.
gloss: Add the directed and confounding dependencies introduced by partially projecting lossy variables.
relation: Extends the C-DAG to support counterfactual inference under AIC violations.

quote: In words, a query Q is considered τ -ID if, for any pair of models ML and MH such that both are compatible with GC† and Z, they also match in Q.
formula: \forall M_L\in\Omega_L(G_{\mathcal C}^\dagger),\ M_H\in\Omega_H(G_{\mathcal C}^\dagger),\qquad\left[M_H\text{ is }\mathcal Z\text{-}\tau\text{ consistent with }M_L\right]\Rightarrow Q^{M_L}=\tau(Q)^{M_H}.
assumptions: A projected C-DAG, constructive abstraction and available observational/interventional distributions. Definition 9 prints τ's domain/codomain in reversed order; the surrounding framework uses low-to-high τ.
gloss: Every compatible low/high model pair agreeing with available data also agrees on the target query.
relation: Theorem 3 equates this with ordinary identification of the high-level query from abstracted data.

quote: Given τ : DVL → DVH , we say that (MH , IH ) is a τ -abstraction of (ML , IL ) if:
formula: \tau\text{ surjective};\quad\exists\tau_U:\mathcal D_{\mathbf U_L}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal D_{\mathbf U_H}\ \forall\mathbf u_L,i\in\mathcal I_L:\ \tau(M_{L[i]}(\mathbf u_L))=M_{H[\omega_\tau(i)]}(\tau_U(\mathbf u_L));\quad\mathcal I_H=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_L).
assumptions: SCMs and allowed intervention sets; the paper additionally assumes P(UH)=τU#P(UL). Contexts and interventions are independently universally quantified.
gloss: A surjective state/context correspondence preserves every allowed intervention outcome.
relation: Borrowed from Beckers and Halpern; projected abstraction is a partial projection of such an abstraction.

quote: The following definitions about τ -abstractions from Beckers & Halpern (2019) set the groundwork for many discussions on abstraction theory.
formula: (M_H,\mathcal I_H)\text{ is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }(M_L,\mathcal I_L),\qquad\mathcal I_H=\mathcal I_H^*.
assumptions: I*H is the set of all high-level interventions. This is the condition as restated in this paper.
where: Appendix A.3, Definition 15, [P173]; introductory sentence in [P171]
gloss: Require the abstraction to include every high-level intervention.
relation: Borrowed from Beckers and Halpern (2019, Def. 3.15) as restated here (without requiring the induced low-level intervention set); strengthens τ-abstraction; required by constructive τ-abstraction.

quote: MH is a constructive τ -abstraction of ML if MH is a strong τ -abstraction of ML , and there exists a partition of VL , C = {C1 , C2 , . . . , Cn+1 } (where n = |VH |) with nonempty C1 to Cn , such that τ can be decomposed as τ = (τC1 , τC2 , . . . , τCn ), where each τCi : DCi → DVH,i maps the ith partition to the ith variable of VH .
formula: M_H\text{ strong }\tau\text{-abstraction of }M_L;\quad\mathbf V_L=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n+1}C_i,\ C_i\ne\varnothing\ (i\le n);\quad\tau=(\tau_{C_1},\ldots,\tau_{C_n}),\quad\tau_{C_i}:\mathcal D_{C_i}\to\mathcal D_{V_{H,i}}.
assumptions: A strong abstraction and a disjoint low-level variable partition.
gloss: A strong causal abstraction whose state map operates independently on disjoint variable clusters.
relation: Borrowed from Beckers and Halpern; distinguished from a constructive abstraction function alone.

quote: Given a causal diagram G = ⟨V, E⟩ and an admissible clustering C = {C1 , . . . , Ck } of V, construct a graph GC = ⟨C, EC ⟩ over C with a set of edges EC defined as follows:
formula: C_i\to C_j\in E_{\mathcal C}\iff\exists V_i\in C_i,V_j\in C_j:\ V_i\to V_j\in E;\qquad C_i\leftrightarrow C_j\in E_{\mathcal C}\iff\exists V_i\in C_i,V_j\in C_j:\ V_i\leftrightarrow V_j\in E.
assumptions: A low-level causal diagram and an admissible clustering.
gloss: Collapse variable clusters to nodes while retaining cross-cluster directed and confounding edges.
relation: Base graph for the partially projected C-DAG; insufficient under general AIC violations.

quote: In words, a high-level variable is an AIC violator if two of its values that have different effects on its children are clustered together (e.g., X is an AIC violator in Ex. 1).
formula: V_{H,i}\in\mathbf V_H^\dagger\iff\exists V_{H,j}:V_{H,i}\in\operatorname{Pa}_{V_{H,j}},\ \exists\mathbf u,\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2\text{ differing only on }C_i\text{ for which the AIC equality fails at }C_j.
assumptions: A low-level SCM, constructive abstraction and its clusters; the compared values witness an AIC violation.
gloss: Identify macrovariables whose merged distinctions still matter to downstream mechanisms.
relation: Localizes failures of AIC; determines which nodes trigger projected C-DAG edge additions.

quote: M′ is called an SCM projection of M over W.
formula: M'=\langle\mathbf U,\mathbf W,\mathcal F',P(\mathbf U)\rangle,\qquad\forall\mathbf u,\mathbf X\subseteq\mathbf W,\mathbf x\in\mathcal D_{\mathbf X}:\quad M_{\mathbf x}(\mathbf u)[\mathbf W]=M'_{\mathbf x}(\mathbf u).
assumptions: An SCM and a subset of retained endogenous variables; removed mechanisms are substituted into downstream mechanisms.
gloss: Remove variables while preserving all intervention outcomes on the retained variables in each context.
relation: Special case of partial SCM projection with no retained-variable information loss.

quote: A directed acyclic graph (possibly with bidirected edges) G is a Counterfactual Bayesian Network for P∗∗ if:
formula: \begin{aligned}P\!\left(\bigwedge_{W_{\mathbf{pa}_w}\in\mathbf W_*}W_{\mathbf{pa}_w}\right)&=\prod_{j=1}^\ell P\!\left(\bigwedge_{W_{\mathbf{pa}_w}\in\mathbf Z_j^*}W_{\mathbf{pa}_w}\right),\\P(Y_{\mathbf{pa}_y,\mathbf z},\mathbf W_*)&=P(Y_{\mathbf{pa}_y},\mathbf W_*),\\P(Y_{\mathbf z}=y,\mathbf X_{\mathbf z}=\mathbf x,\mathbf W_*)&=P(Y_{\mathbf z\mathbf x}=y,\mathbf X_{\mathbf z}=\mathbf x,\mathbf W_*).\end{aligned}
assumptions: The first line partitions counterfactuals by c-components; the second uses nonparents Z; the third uses X⊆PaY and Z disjoint from X∪{Y}.
gloss: A graph correctly encodes counterfactual independence, exclusion and consistency restrictions.
relation: Supplies the formal meaning of graphical sufficiency for projected C-DAGs.

quote: We say that a causal query Q is identifiable (ID) from the available data Z and the causal diagram G if Q(M1 ) = Q(M2 ) for every pair of models M1 , M2 ∈ Ω∗ such that M1 and M2 both induce G and Z(M1 ) = Z(M2 ).
formula: \forall M_1,M_2\in\Omega^*:\quad[G(M_1)=G(M_2)=G\ \land\ \mathcal Z(M_1)=\mathcal Z(M_2)]\Rightarrow Q(M_1)=Q(M_2).
assumptions: A model class on common endogenous variables, a causal diagram and available distributions.
gloss: The target query is fixed by the graph and data across all compatible models.
relation: Classical counterpart of abstract identification; Theorem 3 establishes their duality.

quote: This notation means that, during the forward computation of the DNN, the activations of the neurons in ψ are fixed to the specified values cψ , while the rest of the network operates as usual.
formula: f_N^{\psi_{L+1}}(\mathbf x,(\mathbf h_\psi\leftarrow\mathbf c_\psi)).
assumptions: Access to internal activations during computation and a specified replacement value.
gloss: Override selected activations during an otherwise ordinary forward pass.
relation: Basis for ordinary and distributed intervention correspondence.

quote: In words, an abstraction map translates the inner states of a neural network into an algorithms’ inner states.
formula: \tau:\mathcal H\to\mathcal N,\qquad\mathcal H=\prod_{\psi\in\psi_{\mathrm{int}}}\mathcal H_\psi,\qquad\mathcal N=\prod_{\eta\in\eta_{\mathrm{int}}}\mathcal V_\eta.
assumptions: A neural network and a deterministic acyclic algorithm; the defined state products exclude inputs and include outputs.
gloss: Translate complete internal network states into algorithmic states.
relation: Constructive and distributed abstraction maps impose additional structure on τ.

quote: Intuitively, ωτ maps a DNN intervention IN to an algorithmic one IA if the sets of states they induce on N and A, respectively, are the same.
formula: \omega_\tau(\mathbf h_\psi\leftarrow\mathbf c_\psi)=\begin{cases}\mathbf v_\eta\leftarrow\mathbf c_\eta,&\mathcal N_{\mathbf v_\eta=\mathbf c_\eta}=\{\tau(\mathbf h):\mathbf h\in\mathcal H_{\mathbf h_\psi=\mathbf c_\psi}\},\\\text{undefined},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
assumptions: A state abstraction map and intervention restriction sets.
gloss: Match interventions by the state restrictions they express after abstraction.
relation: Specializes Beckers and Halpern's induced intervention map to algorithms and neural networks.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: Definition 1 (from Beckers and Halpern, 2019). An algorithm A is a τ -abstraction of a neural network N iff: τ is surjective; I A = ωτ (I N ); 3 and there exists a surjective τηx such that:
formula: \tau\text{ surjective},\quad\mathcal I_A=\omega_\tau(\mathcal I_N),\quad\exists\tau_{\eta_x}\text{ surjective}\ \forall\mathbf x\in\mathcal X,I_N\in\mathcal I_N:\quad\tau(f_N^{\psi_{\mathrm{int}}}(\mathbf x,I_N))=f_A^{:\eta_{\mathrm{int}}}(\tau_{\eta_x}(\mathbf x),I_A),\quad I_A=\omega_\tau(I_N).
assumptions: Specified intervention sets; algorithm and network execution under corresponding interventions; the paper subsequently fixes input mapping to identity and output mapping to argmax.
gloss: Network states and algorithm states agree under every corresponding allowed intervention.
relation: Specializes τ-abstraction to algorithm–DNN pairs.

quote: We further say that A is a strong τ -abstraction of N if it is a τ -abstraction and I A is maximal, meaning that any intervention is allowed on algorithm A.
formula: A\text{ is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }N,\qquad\mathcal I_A=\mathcal I_A^*.
assumptions: All algorithmic interventions are admitted; neural interventions are their induced counterparts.
gloss: Require causal agreement for every intervention on the algorithm.
relation: Strengthens τ-abstraction; weakened by input-restricted τ-abstraction.

quote: In other words, constructive abstraction maps compute the value vη of each node η ∈ η int in A using non-overlapping sets of neurons ψ η from N, with set ψ⊥ being left unused.
formula: \psi_{\mathrm{int}}=\left(\bigsqcup_{\eta\in\eta_{\mathrm{int}}}\psi_\eta\right)\sqcup\psi_\bot,\quad\psi_\eta\ne\varnothing,\qquad\tau(\mathbf h)=[\tau_\eta(\mathbf h_{\psi_\eta})]_{\eta\in\eta_{\mathrm{int}}}.
assumptions: A disjoint neuron partition and per-node abstraction maps.
gloss: Decode each algorithmic variable from its own nonoverlapping neuron set.
relation: Neuron-aligned special case of distributed abstraction map.

quote: Definition 2 (from Beckers and Halpern, 2019). An algorithm A is a constructive abstraction of a neural network N iff there exists an τ : for which A is a strong τ -abstraction of N; and τ is constructive.
formula: \exists\tau:\quad A\text{ is a strong }\tau\text{-abstraction of }N\ \land\ \tau\text{ is constructive}.
assumptions: A constructive neuron partition; all algorithmic interventions; the paper's fixed input/output conventions.
gloss: A fully intervention-preserving abstraction with algorithmic variables localized to disjoint neuron sets.
relation: Special case of distributed abstraction using the identity alignment map.

quote: In words, a distributed abstraction map computes the value vη of each node η ∈ η int in A using non-overlapping partitions of latent variables ψ ϕη from N, with partition ψ⊥ϕ remaining unused.
formula: \phi(\mathbf h)=[\phi_\ell(\mathbf h_{\psi_\ell})]_\ell,\qquad\phi_\ell:\mathbb R^{|\psi_\ell|}\overset{\mathrm{bij}}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{|\psi_\ell|};\qquad\tau(\mathbf h)=[\tau_\eta(\phi(\mathbf h)_{\psi_\eta^\phi})]_{\eta\in\eta_{\mathrm{int}}}.
assumptions: Layerwise bijections respecting computational order; a partition of transformed coordinates with nonempty per-node cells and an optional unused cell.
gloss: Invertibly transform each layer, then decode algorithmic variables from separate transformed-coordinate blocks.
relation: Generalizes constructive abstraction maps beyond neuron alignment.

quote: These interventions are performed by first mapping the hidden state hψ to the latent variables hψϕ = ϕ(hψ ), intervening on a subset ψ ϕη by replacing hψϕη with desired values cψϕη , and then mapping these intervened latent variables back to the original neuron base via h′ψ = ϕ−1 (h′ψϕ ).
formula: \mathbf h'_\psi=\phi^{-1}\!\left(\operatorname{replace}_{\psi_\eta^\phi}(\phi(\mathbf h_\psi),\mathbf c_{\psi_\eta^\phi})\right).
assumptions: An invertible alignment map and a selected latent-coordinate block.
gloss: Patch activations in transformed coordinates and invert the transformation.
relation: Generalizes neuron-level intervention; operational counterpart of distributed abstraction maps.

quote: Definition 6. An algorithm A is a distributed abstraction of a neural network N iff there exists an τ : for which A is a strong τ -abstraction of N; and τ is a distributed abstraction map.
formula: \exists\tau:\quad A\text{ is a strong }\tau\text{-abstraction of }N\ \land\ \tau\text{ is a distributed abstraction map}.
assumptions: Layerwise invertible alignment, blockwise decoding and all algorithmic interventions.
gloss: A full causal abstraction expressed through distributed, invertibly transformed features.
relation: Generalizes constructive abstraction; input-restricted distributed abstraction weakens its intervention coverage.

quote: Geiger et al. (2024b) thus restrict their analyses to what we term here input-restricted interventions: the set of interventions which are themselves producible by a set of other input-restricted interventions.
formula: c_{\psi'}=f_N^{\psi'}(\mathbf x')\quad\text{or}\quad c_{\eta'}=f_A^{:\eta'}\!\left(\mathbf x',\left(v_{\eta''}\leftarrow f_A^{:\eta''}(\mathbf x'')\right)\right)\quad\text{(intervention values produced by other input-restricted computations)}
assumptions: Intervention values arise from valid inputs and recursively allowed interventions; use the maximal recursively generated intervention set.
gloss: Only patch values obtainable from actual or recursively intervened computations.
relation: Includes interchange-style interventions; excludes arbitrary values throughout the hidden-state space.

quote: This leads to the definition of input-restricted τ -abstraction: a weakened notion of strong τ -abstraction, where intervention sets are restricted to input-restricted interventions.
formula: A\text{ is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }N\text{ using maximal input-restricted }\mathcal I_A,\mathcal I_N.
assumptions: The recursively generated input-restricted intervention sets and the τ-abstraction commutation condition.
gloss: Require causal agreement only for interventions obtainable from computations on valid inputs.
relation: Weakens strong τ-abstraction; used in the main vacuity theorem.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: Definition 7 (inspired by Geiger et al., 2024b). An algorithm A is an input-restricted distributed abstraction of a neural network N iff there exists an τ : for which A is an input-restricted τ -abstraction of N; and τ is a distributed abstraction map.
formula: \exists\tau:\quad A\text{ is an input-restricted }\tau\text{-abstraction of }N\ \land\ \tau\text{ is a distributed abstraction map}.
assumptions: Layerwise bijective alignment, nonempty latent blocks, surjective abstraction, matching maximal input-restricted intervention sets and commuting executions.
where: §3.2, Definition 7, [P101]; Appendix F.2, Alternative Definition 1 and Eq. 35, [P529]–[P536]
gloss: A distributed causal interpretation validated over recursively obtainable intervention values.
relation: Main target of the vacuity theorem; restricted further by input-restricted V-abstraction.

quote: Finally, we further introduce input-restricted V-abstractions: input-restricted distributed abstractions for which we restrict alignment maps ϕ to be in a specific variational family V. The case of linear alignment maps, will be particular important here—as it relates to the linear representation hypothesis—and we will thus explicitly label it as input-restricted linear abstraction.
formula: \exists\phi\in\mathcal V\text{ witnessing input-restricted distributed abstraction};\qquad\mathcal V_{\mathrm{linear}}=\{\phi:\phi\text{ is linear}\}.
assumptions: A prescribed alignment-map family; experiments instantiate the linear family with orthogonal matrices.
gloss: Limit which transformations may witness the abstraction, with linear maps as a named special case.
relation: Restricts unrestricted distributed abstraction and makes the representation-encoding assumption explicit.

concepts: causal abstraction; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports
quote: We evaluate the effectiveness of an alignment map ϕ using the interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) metric proposed by Geiger et al. (2024b).
formula: \operatorname{IIA}(\phi)=\frac1{|\mathcal D_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_n\mathbf1\!\left[\arg\max_{y'\in\mathcal Y}p_N^\phi(y'\mid\mathbf x_\varnothing^{(n)},I_N^{(n)})=f_A(\mathbf x_\varnothing^{(n)},I_A^{(n)})\right].
assumptions: Held-out base/source/intervention examples and an algorithm supplying corresponding intervened labels.
where: §5, Evaluation Metric, [P116]; corresponding-intervention construction in §3.3, Eqs. 7–8, [P104]
gloss: How often the intervened network predicts the intervened algorithm's output.
relation: Empirical proxy for input-restricted distributed abstraction; high scores can arise even when the network lacks the original task capability.

quote: An intervention is a partial distribution I over a set of variables V ′ ⊆ V that replaces each CPD Pr(Y | PaY ; θY ) with a new CPD I(Y | Pa∗Y ; θY∗ ) for each Y ∈ V ′ .
formula: \forall Y\in\mathbf V'\subseteq\mathbf V:\quad\Pr(Y\mid\operatorname{Pa}_Y;\theta_Y)\longmapsto I(Y\mid\operatorname{Pa}^*_Y;\theta_Y^*).
assumptions: SCG mechanisms and replacement CPDs; interventions preserve Markov compatibility and the causal graph's admissible structure.
gloss: Replace selected variable mechanisms to ask how behaviour or outcomes would change.
relation: Ordinary intervention specialized by Context-Conditional Intervention; used in belief and intention tests.

quote: An agent i responds [29] to a proposition ϕ if they act differently when they observe that ϕ is i true to when they observe that ϕ is false,
formula: D^i_{\phi=\bot}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\ne D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e).
assumptions: Single-decision SCG; access to the unique observation-conditioned policy; intervene on the observation, not the proposition; proposition contains no decision descendants.
gloss: The agent changes its decision when told the proposition is true versus false.
relation: Prerequisite for Belief and Ignorance; differs from intervention on an underlying variable in Hammond et al.'s response incentive.

quote: Then, in words, for a proposition ϕ to which i responds, i believes ϕ if they act as though they observe ϕ is true.
formula: \operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\iff \bigl[D^i_{\phi=\bot}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\ne D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\bigr]\land\bigl[D^i(\pi,\mathbf e)=D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\bigr].
assumptions: As for response; policy profile and exogenous setting fixed. This operationalizes acceptance; nonresponse makes belief unidentifiable.
gloss: A responsive agent believes a proposition when its actual action matches its action after observing that proposition as true.
relation: Used by Deception and Ignorance; alternative to mental-state or credence-based belief.

quote: An agent has a true belief about ϕ if they believe ϕ and ϕ is true (similarly for a false belief).
formula: \operatorname{TrueBel}_i(\phi)=\operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi)\land\phi;\qquad \operatorname{FalseBel}_i(\phi)=\operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi)\land\neg\phi.
assumptions: Belief as in Definition 3.1 and the actual truth value of the proposition in the SCG setting.
gloss: Classifies an accepted proposition by whether it is actually true.
relation: Specializations of Belief; false belief is required for Deception and lack of true belief defines Ignorance.

quote: First, we define a context-conditional intervention which only occurs in some settings.
formula: Y_{I\mid w}(\pi,\mathbf e)=\begin{cases}Y_I(\pi,\mathbf e)&\mathbf e\in w,\\Y(\pi,\mathbf e)&\mathbf e\notin w.\end{cases}
assumptions: An intervention I, SCG, policy profile, and specified subset w of exogenous settings.
gloss: Apply an intervention only in selected exogenous circumstances.
relation: Restricts an ordinary intervention to selected settings; used by Intention and renamed Contextual Intervention in Ward et al. (2024).

quote: Informally, an agent intended to cause an outcome X = x with its policy, if guaranteeing that another policy would cause X = x would make that policy just as good for the agent.
formula: \exists\hat\pi^i\in\operatorname{REF}(\pi^i),\ \mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf X,\ (w_Y\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E))_{Y\in\mathbf Y}:\quad \mathbf e\in\bigcap_{Z\in\mathbf X}w_Z,\qquad \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_{(\hat\pi^i,\pi^{-i})}\!\left[U_{\{Y_{\pi\mid w_Y}\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}}\right],\quad \mathbf Y\text{ and every }w_Y\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: Known causal model, utilities, reference alternative policies, and contextual interventions; other agents' policies fixed. Agents share the objectively correct causal model.
gloss: The outcome helps explain choosing this policy: securing it under an alternative removes the alternative's disadvantage.
relation: Refines H&KW Intention to influence and replaces Intention to bring about; implies Actual causality; antecedent of Deception.

quote: Following Carson [15], Mahon [58], we say that an agent S deceives another agent T if S intentionally causes T to believe ϕ, where ϕ is false and S does not believe that ϕ is true.
formula: \operatorname{Dec}_{S,T}(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\iff \operatorname{IntCause}_S\!\left(D^T=D^T(\pi,\mathbf e);\pi^S,\mathbf e\right)\land \operatorname{Bel}_T(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\land\neg\phi(\pi,\mathbf e)\land\neg\operatorname{Bel}_S(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e).
assumptions: SCG and setting; intention and behavioural belief tests; correct common-prior causal model. Success is required; S need not believe the negation and may be ignorant or nonresponsive.
gloss: An agent intentionally produces another agent's false belief without itself believing that proposition.
relation: Combines Intention and Belief; excludes accidental misleading and unintended side effects; permits deception without lying.

quote: Under π, in e, for agent i and proposition ϕ to which i responds, i is ignorant about ϕ if they do not have a true belief about ϕ.
formula: \operatorname{Ign}_i(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\iff \operatorname{Respond}_i(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\land\neg\operatorname{TrueBel}_i(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e).
assumptions: Response to the proposition and knowledge of its truth value; nonresponsive agents' ignorance is not identified.
gloss: A responsive agent lacks a true belief about the proposition.
relation: Defined through True belief; distinguished from false belief and from merely concealing information.

quote: What it means for an agent to intentionally influences a variable X is that, if the effect the agent has on X was guaranteed to to happen anyway, then they would not mind choosing an alternative policy.
formula: \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf X\text{ subset-minimal}:\quad\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_{(\hat\pi^i,\pi^{-i})}[U_{\mathbf Y_\pi}].
assumptions: Utilities, fixed other-agent policies, a chosen alternative policy, and nested interventions fixing outcomes under the actual policy.
gloss: The agent prefers its policy because of its effects on a minimal collection of variables.
relation: Adaptation of Halpern–Kleiman-Weiner; variable-level precursor to Intention and prerequisite of Intention to bring about.

quote: In words, an agent i intends to bring about X = x with policy π i if 1) agent i intends to influence X with π i , 2) X = x is a possible outcome under π, 3) X = x is an optimal outcome for i under π.
formula: \operatorname{Influence}_i(\mathbf X;\pi^i,\hat\pi^i)\ \land\ \Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x)>0\ \land\ \forall\mathbf x'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf X)\text{ with }\Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x')>0:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x'}]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x}].
assumptions: SCG, utility, an alternative policy, intervention access, and positive probability of the intended outcome.
gloss: Among possible outcomes of an intentionally influenced variable, identifies utility-maximizing outcomes as intended.
relation: Adapted H&KW definition criticized and replaced by Intention; may label uninfluenceable best outcomes intentional.

quote: First we adapt the notion of actual causality to SCGs.
formula: \mathbf C(\pi,\mathbf e)=\mathbf c,\quad (M,\pi,\mathbf e)\models\phi;\qquad \exists\mathbf Z\subseteq\mathbf V,\ \mathbf c'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf C):\ \mathbf z=\mathbf Z(\pi,\mathbf e),\ (M_{\mathbf C=\mathbf c',\mathbf Z=\mathbf z},\pi,\mathbf e)\models\neg\phi;\qquad \mathbf C\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: Known SCG, fixed policy profile and exogenous setting; interventions on the proposed cause while holding contingency variables at their actual values.
gloss: An actual event is a minimal cause when changing it defeats the effect, possibly holding other events at their actual values.
relation: Adaptation of Halpern's modified actual-causality definition; Intention implies Actual causality (Theorem 3.6).

quote: An intervention is a new set of structural functions I over a set of variables 𝒀 ⊆ 𝑽 that replaces the structural function 𝑓 𝑌 with a new function I𝑌 for each 𝑌 ∈ 𝒀 , which may have a different domain, i.e., may change the parents of the variables in 𝒀 .
formula: \forall Y\in\mathbf Y\subseteq\mathbf V:\quad f^Y\longmapsto I^Y;\qquad Y_I\text{ denotes the intervened variable, and }Y_{X=x}\text{ a hard intervention}.
assumptions: SCIM structural functions and specified replacements; new parent sets must permit a well-defined causal model.
gloss: Replace selected causal functions, possibly changing their parent variables.
relation: General intervention on which Contextual Intervention and the two formal intention definitions are based.

quote: An agent intended to cause outcomes 𝒐 in setting 𝒆 with action 𝑎, if (1) There is a super-set of outcomes 𝒚 ⊇ 𝒐 and a set of settings 𝒘 ⊇ 𝒆 in which 𝒚 is caused; (2) Guaranteeing that another action 𝑎 ′ also caused 𝒚 in 𝒘 would make 𝑎 ′ just as good as 𝑎; (3) No proper subsets of 𝒚 and 𝒘 make 𝑎 ′ just as good as 𝑎.
assumptions: Random settings, alternative action, and counterfactual guarantees restricted to selected settings; minimal outcome and setting sets.
gloss: Only outcomes in circumstances essential to the reason for acting count as intended.
relation: Refines Operationalisation II by excluding coincidental outcomes; formalized by Subjective Intention.

quote: First, we define a contextual intervention which only occurs in some exogenous settings.
formula: I^Y_{\mathbf w_Y}(\mathbf{pa}_Y,\mathbf e)=\begin{cases}I^Y(\mathbf{pa}_Y)&\mathbf e\in\mathbf w_Y,\\f^Y(\mathbf{pa}_Y)&\mathbf e\notin\mathbf w_Y,\end{cases}\qquad I^Y_{\mathbf w_Y}:\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf{Pa}_Y\cup\mathbf E)\to\operatorname{dom}(Y).
assumptions: SCIM structural functions and selected exogenous settings. The intervened function may depend on every exogenous variable and make the model non-Markovian.
gloss: Apply a replacement mechanism only in chosen exogenous circumstances.
relation: Same construction as Context-Conditional Intervention in Ward et al. (2023); supports Subjective and Behavioural Intention.

quote: The agent intentionally causes the outcomes of 𝑶 in setting 𝒆 with 𝜋 if the following conditions are met.
formula: \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf O,\ W=\{\mathbf w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y},\ \hat\pi\in\operatorname{REF}(\pi):\quad \mathbf w_Y\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E),\quad \mathbf e\in\bigcap_{O\in\mathbf O}\mathbf w_O,\quad \mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right]\le\mathbb E_{\hat\pi}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{\mathbf Y_\pi\mid W}\right],\quad\mathbf Y\text{ and each }\mathbf w_Y\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: Single-decision subjective SCIM, utility function, actual policy and reference alternatives; contextual interventions. Model need not match reality.
gloss: An intended outcome belongs to a minimal collection of effects that justify the policy over an alternative.
relation: Formalizes Operationalisation III; refines H&KW Intention to influence/bring about; equivalent to Behavioural Intention under Theorem 14's conditions.

quote: Following this, we represent an adaptive agent as a policy oracle which maps interventions in a SCIM to policies [32].
formula: \Gamma:\mathcal I_M\to\Pi_M;\qquad \Gamma\text{ robustly optimal}\iff\forall I\in\mathcal I_M,\ \Gamma(I)\in\arg\max_\pi\mathbb E^{M_I}_\pi\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right].
assumptions: A set of interventions and available policies in a SCIM; utilities needed only for robust optimality, not for an arbitrary policy oracle.
gloss: Represents how an agent chooses policies as its environment changes; robust optimality requires utility maximization under every intervention.
relation: Agent representation used by Behavioural Intention; robust optimality helps equate it to Subjective Intention.

quote: The following definition is similar to Definition 6, except that we replace condition 2) with a requirement that the agent should observably change its behaviour when the intended outcomes are fixed.
formula: \pi:=\Gamma(M),\quad \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf O,\ W=\{\mathbf w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}:\ \mathbf e\in\bigcap_{O\in\mathbf O}\mathbf w_O,\quad \Gamma(M)\ne\Gamma(M_{\mathbf Y_\pi\mid W}),\quad \mathbf Y\text{ and every }\mathbf w_Y\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E)\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: Intervention access and policy oracle; no utility variables required. Interpretation as subjective intent requires robust optimality, stable causal representation, and Theorem 14's tie-breaking assumption.
gloss: If guaranteeing selected outcomes changes the agent's policy, those outcomes reveal its reasons for acting.
relation: Behavioural counterpart of Subjective Intention; equivalent under robust optimality and specified preference for the baseline policy on ties.

quote: Condition (2) does most of the work. It is a necessity condition capturing the “but-for" clause, that is, but for the fact that 𝑪 = 𝒄 occurred, 𝑶 = 𝒐 would not have occurred.
formula: \mathbf C_\pi(\mathbf e)=\mathbf c,\quad\mathbf O_\pi(\mathbf e)=\mathbf o;\qquad\exists\mathbf Z\subseteq\mathbf V,\ \mathbf c'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf C):\ \mathbf z=\mathbf Z_\pi(\mathbf e),\quad\mathbf O_{\mathbf C=\mathbf c',\mathbf Z=\mathbf z,\pi}(\mathbf e)\ne\mathbf o;\qquad\mathbf C\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: SCIM, policy and exogenous setting; interventions holding contingency variables at actual values. PDF Definition 15 prints the final comparison as ≠ O rather than ≠ o; formula makes the outcome comparison explicit.
gloss: A minimal actual event whose alteration changes the outcome under a suitable actual-valued contingency.
relation: Adaptation of Halpern's actual causality; implied by Subjective Intention in the subjective model (Theorem 7).

quote: In a SCIM M there is an ICI on 𝑂 if for all optimal 𝜋 ∗ there exists 𝑑 ∈ 𝑑𝑜𝑚(𝐷) s.t.
formula: \forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M)\ \exists d\in\operatorname{dom}(D):\quad\mathbb E_{\pi^*}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right]\ne\mathbb E_{\pi^*}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{O_{D=d}}\right].
assumptions: Single-decision SCIM; known utility, optimal policies, and nested counterfactual intervention changing only the decision's influence through O.
gloss: For every optimal policy, separately changing the decision's influence through this variable changes utility.
relation: Adapted from Everitt et al.; shares graphical criteria with Subjective Intention but quantifies over all optimal policies.

quote: The agent intends to influence 𝑿 ⊆ 𝑽 with policy 𝜋 w.r.t. alternative policy 𝜋ˆ if there exists a subset-minimal 𝒀 ⊇ 𝑿 satisfying:
formula: \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf X\text{ subset-minimal}:\quad\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E_\pi[U]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E_{\hat\pi}[U_{\mathbf Y_\pi}].
assumptions: SCIM, utility, actual and alternative policies, and counterfactual guarantees of actual-policy outcomes.
gloss: The policy's effects on a minimal collection of variables make it preferable to an alternative.
relation: Adapted H&KW criterion; coarser than Subjective Intention, which identifies specific intended outcomes and circumstances.

quote: In words, an agent intends to bring about 𝑂 = 𝑜 with policy 𝜋 if 1) the agent intends to influence 𝑂 with 𝜋, 2) 𝑂 = 𝑜 is a possible outcome under 𝜋, 3) 𝑂 = 𝑜 is an optimal outcome under 𝜋.
formula: \operatorname{Influence}_i(\mathbf X;\pi^i,\hat\pi^i)\ \land\ \Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x)>0\ \land\ \forall\mathbf x'\text{ with }\Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x')>0:\quad\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x'}]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x}].
assumptions: Adapted H&KW criterion, utility and alternative policy. Appendix Definition 18 retains multi-agent notation (π = (π^i, π^j)) despite the paper's single-agent setup; the quote is the main-text paraphrase in §5.2 (Definition 18 itself is in the cached text at [P195]).
gloss: An intentionally influenced variable takes a possible outcome that maximizes utility among its possible outcomes.
relation: Builds on Intention to influence; criticized for selecting uninfluenceable best outcomes; replaced by Subjective Intention.

quote: The simplest form of intervention, a hard intervention do(Y = y), sets the values of variables Y to some y.
formula: \Pr_{\mathbf y}(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V)=\begin{cases}1&V\in\mathbf Y,\ v\text{ consistent with }\mathbf y,\\\Pr(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V)&V\notin\mathbf Y,\ \mathbf{pa}_V\text{ consistent with }\mathbf y.\end{cases}
assumptions: Causal Bayesian network and variables to fix; inconsistent variable assignments have probability zero; conditioning on impossible parent assignments is undefined.
gloss: Force selected variables to specified values, leaving other mechanisms unchanged.
relation: Special case of Soft intervention; the action step of counterfactual evaluation.

quote: More generally, a soft intervention, specified using a partial distribution I over variables Y replaces each CPD Pr(Y | PaY ) with a new CPD I(Y | Pa∗Y ; θY∗ ) for each Y ∈ Y , where Pa∗Y may differ from PaY .3
formula: \Pr_I(\mathbf v):=\prod_{Y\in\mathbf Y}I(y\mid\mathbf{pa}^*_Y)\prod_{V\in\mathbf V\setminus\mathbf Y}\Pr(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V).
assumptions: Known causal graph and mechanisms; replacement CPDs and potentially changed parents. SCG interventions require deterministic mechanisms with any fresh randomness made exogenous.
gloss: Replace selected mechanisms, possibly changing what inputs they depend on.
relation: Generalizes Hard intervention; used in interventional and counterfactual queries.

quote: In counterfactual queries, evidence about the actual state of the world informs us about a hypothetical scenario in which some variables have been modified.
formula: \Pr(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf z)=\int_{\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E)}\Pr_I(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf e)\Pr(\mathbf e\mid\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf e.
assumptions: Markovian SCM with independent exogenous noise and deterministic endogenous functions; observation has positive probability. Formula expresses the three steps in Definition 5's following discussion.
gloss: Update hidden circumstances from actual evidence, then evaluate a hypothetical intervention in those same circumstances.
relation: SCM precursor to Counterfactual query in games (Definition 23).

quote: A causal game (CG) M = (G, θ) is a MAID such that for any parameterisation of the decision variable CPDs π, the induced model with joint distribution Prπ (V ) is a CBN.
formula: M=(G,\theta)\text{ is a CG}\iff\forall\pi,\ (G,\theta,\pi)\text{ induces a causal Bayesian network with distribution }\Pr^\pi(\mathbf V).
assumptions: MAID with decision, chance and utility variables; graph represents causal rather than merely statistical relationships.
gloss: A game whose causal interpretation remains valid after any choice of policies.
relation: Causal extension of MAIDs; generalized to counterfactual-capable Structural causal games.

quote: Our key observation is that pre-policy interventions can be modelled as interventions on the mechanism variables in the mechanised CG, which ensures that the effects are propagated through the processes via which agents select their decision rules.
assumptions: Mechanised CG; agents know pre-policy changes before selecting policies; post-policy changes occur without policy adaptation. Timing concerns available information, not chronological play.
gloss: Pre-policy changes let agents adapt their policies; post-policy changes act on the world with those policies fixed.
relation: Two cases of Interventional query and Counterfactual query in games; encoded at mechanism and object levels, respectively.

quote: As for conditional queries, in our definition (which mirrors that introduced for cyclic causal models [8], but where the cyclic dependencies are governed by relations instead of functions [1]) we quantify over the set of rational outcomes that are consistent with the given intervention.
formula: \Pr^R(\mathbf x_I):=\{\Pr^\pi(\mathbf x_I)\}_{\pi\in R(mM_I)},\qquad R^*=\{r_D^*\}_{\Pi_D\in\mathbf Y}\cup\{r_D\}_{\Pi_D\notin\mathbf Y}.
assumptions: Mechanised CG, rationality relations and intervention on object-level or mechanism variables; resulting parameter distributions and rational responses determine R(mM_I).
gloss: Return the intervention's consequences under all rational outcomes of the changed game.
relation: Generalizes causal-model interventions to adaptive agents; observation-free counterpart of Counterfactual query in games.

quote: An SCG can be seen as an SCM without parameters for the decision variables.
formula: M=(G,\theta)\text{ is a Markovian SCG}\iff\forall\dot\pi,\ \Pr^{\dot\pi}(\mathbf V,\mathbf E)\text{ is induced by a Markovian SCM}.
assumptions: A causal game with exogenous and endogenous variables; one independent exogenous parent per endogenous variable; deterministic CPDs after selecting deterministic decision rules.
gloss: Add explicit exogenous randomness so that fixing deterministic policies yields a structural causal model.
relation: Extends Causal game to counterfactuals; subsumes SCMs and single-agent SCIMs.

quote: Given a stochastic decision rule πD (D | PaD ), we may then define a canonical structural representation by setting:
formula: \Pr(E_D^{\pi_D,\mathbf{pa}_D}=d):=\pi_D(d\mid\mathbf{pa}_D),\qquad\dot\pi_D(D=d\mid\mathbf{pa}_D,\mathbf e_D):=\delta_{D,e_D^{\pi_D,\mathbf{pa}_D}},\qquad \mathbf{Pa}_D:=\operatorname{Pa}_D\setminus\{E_D\}.
assumptions: Stochastic behavioural decision rules; independent randomization across different rules and non-exogenous decision contexts; random-field exogenous variables held fixed across worlds.
where: §4.3, Decision Rules as Structural Functions, equation (3), [P258]–[P264]
gloss: Realize each stochastic choice using a separate exogenous draw indexed by policy and decision context.
relation: Makes stochastic policies usable in Structural causal games; a modeling assumption needed for Counterfactual query in games.

quote: The simplest – let us call it the simplicity principle – is to recompute the values of all decision rule variables, i.e., Π(I) = ∅.
formula: \Pi(I)=\varnothing\quad\text{for pre-policy counterfactuals};\qquad\Pi(I)=\Pi\quad\text{for fully post-policy interventions}.
assumptions: An SCG with possibly multiple rational outcomes; pre-policy intervention; do not assume preservation of actual-world equilibrium choices.
gloss: Recompute all policy choices after a pre-policy intervention.
relation: Alternative to Closest possible world principle; supplies invariance set for Definition 23.

quote: When computing counterfactuals in SCGs under the ‘closest possible world’ principle, our basic desideratum is to consider those counterfactual rational outcomes π 0 ∈ R(mMI ) that are consistent with the decision rules used in some actual rational outcome π ∈ R(mM | z) whenever those decision rules are not affected by I.
assumptions: Mechanised SCG, actual evidence, intervention, and R-relevance graph. Appendix B.1 Algorithm 1 propagates changes through maximal strongly connected components, retaining components whose rational-response sets remain unchanged.
gloss: Preserve actual-world policy information wherever the intervention leaves rational choices unaffected.
relation: Alternative to Simplicity principle; produces a larger invariant-policy set for Counterfactual query in games.

quote: Given a set of invariant decision rule variables Π(I), the answer produced by the three-step process given above can be written as follows.
formula: \Pr^R(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf z):=\left\{\int_{\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E')}\Pr^{\pi'}(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf e,\mathbf e^*)\Pr(\mathbf e^*)\Pr^\pi(\mathbf e\mid\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf e'\right\}_{(\pi,\pi')\in R(mM_I\mid\mathbf z)},\quad R(mM_I\mid\mathbf z):=\{(\pi,\pi')\in R(mM\mid\mathbf z)\times R(mM_I):\pi(I)=\pi'(I)\}.
assumptions: Mechanised SCG, rationality relations, deterministic mechanisms or canonical structural policy representation, positive-probability observation, and an explicit invariance principle. E*=E'\E captures fresh independent intervention noise.
gloss: Combine actual evidence with hypothetical changes, returning every compatible actual/counterfactual policy pair's answer.
relation: Generalizes SCM counterfactuals to adaptive multi-agent games; contains pre- and post-policy cases; depends on the chosen invariance principle.

quote: The following definition is adapted from [39], and formalises the extent to which an agent is blameworthy for causing an event.
formula: \operatorname{db}_S(d,d',\phi):=\delta_{d,d',\phi}\frac{S-\max(c^i(d')-c^i(d),0)}{S},\quad\delta_{d,d',\phi}:=\max(0,\Pr^\pi(\phi_d)-\Pr^\pi(\phi_{d'})),\quad c^i(d):=\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U]-\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_d],\quad S>\max_d c^i(d),\quad\operatorname{db}_S(d,\phi):=\max_{d'}\operatorname{db}_S(d,d',\phi).
assumptions: Known SCG, policy profile, decision and alternatives, proposition, agent utilities, and cost-sensitivity S.
gloss: Blame increases with the decision's effect on an event's probability and decreases when avoiding it would have been costly.
relation: Adapts Halpern–Kleiman-Weiner blameworthiness to SCGs; distinct from actual causation and from Intention to bring about.

quote: In the same work as above, the authors also formalise the question of whether or not an agent intends to bring about an event, which we adapt below for use with SCGs.
formula: \exists\mathbf Z\supseteq\mathbf Y\text{ subset-minimal}:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_d]\le\max_{d'\in\operatorname{alt}(d)}\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{d',\mathbf z_d}];\quad \Pr^\pi(\mathbf y_d)>0;\quad\forall\mathbf y'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf Y)\text{ with }\Pr^\pi(\mathbf y'_d)>0:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{\mathbf y'}]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{\mathbf y}].
assumptions: SCG with fixed policy profile, utilities, reference alternative decisions, and nested counterfactuals; game structure and prior are common knowledge.
gloss: Intended outcomes belong to minimally influential variables, are achievable, and maximize utility among the possible outcomes.
relation: Adapts H&KW action-level intention; related to Ward's policy-level Intention to influence and Intention to bring about.

quote: X has a response incentive (RI) if all optimal policies π ∗ respond to X, and a graph G admits a RI on X if there is a SCIM over G that has a RI on X.
formula: \operatorname{Respond}(\pi,X)\iff\exists x\in\operatorname{dom}(X),\mathbf e\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E):\Pr^\pi(D_x\mid\mathbf e)\ne\Pr^\pi(D\mid\mathbf e);\qquad\operatorname{RI}_M(X)\iff\forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M),\operatorname{Respond}(\pi^*,X).
assumptions: Single-agent, single-decision SCIM; optimal policies and intervention access while fixing exogenous context; graph admission existentially quantifies over SCIM parameterizations.
gloss: Every optimal policy must sometimes change its decision when the variable is changed.
relation: Distinct from Ward's response to an observed proposition; complements Instrumental control incentive's influence-on-the-world criterion.

quote: In a single-decision SCIM M, there is an instrumental control incentive (ICI) on a variable X in decision context paD if for all optimal policies π ∗ , there exists some d ∈ dom(D) such that:
formula: \forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M)\ \exists d\in\operatorname{dom}(D):\quad\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E^{\pi^*}[U_{X_d}\mid\mathbf{pa}_D]\ne\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E^{\pi^*}[U\mid\mathbf{pa}_D].
assumptions: Single-agent, single-decision SCIM, utility and optimal policies, specified decision context, and nested counterfactual intervention through X. Graph admission means some parameterized SCIM has such an incentive.
gloss: Changing the decision's influence through this variable changes expected utility under every optimal policy.
relation: Context-specific version of the ICI reproduced in Ward et al. (2024); shares intention's decision-to-variable-to-utility graphical pattern.

quote: In order to provide values for the decision rule variables, we introduce a set of rationality relations R = {rD }D∈D that describe assumptions about how the agents choose decision rules.
formula: mM=(m\mathcal G,\theta,R),\quad m\mathcal G=(N,\mathbf V\cup\mathbf M,m\mathcal E),\quad m\mathcal E:=\mathcal E\cup\{(M_V,V)\}_{V\in\mathbf V}\cup\mathcal E',\quad \mathcal E'\subseteq\bigcup_{D\in\mathbf D}(\mathbf M\setminus\Pi_D)\times\Pi_D,\quad r_D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf{Pa}_{\Pi_D})\times\operatorname{dom}(\Pi_D)\text{ serial};\qquad \text{e.g. }\pi_D\in r^{BR}_D(\mathbf{pa}_{\Pi_D})\iff\pi_D\in\arg\max_{\hat\pi_D\in\operatorname{dom}(\Pi_D)}\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_{(\hat\pi_D,\pi_{-D})}[U].
assumptions: A MAID with known parameters (common prior); mechanism variables Θ_V for parameters and Π_D for decision rules; rationality relations (e.g. best response) stating how each agent picks its rule given the other mechanism variables. The mechanised graph may be cyclic.
gloss: Adds a variable for each parameter and decision rule, plus relations saying how agents choose rules, so interventions can propagate into the agents' policy choices.
relation: Substrate for Pre-policy interventions and for the rational outcomes over which Interventional query and Counterfactual query in games quantify; plays the role that the policy oracle plays in Ward et al. (2024).

quote: The local explanation for model f at instance x is some relevant property of x, denoted e(x). The selected property should ideally be enough, on its own, to predict label f (x).
formula: f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y,\qquad e:\mathcal X\to\mathcal E,\qquad \text{local explanation at }x=e(x).
assumptions: Classifier and explanation function; randomized explainers may be fixed to one seed. Explanations are properties, not necessarily subsets of raw features.
gloss: A property of an instance offered as sufficient information for predicting the model's label.
relation: Framework underlying consistency, sufficiency, and intelligibility.

quote: The consistency of explainer e for model f at instance x, with respect to distribution µ, is defined as
formula: C_\pi:=\{x\in\mathcal X:e(x)=\pi\},\quad\pi=e(x),\qquad m_c(x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|C_\pi}\bigl(f(x')=f(x)\bigr).
assumptions: Classifier, explainer and deployment distribution; conditional sampling among instances receiving exactly the same explanation; conditional distribution must be defined.
gloss: How often another instance receiving this explanation has the same predicted label.
relation: One component of faithfulness; differs from Local sufficiency, which conditions on applicability rather than assignment.

quote: The global consistency of explanation system (f, e), with respect to distribution µ over X , is
formula: m_c:=\mathbb E_{x\sim\mu}[m_c(x)]=1-E_G.
assumptions: Classifier, explainer, deployment distribution, and defined local consistency almost surely.
gloss: Average label agreement among points assigned the same explanation; equivalently, Gibbs-decoder accuracy.
relation: Averages Local consistency; equals accuracy of the Gibbs decoder and bounds optimal deterministic decoding error.

quote: To start with, we say that explanations E are intelligible if for any instance x ∈ X and property π ∈ E, it is possible to assess whether π applies to x.
formula: A:\mathcal X\times\mathcal E\to\{0,1\},\qquad C_x:=\{x'\in\mathcal X:A(x',e(x))\}.
assumptions: An applicability relation based solely on the instance and explanation, independent of true or predicted label. Human checkability is desirable but not required by the definition.
gloss: One can decide whether an explanation's property holds for an instance.
relation: Required to define Local sufficiency; explicitly scoped rules supply a direct applicability relation.

quote: The local sufficiency of explainer e for model f at instance x, with respect to distribution µ, is defined as
formula: C_x:=\{x'\in\mathcal X:A(x',e(x))\},\qquad m_s(x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|C_x}\bigl(f(x')=f(x)\bigr).
assumptions: Classifier, explainer, intelligible applicability relation, and deployment distribution; defined conditional distribution over applicable instances.
gloss: How often another instance satisfying the stated property has the same predicted label.
relation: Complementary to Local consistency; equals anchor precision for anchor explanations.

quote: The global sufficiency of explanation system (f, e), with respect to distribution µ on X , is equal to ms = Ex∈µ X [ms (x)].
formula: m_s:=\mathbb E_{x\sim\mu}[m_s(x)].
assumptions: Classifier, explainer, deployment distribution and applicability relation; local sufficiency defined almost surely.
gloss: Average sufficiency of the explanations issued on the deployment distribution.
relation: Averages Local sufficiency; equals average anchor precision; need not exceed or fall below Global consistency.

quote: With this in place, there are two natural ways to define the decoder: (i) the (randomized) Gibbs decoder that, given explanation π, returns a label y with probability Pr(y|π), and (ii) the optimal deterministic decoder that returns the label y that maximizes Pr(y|π).
formula: p(y\mid\pi):=\Pr_{x\sim\mu|C_\pi}(f(x)=y),\quad d_G(\pi)\sim p(\cdot\mid\pi),\quad d_O(\pi)\in\arg\max_y p(y\mid\pi),\quad E_d:=\Pr_x(f(x)\ne d(e(x))),\quad E_O\le E_G\le2E_O.
assumptions: Distribution of predicted labels conditional on explanation; unrestricted optimal decoder, not a bounded human or learned simulator.
where: §2.1, Relation to decoding and Claim 1, [P37]–[P40]; Appendix A.1 [P166]
gloss: Recover the model's label from its explanation by conditional sampling or by the most likely label.
relation: Global consistency is exactly Gibbs-decoder accuracy; optimal deterministic decoding is within a factor of two in error.

quote: The quality of an anchor is typically formalized using the notion of precision, which is the probability, over the distribution µ, that a random instance in Hx has label f (x), that is, Prx0 ∈µ Hx [f (x0 ) = f (x)].
formula: \operatorname{precision}(H_x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|H_x}[f(x')=f(x)].
assumptions: Explicit hyperrectangle H_x containing x, classifier, and deployment distribution; conditional distribution on H_x exists.
gloss: Agreement with the target label among points inside the anchor region.
relation: Special case of Local sufficiency; mean precision equals Global sufficiency.

quote: To formalize it, we say an explanation system (f, e) has explicitly scoped rules if each explanation π is a description of a region Sπ ⊆ X of the instance space. For a given point x, the explanation π = e(x) has the property that x ∈ Sπ . The terminology “explicitly scoped” means that subset Sπ is specified in a form where it is easy to check whether a specific point lies in it or not.
formula: \pi=e(x)\implies x\in S_\pi\subseteq\mathcal X,\qquad A(x,\pi)\iff x\in S_\pi.
assumptions: Explanation supplies an explicit region with easy membership checks and contains its explained instance.
gloss: Each explanation declares a region of inputs, and membership can be checked directly.
relation: A subclass of Intelligible explanations; includes decision-tree paths, anchors, and highlighted text.

quote: In this case, the “explanation” x0 gives information about the nature of predictions in the vicinity of x. Specifically, it asserts that any point in the open ball B(x, d(x, x0 )) has label f (x).
formula: x'\in\arg\min_{z:f(z)\ne f(x)}d(x,z).
assumptions: Classifier, input metric, and existence of a nearest oppositely classified instance; closest-point formulation specializes to binary classification.
gloss: A nearby input with a different model prediction, concretized as the nearest such input.
relation: Can be converted to an explicitly scoped open-ball rule and assessed using sufficiency; unlike SCM counterfactuals, no causal mechanism is required.

quote: This generalizes both types of faithfulness: for consistency, take R(x, π) to mean e(x) = π and for sufficiency take R(x, π) ≡ A(x, π).
formula: m_\mu^R:=\Pr_{X,X'\sim\mu}\bigl(f(X')=f(X)\mid R(X',e(X))\bigr).
assumptions: Classifier, explainer, relation R and deployment distribution. This is the main-text printed formula; Appendix A.2 instead writes E_X[q(f(X)|e(X))], matching the intended average of local conditional scores. The two sampling orders are not generally identical.
gloss: Use one relation-based agreement criterion to express both consistency and sufficiency.
relation: Generalizes the two faithfulness components; target of the global estimator, subject to the printed conditioning ambiguity.

quote: Our estimator for mR µ is then
formula: \widehat M:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{N_{e(x_i)}>1\}\frac{N_{e(x_i),f(x_i)}-1}{N_{e(x_i)}-1},\quad N_\pi:=|\{i:R(x_i,\pi)\}|,\quad N_{\pi,y}:=|\{i:R(x_i,\pi),f(x_i)=y\}|.
assumptions: Independent unlabeled samples from the deployment distribution plus queries to f and e; countable explanation space; computable R with self-applicability. Terms with no other matching point contribute zero.
gloss: Average leave-one-out label agreement among examples sharing an explanation or satisfying its property.
relation: Estimates the average local version of Generic faithfulness; specializes to Global consistency or Global sufficiency.

quote: To estimate consistency it returns the fraction of instances with similar label out of all instances with similar explanation. To estimate sufficiency, it returns the fraction of instances with similar label out of all examples that e(x) applied to.
formula: \widehat m_c(x)=\frac{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{e(x')=e(x),\,f(x')=f(x)\}}{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{e(x')=e(x)\}},\qquad \widehat m_s(x)=\frac{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{A(x',e(x)),\,f(x')=f(x)\}}{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{A(x',e(x))\}}.
assumptions: Sample S from µ and positive denominators. These are the fractions specified in the prose and counters; the PDF algorithm's last line mistakenly returns sufcounter/sufcounter rather than sufcounter/suftot.
gloss: Estimate each local score by the matching-label fraction among its relevant sampled inputs.
relation: Empirical counterparts of Local consistency and Local sufficiency; conditional sampling gives the stated Hoeffding sample bound.

quote: Let ϕ represent a propositional formula, and let τA,B represent a term. τA,B is a prime implicant of ϕ if,
formula: \tau_{A,B}\models\phi,\qquad\forall\tau_{C,D}:\ (\tau_{A,B}\models\tau_{C,D}\land\tau_{A,B}\not\equiv\tau_{C,D})\implies\tau_{C,D}\not\models\phi.
assumptions: Propositional formula and consistent conjunctions of literals; a weaker term deletes literals. The first condition alone defines an implicant.
gloss: A sufficient conjunction of facts from which no literal can be removed without losing sufficiency.
relation: Logical basis of Abductive explanations and Global abductive explanations; distinct from Prime implicate.

quote: For completeness, we also mention prime implicates. Let ϕ be a propositional formula, and let ωA,B be a clause. ωA,B is a prime implicate of ϕ if,
formula: \phi\models\omega_{A,B},\qquad\forall\omega_{C,D}:\ (\omega_{C,D}\models\omega_{A,B}\land\omega_{A,B}\not\equiv\omega_{C,D})\implies\phi\not\models\omega_{C,D}.
assumptions: Propositional formula and clauses. PDF condition 2 ends with τ_C,D rather than ω_C,D, an apparent symbol typo; formula states the clause-minimality condition described by the definition.
gloss: A necessary clause implied by the formula that cannot be strengthened by removing a literal.
relation: Dual to Prime implicant through minimal hitting sets; negated prime implicates define Counterexamples, not local Contrastive explanations.

quote: Informally, an MUS provides some irreducible information that suffices to be added to the background knowledge B to attain an inconsistent formula; thus, an MUS represents an explanation for the causes of inconsistency.
formula: \phi=\mathcal B\cup\mathcal S\models\bot,\quad\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal S,\quad\mathcal B\cup\mathcal M\models\bot,\quad\forall\mathcal M'\subsetneq\mathcal M,\ \mathcal B\cup\mathcal M'\not\models\bot.
assumptions: Consistent hard background constraints B; removable soft constraints S with B∪S inconsistent; sound and complete satisfiability reasoning.
gloss: An irreducible subset of soft constraints that conflicts with the fixed background.
relation: AXp computation reduces to MUS extraction; MUSes are minimal hitting sets of MCSes.

quote: Alternatively, one might be interested in correcting the formula, removing some clauses to achieve consistency.
formula: \mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S,\quad\mathcal B\cup(\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal C)\not\models\bot,\quad\forall\mathcal C'\subsetneq\mathcal C,\ \mathcal B\cup(\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal C')\models\bot.
assumptions: Hard background B and removable soft constraints S forming an inconsistent theory.
gloss: An irreducible set of constraints whose removal makes the theory consistent.
relation: CXp computation reduces to MCS extraction; dual to MUSes and complementary to MSSes.

quote: Logic-based abduction can be viewed as the problem of finding a (minimimum or minimal) subset of hypotheses, which is consistent with some background theory, and such that those hypotheses are sufficient for some manifestation.
formula: \mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal H,\qquad\mathcal T\land\mathcal E\models\mathcal M,\qquad\mathcal T\land\mathcal E\not\models\bot.
assumptions: PAP=(X,H,M,T,ς): finite atoms, hypothesis clauses, manifestations, background theory, and nonnegative hypothesis costs. Minimum-cost or subset-minimal solutions may additionally be requested.
gloss: A consistent collection of hypotheses that entails the observations to be explained.
relation: General abduction framework instantiated by AXp's; prime-implicant computation is also an abduction instance.

quote: Thus, given an instance (v, c), a (weak) AXp is a subset of features which, if fixed to the values dictated by v, then the prediction is guaranteed to be c, independently of the values assigned to the other features.
formula: \operatorname{WeakAXp}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c).
assumptions: Known classifier, target instance with c=κ(v), and feature space; all unselected-feature combinations are allowed unless input constraints are explicitly added.
gloss: Fixing the selected features guarantees the original prediction for every completion of the remaining features.
relation: Sufficiency criterion underlying AXp; generalized by WeakPAXp, input-constraint-aware AXp, and WeakLAXp.

quote: Moreover, X ⊆ F is an AXp if, besides being a weak AXp, it is also subsetminimal, i.e.
formula: \operatorname{AXp}(X):=\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X');\qquad\operatorname{AXp}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X)\land\forall t\in X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X\setminus\{t\}).
assumptions: Weak AXp setup; subset minimality, not necessarily smallest cardinality. Monotonicity makes checking single-feature deletions sufficient.
gloss: An irreducible set of feature values sufficient to guarantee the prediction.
relation: Boolean case equals PI-explanation; local prime implicant; minimal hitting-set dual of CXp; obtainable via MUS extraction.

quote: Thus, given an instance (v, c), a (weak) CXp is a subset of features which, if allowed to take any value from their domain, then there is an assignment to the features that changes the prediction to a class other than c, this while the features not in the explanation are kept to their values (ceteris paribus).
formula: \operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y):=\exists\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\notin Y}(x_i=v_i)\right]\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c).
assumptions: Known classifier and target instance; selected features may vary over their domains, all other features fixed.
gloss: Changing only the selected features can produce a different prediction.
relation: Existential counterpart of Weak AXp and precursor to CXp; a feature-set counterfactual rather than an SCM intervention.

quote: Furthermore, a set Y ⊆ F is a CXp if, besides being a weak CXp, it is also subset-minimal, i.e.
formula: \operatorname{CXp}(Y):=\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y)\land\forall Y'\subsetneq Y,\neg\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y');\qquad\operatorname{CXp}(Y)\iff\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y)\land\forall t\in Y,\neg\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y\setminus\{t\}).
assumptions: Weak CXp setup and subset-minimality; monotonicity permits single-feature deletion tests.
gloss: An irreducible set of features that can be changed to change the prediction.
relation: Minimal hitting-set dual of AXp; reducible to MCS extraction; not a prime implicate or global Counterexample.

quote: The set of literals of π is a global abductive explanation of the prediction c.
formula: \pi\text{ is a prime implicant of }[\kappa(\mathbf x)=c],\qquad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \pi(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c).
assumptions: Known classifier and target class; a consistent term of feature literals, irreducible under literal deletion; no fixed target instance.
gloss: A minimal sufficient rule guaranteeing a class across all inputs satisfying the rule.
relation: Global counterpart of AXp; corresponds to a prime implicant and is incompatible with every Counterexample for that class.

quote: The set of literals in η is referred to as a counterexample (CEx) for the prediction c, and represents the negation of a prime implicate for the predicate [κ(x) = c]. Clearly, both global AXp’s and CEx’s are irreducible (and so subset-minimal).
formula: \neg\eta\text{ is a prime implicate of }[\kappa(\mathbf x)=c];\qquad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \eta(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf v)\ne c).
assumptions: Classifier and target class; η is a term. Displayed formula preserves the PDF's κ(v); its prose and prime-implicate definition instead require κ(x), an apparent variable typo.
gloss: A minimal conjunction ruling out the target class, expressed as a negated prime implicate.
relation: Global, class-level alternative to local CXp; every CEx breaks every Global AXp.

quote: A conflict set is a (subset)-minimal set CS of Comp such that,
