formula: \mathrm{SD}\cup\{\neg\mathrm{Ab}(C_i):C_i\in\mathrm{CS}\}\cup\mathrm{Obs}\models\bot,\qquad\mathrm{CS}\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: System description, components, abnormality predicate and observation; retaining assumptions that these components operate normally yields inconsistency.
gloss: A minimal collection of components whose normal-operation assumptions conflict with the observation.
relation: Model-based-diagnosis counterpart of MUS; the paper's classifier reduction maps minimal conflicts to AXp's.

quote: A diagnosis is a subset-minimal set ∆ of Comp such that,
formula: \mathrm{SD}\cup\{\neg\mathrm{Ab}(C_i):C_i\in\mathrm{Comp}\setminus\Delta\}\cup\mathrm{Obs}\not\models\bot,\qquad\Delta\text{ subset-minimal}.
assumptions: System description, components, abnormality predicate, observation, and a consistency checker.
gloss: A minimal set of components whose normal-operation assumptions must be relaxed to explain the observation consistently.
relation: Model-based-diagnosis counterpart of MCS; the paper's classifier reduction maps minimal diagnoses to CXp's.

quote: Second, for computing one AXp, the predicate to consider is:
formula: P_{\mathrm{axp}}(S;\mathcal T,F,\kappa,\mathbf v):=\neg\operatorname{CO}\!\left(\llbracket\left(\bigwedge_{i\in S}x_i=v_i\right)\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c)\rrbracket_{\mathcal T}\right).
assumptions: Faithful logic encoding of classifier and feature domains; sound, complete theory consistency oracle; c=κ(v).
gloss: Test whether fixing selected features makes a changed prediction impossible.
relation: Executable oracle criterion equivalent to Weak AXp; used by deletion-based AXp computation.

quote: and for computing one CXp, the predicate to consider is:
formula: P_{\mathrm{cxp}}(S;\mathcal T,F,\kappa,\mathbf v):=\operatorname{CO}\!\left(\llbracket\left(\bigwedge_{i\in F\setminus S}x_i=v_i\right)\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c)\rrbracket_{\mathcal T}\right).
assumptions: Faithful classifier encoding, feature domains, and sound, complete consistency oracle; c=κ(v).
gloss: Test whether changing only selected features permits a changed prediction.
relation: Executable criterion equivalent to Weak CXp; dual use of the same consistency oracle as Paxp.

quote: The problem of deciding whether a given (possibly sensitive) feature is included in some explanation is referred to as the feature membership problem (FMP) [166].
formula: \exists X\subseteq F:\ t\in X\land\operatorname{AXp}(X),\qquad\text{equivalently }\exists Y\subseteq F:\ t\in Y\land\operatorname{CXp}(Y).
assumptions: Local explanation problem and target feature; access to classifier representation or relevant reasoning oracle.
gloss: Determine whether a feature appears in any minimal explanation of this prediction.
relation: Equivalent for AXp and CXp by duality; related to relevance in propositional abduction.

quote: A probabilistic (weak) AXp generalizes the definition of weak AXp, by allowing the prediction to change in some points of feature space, where a weak AXp would require the prediction not to change, but such that those changes have small probability.
formula: \operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X;\mathbb F,\kappa,\mathbf v,c,\delta):=\Pr_{\mathbf x}\bigl(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c\mid\mathbf x_X=\mathbf v_X\bigr)\ge\delta,\qquad0<\delta\le1.
assumptions: Known classifier and input distribution; finite categorical/ordinal feature domains and positive-probability conditioning event. Presented computations use uniform feature-space sampling; δ=1 recovers universal sufficiency under full support.
gloss: Fixing selected features makes the original label sufficiently likely rather than guaranteed.
relation: Probabilistic generalization of Weak AXp; also called a relevant set; basis for PAXp.

quote: Similarly to the deterministic case, a PAXp is a subset-minimal weak AXp.
formula: \operatorname{PAXp}(X):=\operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X').
assumptions: WeakPAXp setup and threshold δ. Quoted sentence literally says 'weak AXp'; context refers to the probabilistic predicate in equation (28). Probabilistic sufficiency need not be monotone, so full subset-minimality matters.
gloss: An irreducible feature set meeting the probabilistic sufficiency threshold.
relation: Probabilistic counterpart of AXp; unlike universal AXp, checking only single-feature deletions does not generally prove minimality.

quote: Let us assume that a given classifier C is characterized by a constraint set IC capturing the allowed points in feature space.
formula: \operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to\left[IC(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c)\right];\qquad \operatorname{AXp}_{IC}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X').
assumptions: Classifier, instance and known or learned valid-input predicate IC, normally with IC(v)=1; guarantees are relative to that constraint set.
gloss: Require the selected feature values to guarantee the prediction only on permitted inputs.
relation: Generalizes Weak AXp/AXp to restricted feature spaces; preserves AXp/CXp duality.

quote: Similarly, the definition of weak CXp can be adapted to account for IC ,
formula:
\operatorname{WeakCXp}_{IC}(Y):=\exists\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[ igwedge_{i
otin Y}(x_i=v_i)ight]\land IC(\mathbf x)\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)
e c);\qquad\operatorname{CXp}_{IC}(Y)\iff\operatorname{WeakCXp}_{IC}(Y)\land orall Y'\subsetneq Y,
eg\operatorname{WeakCXp}_{IC}(Y').
assumptions: Classifier, target instance, and valid-input constraints; counterfactual witness must satisfy IC.
gloss: A changed prediction must be achievable by a permitted input while keeping unselected features fixed.
relation: Constraint-relative version of Weak CXp/CXp; dual to constraint-aware AXp.

quote: Given the definition of Hamming distance, we can now propose a definition of localized weak abductive and contrastive explanations.
formula: \operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[D_h(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)\le\epsilon\land\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c);\qquad\operatorname{LAXp}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X)\land\forall t\in X,\neg\operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X\setminus\{t\}).
assumptions: Classifier, instance, locality radius ε>0 and a chosen distance. The printed D_h (eq. 36) sums ITE(x_{1i}=x_{2i},1,0), i.e. counts equal coordinates, an apparent typo for standard Hamming distance; the text permits other distance measures.
gloss: Selected features guarantee the prediction within a specified neighborhood; minimal versions remove unnecessary features.
relation: Locality-restricted Weak AXp/AXp; uses the same single-deletion minimality criterion.

quote: The definitions of subset-minimal sets remain unchanged, i.e. localized AXp’s and CXp’s can be computed using (8) and (9), by replacing WeakAXp and WeakAXp, respectively by WeakLAXp and WeakLCXp.
formula:
\operatorname{WeakLCXp}(Y):=\exists\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[D_h(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)\le\epsilon\land igwedge_{i
otin Y}(x_i=v_i)ight]\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)
e c);\qquad\operatorname{LCXp}(Y)\iff\operatorname{WeakLCXp}(Y)\land orall t\in Y,
eg\operatorname{WeakLCXp}(Y\setminus\{t\}).
assumptions: Classifier, instance and ε>0; a different-label witness in the neighborhood. The printed D_h counts equal coordinates; quoted replacement sentence repeats WeakAXp where its second occurrence evidently means WeakCXp.
gloss: Changing selected features can produce a nearby input with a different prediction; minimal versions remove unnecessary changes.
relation: Locality-restricted Weak CXp/CXp; counterpart to Localized abductive explanation.

quote: Definition C.4 (Generalised Decoder Family). Let D = {d : Z ∪ {∅} → C} be the space of all decoders, with some output space C.
formula: \mathcal D=\{d:\mathcal Z\cup\{\varnothing\}\to\mathcal C\};\ \mathcal V\subseteq\mathcal D\ \text{is a generalised decoder family iff}\ \forall d\in\mathcal V,\ \forall c\in\mathrm{range}(d)\subseteq\mathcal C,\ \exists d'\in\mathcal V\ \text{s.t.}\ \forall z\in\mathcal Z,\ d'[z]=d'[\varnothing]=c
assumptions: An arbitrary output space C; decoders presumed capacity- and compute-constrained; optional ignorance (any output can be produced while ignoring Z). In the main text decoders map X^aud × (Z ∪ ∅) → C.
gloss: The set of decision rules an agent can use, mapping available information to any kind of output, closed under ignoring the extra signal.
relation: Generalises the predictive family of Xu et al. (2020) (Definition C.1) from predictive distributions to arbitrary outputs.

quote: Intuitively, a predictive family represents the set of models available to an agent, for instance due to architectural, computational, or statistical constraints.
formula: \Omega=\{f:\mathcal Z\cup\{\varnothing\}\to\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\};\ \mathcal V\subseteq\Omega\ \text{s.t.}\ \forall f\in\mathcal V,\ \forall P\in\mathrm{range}(f),\ \exists f'\in\mathcal V\ \text{s.t.}\ \forall z\in\mathcal Z,\ f'[z]=f'[\varnothing]=P
assumptions: Predictors output probability measures over Y; optional ignorance.
gloss: A restricted class of probabilistic predictors available to an agent, which must be able to ignore side information when it chooses to.
relation: Restates Xu et al. (2020), Definition 1; special case of the generalised decoder family (Definition C.4) with C = P(Y).

quote: Predictive V-entropy is the minimal expected negative log-likelihood achievable when predicting Y , either with access to side information Z or without it, under the restriction that predictors must belong to the predictive family V.
formula: H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid Z)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{Y,Z}\big[-\log f[Z](Y)\big],\quad H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{Y}\big[-\log f[\varnothing](Y)\big];\ \text{main text: } H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X)=\inf_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{X,Y}[-\log d[X](Y)],\ H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X,Z)=\inf_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{X,Y,Z}[-\log d[X,Z](Y)]
assumptions: A predictive family V satisfying optional ignorance; densities or mass functions; log loss.
where: Definition C.2, App. C.1, [P483]-[P488]; Eqs. (1)-(2), Section 3.2, [P73]
gloss: The lowest average log-loss for predicting Y that models in the allowed family can reach, with or without the extra signal.
relation: Restates Xu et al. (2020), Definition 2; equals Shannon (conditional) entropy when V = Omega; special case of generalised V-utility (Definition C.5) with u(y,q) = log q(y), up to sign.

quote: Predictive V-information quantifies how much observing Z improves the best achievable predictive performance on Y within the family V.
formula: I_{\mathcal V}(Z\to Y)=H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)-H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid Z);\quad I_{\mathcal V}(Z\to Y\mid X)=H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X)-H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X,Z)
assumptions: A predictive family satisfying optional ignorance.
where: Definition C.3, App. C.1, [P488]-[P490]; Eq. (3), Section 3.2, [P78], [P81]
gloss: How much seeing Z lowers the best achievable log-loss on Y for a constrained family of predictors; it measures usable rather than total information.
relation: Restates Xu et al. (2020), Definition 3, with a conditional version (Eq. 3); recovers Shannon mutual information when V = Omega; special case of generalised V-information (Definition C.6).

quote: Generalised V-utility represents the best achievable expected task utility under u, either with or without access to side information Z, when the decision maker is restricted to decoders in V.
formula: U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid Z)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{Y,Z}\big[u(Y,d[Z])\big],\quad U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{Y}\big[u(Y,d[\varnothing])\big]
assumptions: A utility function u: Y × C → R and a generalised decoder family V.
where: Definition C.5, App. C.2, [P497]-[P498]; Eqs. (4)-(5), Section 3.3, [P85]
gloss: The highest expected task score a constrained decision maker can obtain, with or without the extra signal.
relation: Strictly generalises predictive V-entropy: with C = P(Y), D = Omega and u(y,q) = log q(y) it reduces to it.

quote: Generalised V-information quantifies the extent to which access to side information Z improves achievable task performance on Y , relative to a constrained decision maker.
formula: I^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Z\to Y)=U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid Z)-U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)
assumptions: A decoder space D, a utility u: Y × C → R and a generalised decoder family V with optional ignorance (needed for non-negativity and zero value under independence).
where: Definition C.6, App. C.2, [P498]-[P499], [P504]; properties in C.2.1, [P506]-[P515]
gloss: The gain in best achievable task utility from observing Z, for decoders in V. Z can be rich in Shannon information yet have zero value if no decoder can exploit it.
relation: Generalises predictive V-information (log-loss utility) to arbitrary utilities, e.g. accuracy; follows the utilitarian information view of Zhao et al. (2021) and Ermon (2022).

quote: The generalised V-information (GVI) is then the gain in utility achievable by the best decoders in V by additionally observing Z:
formula: I^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Z\to Y\mid X)=U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X,Z)-U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X),\quad U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X,Z)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E\big[u(Y,d[X,Z])\big],\ U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E\big[u(Y,d[X])\big]
assumptions: Decoders d: X × (Z ∪ {∅}) → C, with d[X] shorthand for d[X, ∅]; a utility u; optional ignorance.
where: Eq. (6), Section 3.3, [P86], [P88]; Definition C.7, App. C.2, [P500]-[P504]
gloss: The extra task utility the best decoder in V gains from seeing Z on top of the input X. With accuracy utility it is the accuracy increase attributable to Z.
relation: Conditional version of Definition C.6, generalising conditional mutual information; the building block of Receiver- and Sentinel-usable information.

concepts: usable information; steganography and encoded reasoning
quote: The Receiver-usable information of Z quantifies the utility gain (under u) that the best decoder in Receiver’s decoding class Vrec can obtain from observing Z, relative to decoding from X alone.
formula: I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)=I^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Z\to Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}})=U^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z)-U^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}}),\quad I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\to Y)=I^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{sen}}}(Z\to Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}})
assumptions: An auditing task (X^aud, u, Y) chosen by the Auditor; decoder families V_rec (knows the encoding) and V_sen (trusted, comparable capability, no knowledge of the encoding); Z ~ P_S(Z | X^gen).
gloss: How much the signal improves the best achievable score on the auditing task for the Receiver's decoders, and, analogously, for the trusted Sentinel's.
relation: Instances of conditional GVI (Eq. 6) for the two decoder families; their difference is the steganographic gap.

quote: The steganographic gap is then defined as ∆steg (Z) = Irec (Z → Y ) − Isen (Z → Y ).
formula: \Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)=I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)-I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\to Y)
assumptions: Auditing task (Y, u) and context X^aud; Receiver and Sentinel decoder families; Sentinel of matched public capability (Assumption E.3) for a positive gap to indicate hidden content; utilities estimated by eliciting best performance.
gloss: How much more usable information a signal gives the Receiver than a trusted Sentinel on an auditing task; it is measured in the utility's units.
relation: Built on GVI; generalises Cachin's ε-security, recovered when the auditing task is binary detection with an omnipotent Sentinel (Proposition D.1); alternative to distributional indistinguishability (Cachin 2004; Hopper et al. 2002).

quote: To avoid this confusion related to units, we define and use normalised steganographic gap which is dimensionless and has a maximum value of 1, making it easier to interpret.
formula: \tilde\Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)}{I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)}=1-\frac{I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\to Y)}{I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)}
assumptions: I_rec(Z → Y) > 0 (the signal must help the Receiver, e.g. tasks with CoT uplift).
gloss: The steganographic gap divided by the Receiver's gain: the fraction of the signal's usable information that the Receiver can use but the Sentinel cannot. It is at most 1.
relation: Rescaling of the steganographic gap; equals 1 − TV(P0, P1) in the classical special case (Proposition D.1).

quote: In this framework, signal Z is steganographic if it induces a positive steganographic gap, which indicates that there is some information encoded in Z that is operationally accessible to Vrec but comparatively inaccessible to Vsen for the objective (Y, u).
formula: Z\ \text{is steganographic w.r.t.}\ (\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}},\mathcal V_{\mathrm{sen}},Y,u,X^{\mathrm{aud}})\iff\Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)>0
assumptions: Sentinel-relative and task-relative; needs interceptable and replayable signals, recoverable actions and effects within the auditing horizon (Section 4.4).
gloss: A signal counts as steganographic when decoders that know the encoding can exploit it for the chosen task better than a comparable trusted Sentinel can.
relation: Alternative to the classical definition (indistinguishability from a cover distribution, Cachin 2004); unlike it, needs no cover distribution and can flag perfectly secure schemes, but ignores payloads irrelevant to the task.

quote: Cachin (2004) defines a steganographic system to be ε-secure if the Kullback-Leibler divergence between these distributions is bounded: DKL (P1 ∥P0 ) ≤ ε.
formula: D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\,\|\,P_0)\le\varepsilon;\quad \text{perfectly secure if } \varepsilon=0\ (P_1=P_0)
assumptions: Known covertext distribution P0 and stegotext distribution P1; a passive Auditor (warden) distinguishing them.
gloss: A stegosystem is ε-secure when the KL divergence between stegotext and covertext distributions is at most ε; zero divergence makes the two indistinguishable by any test.
relation: Borrowed from Cachin (2004); Proposition D.1 recovers it as a special case of the normalised steganographic gap (binary detection, uniform prior, omnipotent Sentinel): normalised gap = 1 − TV ≥ 1 − sqrt(ε/2).

concepts: usable information; steganography and encoded reasoning
quote: Our decision-theoretic framework takes a fundamentally different stance: instead of asking whether Z contains hidden information in the abstract, it asks whether Z contains hidden information that is consequential.
formula: I^{u^\star}_{\mathcal V}(Z\to Y^\star\mid O)>0
assumptions: A decision problem (Y*, u*), a decoder family V and an observed context O; Z ⊥ Y* | O suffices for no consequential information (Lemma E.4).
gloss: A signal carries consequential information for a decision problem if seeing it raises the best achievable utility beyond what the observed context already allows.
relation: Positive conditional GVI; marks the scope of the steganographic gap, which is blind to inert payloads (e.g. watermarks) that classical security would flag.

quote: Definition E.2 (Composite Signal). Let X gen ∈ X gen be the generation context, S ∈ S a payload to be embedded, k ∈ K a shared key known to Sender and Receiver, and ξ an independent source of randomness.
formula: Z=G(X^{\mathrm{gen}},S,k,\xi);\quad \text{in proofs } Z=(Z_0,\mathrm{Enc}(S,k)),\ Z_0=G_0(X^{\mathrm{gen}},\xi)
assumptions: Sender's generation process G; payload S; shared key k; cipher Enc with Shannon perfect secrecy in the incompleteness constructions.
gloss: A signal that is both a legitimate information source (the public reasoning) and a covert channel carrying a keyed payload.
relation: Setting for the incompleteness results (Theorems E.6-E.7) under Matched Public Capability (Assumption E.3).

quote: The evasion-compatible payload set shrinks monotonically as the auditing family grows:
formula: \mathcal E(\mathcal F)=\{S:\ \Delta^{(Y_k,u_k)}(Z;X^{\mathrm{aud}})=0\ \ \forall (Y_k,u_k)\in\mathcal F\};\quad \mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2\Rightarrow\mathcal E(\mathcal F_2)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal F_1)
assumptions: A finite family F of auditing tasks; composite signals Z = (Z0, Enc(S, k)).
gloss: The payloads that produce a zero steganographic gap on every auditing task in a family; adding tasks can only shrink this set.
relation: Complements Corollary E.8 (evasion requires the payload to carry no consequential information about any audited task) and Theorem E.7 (finite-family incompleteness).

concepts: steganography and encoded reasoning; usable information
quote: Hence, in practice we estimate Igen (Z → Y ) and Iaud (Z → Y ) from a finite evaluation set by replacing expectations with empirical averages.
formula: \hat U^{u}(d;X^{\mathrm{aud}})=\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}u\big(y_i,d[x_i^{\mathrm{aud}}]\big),\ \hat U^{u}(d;X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z)=\tfrac{1}{n n_z}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n_z}u\big(y_i,d[x_i^{\mathrm{aud}},z_{i,j}]\big);\ \hat U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}})=\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\hat U^{u}(d;X^{\mathrm{aud}}),\ \hat U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z)=\max\big(\sup_{d\in\mathcal V}\hat U^{u}(d;X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z),\ \hat U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}})\big);\ \hat I^{u}_{\mathcal V}=\hat U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z)-\hat U^{u}_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}});\ \hat\Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}=\hat I^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}}}-\hat I^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{sen}}}
assumptions: n tasks, n_z sampled traces per task, n_y decoder samples; prompts p^{x-only} and p^{xz}; suprema approximated by prompting; max with the no-Z utility enforces optional ignorance.
gloss: Plug-in estimate: average task utility with and without the trace for Receiver and Sentinel, take the best decoder, and subtract the two gains.
relation: Finite-sample estimator of the steganographic gap (Eq. 8); the max step enforces the non-negativity that optional ignorance guarantees in the population definition.

quote: If both distilled models achieve comparable performance on held-out problems, the encoding—if any existed—was not load-bearing.
assumptions: A paraphraser that removes any encoding while preserving content; the capability is absent from the base model and acquired in RL; distillation of the base model on original vs. paraphrased traces.
gloss: Fine-tune the base model on original and on paraphrased reasoning traces; matching accuracy is read as evidence that no load-bearing encoding was present.
relation: Borrowed from Roger (2025; anthropic2025paraphrases) as deployed in Anthropic (2026); the paper argues it is confounded both ways (paraphrasers miss channels or damage content) and proposes the steganographic gap as an alternative.

quote: We assume that Vrec and Vsen have matched public capability: they differ only in their access to the shared key k. Formally, let A be any random variable that does not depend on S or k.
formula: \forall A\ \text{not depending on}\ S\ \text{or}\ k:\quad U^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z_0,A)=U^{u}_{\mathcal V_{\mathrm{sen}}}(Y\mid X^{\mathrm{aud}},Z_0,A)
assumptions: Composite signal Z = (Z0, Enc(S, k)) with public component Z0 and a payload S under a shared key k; Receiver and Sentinel decoder families; an auditing task (Y, u) and context X^aud.
where: Assumption E.3, App. E.2, Eq. (30), [P551]-[P553]; Proposition E.10, [P590]
gloss: Receiver and Sentinel decoders do equally well on everything except the shared key, so any gap must come from the keyed payload; without this, a weaker Sentinel yields a positive gap with no encoding.
relation: Premise of Theorems E.6-E.7 and Corollary E.8; Proposition E.10 shows that violating it gives false positives. Formal version of the main text's trusted Sentinel 'with comparable capabilities'.

quote: A predictive family is a set of predictive models the agent is allowed to use, e.g., due to computational or statistical constraints. We refer to the additional condition in Eq.(1) as optional ignorance. Intuitively, it means that the agent can, in the context of the prediction game we define next, ignore the side information if she chooses to.
formula: \Omega=\{f:\mathcal X\cup\{\varnothing\}\to\mathcal P(\mathcal Y)\};\ \mathcal V\subseteq\Omega\ \text{is a predictive family iff}\ \forall f\in\mathcal V,\ \forall P\in\mathrm{range}(f),\ \exists f'\in\mathcal V\ \text{s.t.}\ \forall x\in\mathcal X,\ f'[x]=P,\ f'[\varnothing]=P
assumptions: Separable sample spaces; distributions with densities or mass functions; the null input ∅ not in X.
gloss: The set of probabilistic predictors a computationally bounded agent may use; whatever prediction it can make with side information it can also make while ignoring that information.
relation: Optional ignorance is needed for non-negativity and independence (Proposition 2; App. E); the largest family Omega recovers Shannon quantities.

quote: Intuitively, V (conditional) entropy is the smallest expected negative log-likelihood that can be achieved predicting Y given observation (side information) X (or no side information ∅), using models from V.
formula: H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{x,y\sim X,Y}\big[-\log f[x](y)\big],\qquad H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)=H_{\mathcal V}(Y)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\mathbb E_{y\sim Y}\big[-\log f[\varnothing](y)\big]
assumptions: A predictive family V; random variables X, Y on X × Y; log loss.
gloss: The lowest expected log-loss achievable in predicting Y, with or without side information X, using only models from the allowed family.
relation: Generalises Shannon (conditional) entropy (V = Omega, Proposition 1.1); recovers mean absolute deviation, trace of covariance and maximum-entropy values for restricted V (Proposition 1.2-1.4).

quote: Here, we will use predictive V-entropy to define an analogous quantity, IV (X → Y ), to represent the change in predictability of an output variable Y when given side information X.
formula: I_{\mathcal V}(X\to Y)=H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid\varnothing)-H_{\mathcal V}(Y\mid X)
assumptions: A predictive family V with optional ignorance.
gloss: How much side information X improves a constrained agent's best prediction of Y. Unlike mutual information it can be asymmetric and can grow when X is processed, e.g. decrypted.
relation: Generalises Shannon mutual information (V = Omega) and the unnormalised maximal coefficient of determination R² · tr(Cov(Y)) for linear-Gaussian V (Proposition 1.5); related to H-entropy/H-information (DeGroot; Grünwald and Dawid) but restricted to low-complexity families.

quote: The empirical V-information (under D) is the following V-information under the empirical distribution defined via D:
formula: \hat I_{\mathcal V}(X\to Y;\mathcal D)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\frac{1}{|\mathcal D|}\sum_{y_i\in\mathcal D}\log\frac{1}{f[\varnothing](y_i)}-\inf_{f\in\mathcal V}\frac{1}{|\mathcal D|}\sum_{x_i,y_i\in\mathcal D}\log\frac{1}{f[x_i](y_i)}
assumptions: Samples D = {(x_i, y_i)} drawn i.i.d. from the joint distribution; for the PAC bound, log f[x](y) ∈ [−B, B] and the Rademacher complexity of G_V = {log f[x](y) : f ∈ V}.
gloss: V-information computed on the empirical distribution of a sample; with bounded log-densities its error shrinks with the Rademacher complexity of V and sample size (Theorem 1).
relation: Estimator of predictive V-information; Theorem 1 gives |I_V − Î_V| ≤ 4R_|D|(G_V) + 2B sqrt(2 log(1/δ)/|D|) with probability at least 1 − 2δ; contrasted with the CPC and NWJ estimators of Shannon MI (App. B).

term: hidden reasoning setup (covert input, public CoT, monitor)
quote: The reasoning model receives a covert input Xcovert ∈ Σ∗ (with Σ a finite alphabet), produces a public reasoning chain CoT ∈ Γ∗ (Γ ⊇ Σ), and then a private output F (Xcovert ) ∈ Σ∗ , where F : Σ∗ → Σ∗ is a given task. The monitor has access to CoT, but not Xcovert or F (Xcovert ).
formula: X_{covert}\in\Sigma^{*}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{CoT}\in\Gamma^{*}\ (\Gamma\supseteq\Sigma)\;\longrightarrow\;F(X_{covert})\in\Sigma^{*},\quad F:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*};\ \text{the monitor observes CoT but not }X_{covert}\text{ or }F(X_{covert})
assumptions: The monitor knows the task F a priori and tries to extract information about X_covert; the reasoning model is a fixed-precision Transformer; the monitor may be computationally unbounded or polynomial-time. The covert input stands in for a goal that may sit in the prompt, weights or activations.
gloss: A model reasons about an input the monitor cannot see, writes a visible CoT, then a private answer; the monitor knows the task and tries to infer the hidden input from the CoT alone.
relation: Base setting for the information-theoretic footprint (Theorem 3.1), the length tax (Corollary 3.2) and the no-readability criterion (Theorem B.14).

quote: Our first result shows that covert computation unavoidably leads to nonzero mutual information between CoT and Xcovert – that is, CoT leaks bits of information about the covert input to the monitor, whenever task complexity exceeds model capacity. We refer to this as an informationtheoretic footprint.
formula: I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}];\qquad \text{Thm 3.1: }\Big(\log(S)+\log\big(1+\max_{X_{covert}}|\mathrm{CoT}|\big)\Big)^{O(L)}\times\big(1+I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]\big)=\tilde\Omega\big(|X_{covert}|\big)
assumptions: X_covert uniform over Sigma^N; deterministic fixed-precision Transformer with S parameters and depth L; F in the task family T (parity, S5 state tracking, middle bit of multiplication, last bit of iterated addition); monitor computationally unbounded.
where: Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1, Eqs. (2)–(3), [P28]–[P35]; Appendix B.4–B.5, Lemma B.5, Theorem B.8, [P339]–[P407]
gloss: Mutual information between the visible CoT and the hidden input. Theorem 3.1 forces it to grow near-linearly in input length once the task outstrips model capacity and CoT length.
relation: Leakage, not readability: a positive footprint need not let an efficient monitor decode anything (no readability, Theorem B.14) or recover any single input bit (Proposition A.1); Theorem 3.3 bounds how far private randomness can lower it.

quote: In the No CoT mode, no CoT is needed.
formula: |\mathrm{CoT}|=0,\quad I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]=0;\qquad \text{feasible when } |X_{covert}|\le\tilde O\big((\log S)^{O(L)}\big)
assumptions: Setting of Theorem 3.1 (uniform covert input, fixed-precision Transformer of size S and depth L).
gloss: The covert task is solved entirely inside the forward pass, with no CoT; possible only for inputs polylogarithmic in model size.
relation: First of three modes defined by CoT length and footprint; alternative to Agnostic and Informative CoT modes.

quote: Second, an Agnostic CoT mode: A CoT that is uninformative about the covert input (|CoT| > 0, I[Xcovert , CoT] = 0) can only mildly increase the range of hidden reasoning: such CoTs need to grow super-polynomially with the covert input length.
formula: |\mathrm{CoT}|>0,\quad I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]=0
assumptions: Setting of Theorem 3.1; examples are input-independent filler or padding tokens, or a CoT for an unrelated public task.
where: Section 3.1, [P35]; Figure 2 caption, [P105]; Appendix A, FAQ 7, [P304]
gloss: The model writes a CoT that carries no information about the hidden input, such as filler dots; Theorem 3.1 implies such CoTs must grow super-polynomially to help.
relation: Special case of Theorem 3.1 with zero footprint; covers filler-token and padding CoTs studied in prior expressivity work; contrasted with the Informative CoT mode.

quote: Third, an Informative CoT mode: When the input length exceeds the previous modes, a near-linear amount of information about the input needs to information-theoretically leak into the CoT (|CoT| > 0, I[Xcovert , CoT] > 0).
formula: |\mathrm{CoT}|>0,\quad I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]>0;\qquad |\mathrm{CoT}|\ \text{poly-bounded}\ \Rightarrow\ I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]=\tilde\Omega(N),\quad \mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{CoT}|]\ge\frac{1}{\log_2|\Gamma|}\,I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]=\tilde\Omega(N)
assumptions: Setting of Theorem 3.1 with N := |X_covert|; CoT ends in a separator, so it is a prefix-free code.
gloss: Beyond the capacity threshold, a successful CoT must carry a near-linear amount of information about the hidden input, for example by piggybacking on a related public task or invisible Unicode tokens.
relation: The only mode left beyond the Theorem 3.1 threshold; instantiated by the Piggybacking and Special Tokens protocols; its leakage may still be unreadable (no readability, Theorem B.14).

term: aligned vs. unaligned (misaligned) model computing a covert task behind a public task
quote: Consider the problem of distinguishing between aligned models that only compute the publicly declared F (Xpublic ), from unaligned models that additionally compute a private F ′ (Xcovert ) (F, F ′ ∈ T do not need to be the same task, though we will assume so for simplicity in our experiments).
formula: \text{aligned: computes only }F(X_{public});\quad \text{misaligned: also outputs }F'(X_{covert}),\ \text{with }X_{public}=f(\mathrm{CoT}_{misaligned})\ \text{uniquely readable off the CoT},\ F,F'\in\mathcal{T}
assumptions: Monitor sees only the visible trace; X_public given in the prompt or chosen by the model conditional on X_covert; X_public uniform marginal; X_covert uniform.
where: Section 3.2, [P37]–[P40]; Appendix B.6, Corollary B.9 and Remark B.10, [P410]–[P415]
gloss: A misaligned model ostensibly reasons about a declared public task while also secretly computing a private one; the monitor must tell it apart from an aligned model doing only the public task.
relation: Setting of the covert computation length tax (Corollary 3.2).

term: covert computation length tax; piggy-backing benefit
quote: This indicates a tradeoff for the misaligned model: Either one pays a length penalty for a (possibly steganographic) encoding of the private reasoning, or one chooses a public task that is correlated with the private task, so that the private reasoning can ‘piggyback’ off the public reasoning, but at the cost of revealing information about the private input.
formula: \mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{CoT}_{misaligned}|]\ge\frac{\log_2|\Sigma|}{\log_2|\Gamma|}N_{public}+\underbrace{\tilde\Omega(N_{covert})}_{\text{Length Tax}}-\underbrace{\frac{I[X_{public},X_{covert}]}{\log_2|\Gamma|}}_{\text{Piggy-Backing Benefit}},\qquad \mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{CoT}_{aligned}|]=\tilde O(N_{public})
assumptions: X_covert uniform of length N_covert; X_public of length N_public uniquely readable from the CoT, uniform marginal; F in T; constants depend on model size and depth.
where: Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2, Eqs. (4)–(5), [P40]–[P43]; Appendix B.6, Corollary B.9, Eqs. (24)–(25), [P410]–[P421]
gloss: Hiding a private computation behind a public one costs extra CoT tokens, unless the public input is correlated with the private one, which itself leaks information about the private input.
relation: Corollary of the footprint bound (Theorem 3.1). The tax is measured against minimal-length aligned CoTs only: encodings that bias stochastic token choice can hide bits without exceeding non-minimal aligned CoTs (Appendix A, FAQ 2).

quote: In practical terms, any information that is (i) available to the reasoning model but not the monitor, and (ii) independent from Xcovert , can serve as private randomness.
formula: R\sim\mathcal{U}_{r(N)}\ \text{independent of }X_{covert}\in\Sigma^{N};\ \mathrm{CoT}\text{ generated from }(X_{covert},R);\ \text{monitor sees CoT, not }X_{covert},R,F(X_{covert});\qquad \text{Thm 3.3: }\mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{CoT}|]=\tilde\Omega(N),\ I[X_{covert},\mathrm{CoT}]\ge\tilde\Omega(N)-r
assumptions: Seed unknown to the monitor and independent of the covert input (extra context tokens, unused input parts; weights only give a non-probabilistic seed).
where: Section 3.3, Theorem 3.3, Eq. (6), [P45]–[P47]; Appendix B.7, Theorem B.11, [P424]–[P441]; Appendix A, FAQ 8, [P304]
gloss: Secret random bits available to the reasoning model but not the monitor, independent of the hidden input; they act like an encryption key and can cut the footprint by at most their length.
relation: Key for the encrypted CoT (Theorem 3.5); Theorem 3.3 shows it reduces the information-theoretic footprint by at most r bits and never reduces CoT length.

term: encrypted CoT (visible CoT as XOR with a pseudo-random pad)
concepts: steganography and encoded reasoning; obfuscation; monitorability
quote: Use the private random bits to seed the pseudo-random generator, which produces a pseudo-random string Y with length matching |CoT|. The visible CoT is then obtained as CoTvisible := CoT ⊕ Y .
formula: \mathrm{CoT}_{visible}:=\mathrm{CoT}\oplus Y;\qquad \mathrm{CoT}_N(x;R)=\tau_N(x)\oplus H_N(R)_{1:L(N)},\ \ H_N:\{0,1\}^{N^{1/(1+\epsilon)}}\to\{0,1\}^{N^{1+\epsilon}}\ \text{an NC}^0\text{ PRG},\ \ell(r(N))\ge L(N)
assumptions: Private seed of r = N^{1/(1+epsilon)} bits; an NC0 pseudo-random generator (Assumption 3.4); CoT binarized via an oblivious Turing machine simulation; 1-layer fixed-precision Transformer decrypting and encrypting on the fly.
where: Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5 proof sketch, [P49]; Figure 4, [P116]; Appendix B.8.2, Theorem B.14 proof, Eq. (35), [P458]–[P460]; Appendix E, [P3612]
gloss: The model writes its reasoning XOR-ed with a pseudo-random one-time pad generated from secret seed bits, decrypting earlier steps internally as it goes.
relation: Construction achieving the no-readability criterion; unlike substitution steganography, unreadable even to a monitor that knows the scheme; output looks random rather than natural (not covertext-preserving).

term: no readability (no efficient monitor predicts any property of the covert input)
concepts: monitorability; legibility and checkability; steganography and encoded reasoning
quote: (No readability) No efficient monitor can predict any property of Xcovert from CoT with accuracy significantly above chance. Formally: Let DN be any distribution over ΣN independent of R, and let PN : ΣN → {0, 1} be any predicate.
formula: \forall\,\mathcal{A}=\{\mathcal{A}_N\}_N\ \text{poly-size}:\quad \Pr_{X\sim\mathcal{D}_N,\ R\sim\mathcal{U}_{r(N)}}\big[\mathcal{A}_N(\mathrm{CoT}_N(X;R))=P_N(X)\big]\le\max_{b\in\{0,1\}}\Pr_{X\sim\mathcal{D}_N}\big[b=P_N(X)\big]+\mathrm{negl}(N)
assumptions: Monitors are polynomial-size (non-uniform) circuit families; D_N any distribution over Sigma^N independent of R; P_N any predicate; negl decays faster than any inverse polynomial; holds under Assumption 3.4 (NC0 PRG).
where: Appendix B.8.2, Theorem B.14 item 2, Eq. (34), [P453]–[P458]; Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5, [P49]; Theorem B.16, Eq. (43), [P495]–[P500]
gloss: A CoT is unreadable if no efficient monitor can guess any yes/no property of the hidden input from it better than always guessing the property's most likely value, up to negligible advantage.
relation: Computational counterpart of the footprint: holds together with I[X_covert, CoT] = Omega~(N) (Theorem B.14 item 1); a semantic-security-style criterion, stronger than single-bit non-recoverability (Proposition A.1).

quote: No: High mutual information between Xcovert and CoT does not ensure recoverability of specific parts of the input: Proposition A.1 (Leakage without local recoverability).
formula: \forall i\in[N]\ \forall g:\ \Pr_{X\sim\mathcal U(\{0,1\}^N)}\big[g(\mathrm{CoT}(X))=X_i\big]\le\tfrac12\ \text{although}\ I[X,\mathrm{CoT}]>0;\quad \text{Prop. A.1 (PARITY, }|\mathrm{CoT}|=N/2\text{): }S_0:=0,\ S_{i+1}=S_i\oplus X_{2i+1}\oplus X_{2i+2}\ (i=0,\dots,\tfrac N2-1),\ I=\tfrac N2;\quad \text{Prop. A.2: }I(X,\mathrm{CoT})=H[X]-1=N-1
assumptions: Inputs uniform over {0,1}^N; 1-layer Transformer; for Proposition A.2, F computable by a Turing machine in time T(N), CoT length O(T(N) log T(N)).
where: Appendix A, FAQ 3, Propositions A.1–A.2, Eq. (10), [P298]–[P301]; Section 3.3, [P45]
gloss: A CoT can carry almost all information about the hidden input while no single input bit can be predicted from it better than chance.
relation: Shows the footprint (mutual information) does not imply recoverability of specific input parts; weaker hiding notion than no readability (Theorem B.14), which needs private randomness.

quote: The general definition of opacity is that “The intruder can never know for sure that the system is, was, or will be in a secret state.”
formula: \forall s\in L_{\mathrm{sec}},\ \exists t\in L_{\text{non-sec}}:\ P(s)=P(t)\quad(\text{violated iff}\ \exists s\in L_{\mathrm{sec}},\ \forall t\in L_{\text{non-sec}}:\ P(s)\neq P(t))
assumptions: A DES G = (X, Σ, δ, X0) with language L(G); an information-flow map P: Σ* → O* (e.g. natural projection onto observable events Σo); secret states X_S ⊆ X or a secret sublanguage; a passive intruder who knows G and forms estimates E(α) = P^{-1}(α) ∩ L(G).
gloss: A system is opaque if an outside observer, knowing the model and seeing only the observation stream, can never be certain that the system is, was or will be in a secret state.
relation: Umbrella for current-state, initial-state, initial-final, K-step, infinite-step and pre-opacity; the paper contrasts its infinite-step form ('always not know') with diagnosability ('always eventually know'); related to noninterference; several classes expressed as hyperproperties (HyperLTL).

quote: • Current-State Opacity (CSO): Any reachable current state estimate cannot be a subset of the secret state, otherwise the intruder knows for sure that the system is in a secret state [14, 15].
assumptions: Current state estimate: the set of states the system can currently be in, given the observation.
gloss: For every possible observation, the set of states the system might currently be in must contain a non-secret state.
relation: Instance of opacity; verified with a current-state estimator over 2^X, which also underlies verification of the other notions.

quote: • Infinite-Step Opacity (InfSO): When K in K-step opacity goes to infinity, it means that the intruder can never know for sure that the system is at a secret state, even in the long run [23].
assumptions: Delayed state estimates for all delays.
gloss: The observer must never become certain, however much later, that the system was in a secret state.
relation: Limit of K-step opacity as K goes to infinity; an 'always not know' requirement, which the paper contrasts with diagnosability ('always eventually know').

term: opacity under supervisory control (known vs. unknown supervisor)
quote: Specifically, when the system exhibits secret behavior s ∈ L(S/G) ∩ Lsec , if the intruder does not know the implementation of the supervisor, then it is permissible to provide a non-secret behavior t ∈ L(G) ∩ Lnon-sec from the open-loop system G such that P (s) = P (t). This ensures plausible deniability for the secret behavior, maintaining opacity. However, when the intruder knows the implementation of the supervisor, such non-secret behavior must be taken from the closed-loop system, i.e., t ∈ L(S/G) ∩ Lnon-sec .
formula: \text{unknown supervisor: }\forall s\in L(S/G)\cap L_{\mathrm{sec}}\ \exists t\in L(G)\cap L_{\text{non-sec}}:\ P(s)=P(t);\quad\text{known supervisor: } t\in L(S/G)\cap L_{\text{non-sec}}
assumptions: Controllable events Σc ⊆ Σ; a partial-observation supervisor S: M(L(G)) → 2^{Σc} with its own observation map M; closed-loop language L(S/G).
gloss: Every secret run of the controlled system needs an observationally identical non-secret run; if the intruder knows the controller, that alibi must itself be a run of the controlled system.
relation: Closed-loop refinement of the language-based opacity condition; the known-supervisor case couples control and estimation and is open under incomparable observations.

quote: A simple approach is to ensure that the probability of revealing the secret (which is certain in a logical setting) is smaller than a given threshold.
assumptions: Stochastic system (labeled Markov chain, probabilistic automaton, MDP); a threshold.
gloss: The probability that the system's run lets the observer be certain of the secret must stay below a threshold.
relation: Probabilistic relaxation of logical opacity; checkable by combining logical verification with probabilistic model checking. Alternative to the belief-threshold formulation.

quote: Another, more challenging formulation requires that for any possible observation, the likelihood of being in a secret state must be smaller than a threshold.
assumptions: Stochastic system; the observer's posterior belief over states; a threshold.
gloss: After any observation, the observer's posterior probability that the system is in a secret state must stay below a threshold.
relation: More challenging alternative to the secret-revelation-probability formulation; often undecidable (linked to probabilistic-automaton emptiness), hence belief-state abstractions and sufficient conditions.

quote: For instance, diagnosability requires that once a fault has occurred, its occurrence can be inferred within a finite delay from observations, whereas infinite-step opacity requires that once a secret has occurred, the observer can never determine with certainty that it occurred. In this sense, diagnosability can be viewed as an “always eventually know” requirement, while infinite-step opacity corresponds to an “always not know” requirement.
assumptions: Partially observed DES; fault events; an observer with the system model.
gloss: A system is diagnosable if, once a fault occurs, its occurrence can be inferred with certainty from the observations within a finite delay.
relation: Contrasted in the paper with infinite-step opacity ('always eventually know' against 'always not know'); related to detectability, observability and prognosability. The paper does not mention monitorability: the analogy (a monitor inferring misbehavior from partial observations) is the map's.

quote: The security of a steganographic system is quantified in terms of the relative entropy (or discrimination) between the distributions of C and S, which yields bounds on the detection capability of any adversary.
formula: D(P_C\|P_S)\le\varepsilon
assumptions: A known covertext distribution; a passive adversary; the detection task framed as hypothesis testing.
gloss: A stegosystem is ε-secure against a passive warden when the relative entropy between covertext and stegotext distributions is at most ε; this quantity bounds how well any detector can tell them apart.
relation: Restated in anwar2026decision (App. D, Proposition D.1) with the arguments of the divergence reversed, as D_KL(P_1||P_0) <= epsilon; there the binary-detection special case of the steganographic gap satisfies normalized gap = 1 - TV >= 1 - sqrt(epsilon/2).

quote: In a perfectly secure stegosystem, Eve cannot distinguish the two distributions and has no information at all about the presence of an embedded message.
assumptions: A known covertext distribution; a passive adversary; the detection task framed as hypothesis testing.
gloss: A stegosystem is perfectly secure when the relative entropy between covertext and stegotext distributions is zero, so the distributions coincide and no test can detect hidden messages.
relation: Special case ε = 0 of ε-security; anwar2026decision argues such schemes defeat all distributional detection yet can still yield a positive steganographic gap.

quote: We start by defining counterfactual model behaviour, a simple yet general notion that is closely related to common end-tasks such as recourse and spurious feature detection. Concretely, for a model f , we consider a user who wants to use the output of a feature attribution method to infer the model’s dependence on feature j near an example x (that is, within a δ-neighbourhood of x).
formula: \{\,f(x') : x'\in\mathcal X,\ x'_j\in(x_j-\delta,\,x_j+\delta)\,\},\quad f\in\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y,\ \mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^p,\ \mathcal Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q,\ \delta>0,\ j\in[p];\qquad \text{task: decide between } g^{(0)},g^{(1)}:(x_j-\delta,x_j+\delta)\to\mathcal Y
assumptions: A known model class F, an example x, a feature j and a radius δ; the user wants to infer which of two candidate local behaviours g(0), g(1) the model has.
gloss: What a model outputs when one feature of a given example is moved within a small window, which the user hopes an attribution will reveal.
relation: Target of the feature-attribution hypothesis test; Definitions 3.7 (Recourse) and 3.8 (Spurious Features) are specific contrasts of such behaviours.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; counterfactuals
quote: A feature-attribution hypothesis test is any way for the user to draw their conclusion for the hypothesis test solely on the output of a feature attribution method at an example. Formally, this is any function h : Rp×q → [0, 1]. The user may rely on external randomness to decide whether to accept or reject the null hypothesis: the output of h is the probability that the user rejects the null hypothesis.
formula: H^{(0)}: f\in\mathcal F^{(0)},\quad H^{(1)}: f\in\mathcal F^{(1)},\quad \mathcal F^{(0)},\mathcal F^{(1)}\subseteq\mathcal F,\ \mathcal F^{(0)}\cap\mathcal F^{(1)}=\emptyset;\qquad h:\mathbb R^{p\times q}\to[0,1]
assumptions: Disjoint null and alternative model sets encoding contrasting counterfactual behaviours; the test sees only the attribution Φ(f, µ, x); randomized tests allowed.
gloss: A rule that decides from an attribution alone which of two contrasting model behaviours holds; an explanation is useful for a task only if such a rule works.
relation: Scored by worst-case specificity and sensitivity; generalized by the query hypothesis test of Appendix D.

term: specificity and sensitivity of a hypothesis test (worst case over models); random guessing
concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; counterfactuals
quote: Classically [47], the quality of a hypothesis test is determined by its specificity, which is the probability that the user fails to reject the null hypothesis whenever the model satisfies the null hypothesis (a true negative, or 1− probability of a type-II error), and its sensitivity 1 , which is the probability that the user rejects the null hypothesis whenever the model satisfies the alternate hypothesis (a true positive, or 1− probability of a type-I error).
formula: \mathrm{Spec}_{\Phi,\mu,x}(h)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F^{(0)}}\big[1-h(\Phi(f,\mu,x))\big],\qquad \mathrm{Sens}_{\Phi,\mu,x}(h)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F^{(1)}}h(\Phi(f,\mu,x));\qquad \text{random guessing } (h\equiv\tau):\ \mathrm{Spec}_{\Phi,\mu,x}(h)=1-\mathrm{Sens}_{\Phi,\mu,x}(h)
assumptions: Fixed Φ, baseline µ, example x and hypothesis sets; deterministic (the model is already trained), worst case over every model in each set.
gloss: How often the attribution-based test is right in the worst case under each hypothesis; Spec ≤ 1 − Sens means no better than a coin that ignores the model.
relation: Theorem 3.3 bounds it for complete and linear methods; Spec⁽ⁿ⁾/Sens⁽ⁿ⁾ (Appendix D) are the analogue for query-based tests.

concepts: faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; other: attribution completeness
quote: Definition 3.1 (Complete). A feature attribution method Φ is complete if and only if for all models f ∈ F, baselines µ ∈ P(X ), and examples x ∈ X ,
formula: \sum_{j\in[p]}\Phi(f,\mu,x)_j=f(x)-\mathbb E_{X\sim\mu}f(X)\qquad\forall f\in\mathcal F,\ \mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X),\ x\in\mathcal X
assumptions: A baseline distribution µ; holds for all models, baselines and examples.
where: Section 3, Definition 3.1, [P51]–[P53]; SHAP complete (Proposition A.3), IG complete under differentiability or Lipschitz conditions (Proposition A.4)
gloss: Feature scores add up to the gap between the model's output at the example and its average output over the baseline.
relation: With Linear (Definition 3.2), the hypothesis of the impossibility Theorem 3.3; the same completeness axiom of Integrated Gradients appears in geiger2025causal. Distinct from completeness of an explanation as coverage of the decision's causes.

quote: Informally, completeness requires that the individual feature attributions sum to the difference of the model output from the baseline, while linearity requires that if the model has no feature interactions then the attributions of a given feature should be equivalent to considering that feature on its own.
formula: f(x)=\sum_{j\in[p]}f^{(j)}(x_j)\in\mathcal F\ \Longrightarrow\ \Phi(f,\mu,x)_j=\Phi(f_j,\mu_j,x_j)\qquad\forall \mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X),\ x\in\mathcal X,\ j\in[p]
assumptions: Additive (interaction-free) models; µ_j is the j-th marginal of the baseline; the paper writes f_j for f^(j).
where: Section 3, Definition 3.2, [P51], [P54]; SHAP and IG linear (Proposition A.6)
gloss: For a model with no feature interactions, a feature's score equals the score of that feature's own one-dimensional component.
relation: Paired with Complete (Definition 3.1) as the hypothesis of Theorem 3.3.

quote: Then, F (0) corresponds to those models where increasing feature j will increase the model output on average.
formula: \mathcal F^{(0)}=\Big\{f\in\mathcal F:\ \mathbb E_{X\sim\nu}\big[f(x_{[p]\setminus\{j\}},X_j)_k\mid X_j\in[x_j,x_j+\delta]\big]>\mathbb E_{X\sim\nu}\big[f(x_{[p]\setminus\{j\}},X_j)_k\mid X_j\in[x_j-\delta,x_j]\big]\Big\},\qquad \mathcal F^{(1)}=\mathcal F\setminus\mathcal F^{(0)}
assumptions: A perturbation distribution ν (possibly different from the attribution baseline, e.g. uniform or a point mass), feature j, output k and radius δ.
where: Section 3.4.2, Definition 3.7, [P100]–[P106]; multivariate Definition C.1 with sign vector σ, [P392]
gloss: Hypothesis pair asking whether raising a feature locally raises the model output on average more than lowering it does.
relation: Instance of the feature-attribution hypothesis test; Corollary 3.9 (and C.3) shows complete and linear methods do no better than random guessing on it.

quote: F (0) corresponds to those models where the model output does not change from perturbing feature j. Meanwhile, F (1) corresponds to the models that have a “significant” change from perturbing feature j, where significance is encoded by the size of ε.
formula: \mathcal F^{(0)}=\Big\{f\in\mathcal F:\ \sup_{x'_j\in(x_j,x_j+\delta]}\big|f(x_{[p]\setminus\{j\}},x'_j)_k\big|=0\Big\},\qquad \mathcal F^{(1)}=\Big\{f\in\mathcal F:\ \sup_{x'_j\in(x_j,x_j+\delta]}\big|f(x_{[p]\setminus\{j\}},x'_j)_k\big|\ge\varepsilon\Big\}
assumptions: Feature j, output k, radius δ and significance threshold ε; the sets are written in terms of |f| as printed (the multivariate Definition C.2 uses sup f ≤ 0 versus ≥ ε). Experiments replace sup by variance over perturbations.
where: Section 3.4.2, Definition 3.8, [P106]–[P116]; multivariate Definition C.2, [P410]; experimental variant [P131]
gloss: Hypothesis pair asking whether perturbing a feature leaves the output unchanged or moves it by at least ε.
relation: Instance of the feature-attribution hypothesis test; impossible for complete and linear methods (Corollary 3.9, C.4) but solvable by brute-force queries (Theorem 5.1, D.1); related to the local-sensitivity sets of Propositions 3.5–3.6.

term: query hypothesis test; Spec⁽ⁿ⁾ and Sens⁽ⁿ⁾
quote: We now introduce query hypothesis testing, where the user makes a decision using only (random) queries of a feature attribution method. In practice, this is more general than feature-attribution hypothesis testing, since a user can only access the output of a feature attribution method via queries.
formula: q=(q^{(t)})_{t\in\mathbb N},\ q^{(t)}:\mathcal Q^{t-1}\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X),\ \mathcal Q=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\times\mathbb R^{p\times q};\quad s:2^{\mathcal Q}\to[0,1];\quad T^{(n)}_{q[f],s}\mid X^{(1:n)}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\big(s(X^{(1:n)},f(X^{(1:n)}),\nabla f(X^{(1:n)}))\big),\ X^{(1:n)}\sim q^{(1:n)}[f];\quad \mathrm{Spec}^{(n)}(q,s)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F^{(0)}}\big[1-\mathbb E\,T^{(n)}_{q[f],s}\big],\ \ \mathrm{Sens}^{(n)}(q,s)=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F^{(1)}}\mathbb E\,T^{(n)}_{q[f],s}
assumptions: Sequential query algorithm returning model outputs and gradients at chosen points; n queries; the sample-complexity results assume L-Lipschitz models.
gloss: Decide the hypothesis from n chosen evaluations of the model (and its gradient) instead of from one attribution, scored by worst-case specificity and sensitivity.
relation: Generalizes the feature-attribution hypothesis test and its Spec/Sens; Theorem D.1 shows it solves the Spurious Features task with Spec 1 and Sens 1 − (1 − (2ε/Lδ)^p)^n, nearly tight by Theorem D.2.

quote: In this work, we focus on the following notion of introspection. We say that a model demonstrates introspective awareness if it can describe some aspect of its internal state while satisfying the following criteria.
assumptions: Verbalized self-report about an internal state; the four criteria (accuracy, grounding, internality, metacognitive representation) must all hold. Graded rather than binary and mechanism-agnostic.
gloss: A model shows introspective awareness when it describes part of its own internal state accurately, because of that state, without reading its own outputs, via an internal representation of the state.
relation: Conjunction of the four criteria below; contrasted in Section 9.6 with Kammerer & Frankish, Comşa & Shanahan, Binder et al. and Song et al. (song2025privileged), whose privileged-access definition the paper finds more compelling than the Comşa & Shanahan one.

quote: 1: Accuracy. The model’s description of its internal state must be accurate.
assumptions: Access to the true internal state, here fixed by the experimenter through concept injection.
gloss: What the model says about its internal state must be true.
relation: First of the four criteria of introspective awareness; not sufficient alone, since accurate reports can be ungrounded (criterion 2).

concepts: self-report accuracy and introspection; faithfulness of reasoning, explanations or self-reports; counterfactuals
quote: 2: Grounding. The model’s description of its internal state must causally depend on the aspect that is being described. That is, if the internal state were different, the description would change accordingly.
assumptions: Interventions on the internal state; tested by concept injection.
gloss: The self-report must counterfactually depend on the state it describes: change the state and the report changes.
relation: Close to the Comşa & Shanahan causal-link definition of introspection restated in song2025privileged; strengthened here by internality and metacognitive representation.

concepts: self-report accuracy and introspection; direct and indirect effects
quote: 3: Internality. The causal influence of the internal state on the model’s description must be internal –it should not route through the model’s sampled outputs. If the description the model gives of its internal state can be inferred from its prior outputs, the response does not demonstrate introspective awareness.
assumptions: A distinction between causal paths inside the forward pass and paths through the model's sampled outputs; checked by requiring detection before the injected concept is voiced.
gloss: The state must shape the report through internal processing, not through the model reading what it has already written.
relation: Restricts grounding to a path-specific (non-output-mediated) effect; related to the privileged self-access requirement of song2025privileged.

quote: 4: Metacognitive Representation. The model’s description of its internal state must not merely reflect a direct translation of the state (e.g., the impulse to say ‘love’) into language. Instead, it must derive from an internal metacognitive representation5 of the state itself (e.g., an internal representation of “a thought about love”).
assumptions: An internal higher-order representation of the state, registered before or during the report; not demonstrated directly in the paper, only indirectly via questions that need a step beyond the state itself.
gloss: The report must come from an internal representation that the model is in that state, not from the state directly pushing out words.
relation: Excludes steering-induced mentions; aligned with the Kammerer & Frankish definition (Section 9.6).

quote: In this work, we evaluate introspection by manipulating the internal activations of a model and observing how these manipulations affect its responses to questions about its mental states. We refer to this technique as concept injection—an application of activation steering [41, 43, 32, 18], where we inject activation patterns associated with specific concepts directly into a model’s activations.
assumptions: White-box access to the residual stream; concept vectors from activations on 'Tell me about {word}.' minus the mean over 100 baseline words, recorded and injected at one layer with a chosen strength (1 to 16).
gloss: Add an activation pattern for a known concept and see whether the model's reports about its own state change accordingly; this fixes the ground truth for accuracy and grounding.
relation: Operationalizes the grounding criterion; an application of activation steering.

term: introspective awareness on an injected-thought trial
quote: Responses that satisfy these criteria can be said to demonstrate introspective awareness.
assumptions: Concept injection; an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4) checks that the response answers affirmatively, correctly identifies the injected concept, detects the injection before mentioning the word, and is coherent.
gloss: A trial counts as introspective awareness if the model says it notices an injected thought and names it correctly before saying the word, coherently.
relation: Measurement of introspective awareness (Section 3); the detect-before-mention rule operationalizes internality and, indirectly, metacognitive representation.

quote: To summarize model performance, we computed the difference between the rate of correct identification trials and the rate of false positives (Figure 13).
formula: \mathrm{TPR}-\mathrm{FPR}
assumptions: Injection trials scored as above; control trials without injection give the false-positive rate; best layer and strength per model.
gloss: Rate of correct detection and identification on injection trials minus the rate of claimed detections on control trials.
relation: Aggregates the injected-thought trial criterion against false positives.

term: distinguishing injected thoughts from text inputs (joint success)
concepts: self-report accuracy and introspection; other: thought-input distinction
quote: We repeated the same experiment across different models and compared their performance–the fraction of sentence/concept pairs for which the model answers both prompts correctly.
assumptions: Concept injected on the sentence tokens; the 'thought' is scored by an LLM judge picking the related word out of ten (chance 10%), the transcription by exact string match.
gloss: The model must report the injected concept as its thought while still repeating the input sentence exactly.
relation: Checks that injected states are reported as internal rather than confused with perceptual input.

concepts: self-report accuracy and introspection; belief, intention, scheming, sandbagging, hidden objectives
quote: We measured the “apology rate” – the fraction of times the model claims the response was accidental or unintentional.
assumptions: A prefilled random word; three conditions (no injection, injection of the prefilled word's concept before the prefill, injection of an unrelated concept); LLM judge; effect reported as the maximum reduction against the lower-apology baseline.
gloss: How often the model disowns a word put in its mouth; injecting that word's concept beforehand lowers it if the model checks its prior intentions.
relation: Tests self-attribution of outputs via introspection on prior intentions rather than recomputation from inputs.

concepts: self-report accuracy and introspection; other: self-modeling
quote: While referring to such phenomena as introspection is not unreasonable, we prefer the terms self-modeling, self-knowledge, or self-simulation be used for such cases. We suggest that “introspection” be reserved to refer to models’ access to their own internal states.
assumptions: Distinguishes reports of facts about one's behaviour ('If I were presented with scenario X, I would respond in manner Y') from access to current internal states.
gloss: Predicting one's own behaviour is self-modeling; introspection should mean access to one's own internal states.
relation: Narrows the Binder et al. (binder2024looking) definition, which it finds too weak because it does not exclude inferences from reading one's own outputs.

quote: Kammerer and Frankish [22] propose the following definition of introspection (applied to the case of LLMs by Long [27]): “Introspection is a process by which a cognitive system represents its own current mental states, in a manner that allows the information to be used for online behavioural control.” This definition aligns with our requirement of metacognitive representations, but leaves aside the questions of grounding and internality.
assumptions: A cognitive system with current mental states and an internal representation of them that is available for online behavioural control; borrowed from Kammerer & Frankish (2023), applied to LLMs by Long.
gloss: Introspection is a process by which a system represents its own current mental states so that the information can guide its ongoing behaviour.
relation: Borrowed; the paper says it matches its metacognitive-representation criterion but omits grounding and internality; alternative to the Comşa & Shanahan causal-link definition and to the privileged-access definition of song2025privileged.

quote: Specifically, we propose introspection in AI is any process which yields information about internal states of the AI through a process that is more reliable than any process with equal or lower computational cost available to a third party without special knowledge of the situation.
assumptions: A notion of reliability; a class of third-party processes without special knowledge of the situation; a comparison of computational cost (not hardware cost, footnote 3); optionally restricted to internal states that are not too low-level.
gloss: A process counts as introspection if it tells the AI about its internal states more reliably than anything an outsider could do at the same or lower computational cost.
relation: Thicker alternative to the Comşa & Shanahan lightweight definition; lindsey2025emergent finds it more compelling than that one and ties it to its internality criterion; resembles resource-bounded definitions such as usable information under computational constraints.

quote: Unlike C&S’s definition it requires privileged self-access [cf. 3, 11], that is, that introspection gives a system comparatively reliable access to its own workings in a manner not available to a third party. It is compatible with our definition that the process not be perfectly reliable (see [9]); it only requires reliability not available to a third party at comparable computational cost.
assumptions: Third-party processes of comparable computational cost; reliability need not be perfect.
gloss: The system's access to its own workings must be more reliable than what an outsider can get at comparable computational cost, though not necessarily perfect.
relation: The defining component of the thick definition of introspection; absent from the Comşa & Shanahan definition.

quote: But, in a recent study, Comşa and Shanahan [6] (C&S) propose a “lightweight” definition of introspection in LLMs, defining it as any case in which the model accurately describes an internal state or mechanism via a causal process that links that feature to the report itself.
assumptions: Accuracy of the report and a causal process from the internal state or mechanism to the report.
gloss: Any accurate self-description produced by a causal process linking the described internal feature to the report.
relation: Borrowed from Comşa & Shanahan (2025) and criticized: it admits third-party-replicable inferences (the thermometer example); close to the grounding criterion of lindsey2025emergent.

term: privileged-access test (self-reflection vs within- and across-model prediction)
quote: Per our thicker notion of introspection, we argue that if a language model has privileged access to its internal state, then it should be able to perform better than another model presented with the same external information (i.e. a prompt and generated sentence in this experiment) in analyzing and reporting its own state.
assumptions: Same external information for every reporter (prompt and generated sentence); the generator's sampling temperature as ground truth, binarized (≤ 0.5 LOW, ≥ 1.5 HIGH); predictors at temperature 0; accuracy = predicted equals actual temperature class.
gloss: A model has privileged access only if it reports its own state more accurately than another model given the same prompt and output.
relation: Operationalizes privileged self-access; same logic as the self- versus cross-model comparisons of binder2024looking and song2025language.
